docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 6 of 17

Students combine gratitude with service, designing and creating something to help or bless others in their community.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Express gratitude for God's blessings

  • Design something to help others

  • Create a service project item

  • Connect engineering skills to Catholic social teaching

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Card-making supplies (paper, markers, stickers)

  • 🎨 Craft supplies

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📋 "People Who Help Us" list

  • ❤️ Heart shapes

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Martin de Porres — He served the poor and sick with great love, giving food and care to everyone in need.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: 1 Thessalonians 5:18; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, we have so much to be thankful for! Help us share our blessings with others. Like St. Martin de Porres, may we serve with love. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude Round — Each person: "I'm thankful for..."
  2. Giving Back — "When we have blessings, we share them!"
  3. St. Martin de Porres — Served the poor in Peru
  4. Today's Project — "We're making something to bless others!"
  5. Design Thinking — "WHO could we help? WHAT would help them?"

docs.title: Main Activity: Service Design Project (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Design Planning (4 minutes)

  • Brainstorm who needs blessing:
  • Elderly in nursing homes
  • Children in hospital
  • Community helpers (firefighters, police)

  • School staff

  • Choose a group to serve

  • Discuss: "What would help them feel loved?"

Part 2: Create (13 minutes)

  • Option A: Thankful Cards
  • Cards for nursing home residents
  • Include drawings, messages, stickers

  • "You are loved!"

  • Option B: Bookmark Gifts

  • Decorated bookmarks for library/school

  • "Thank you for helping us learn!"

  • Option C: Thank You Posters

  • For school helpers (custodians, lunch staff)

  • Class collaboration

  • Focus on quality and kindness in creation

Part 3: Reflection (2 minutes)

  • "How do you think people will feel when they get these?"

  • "Why is it important to think about others?"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw what you created
  2. Write: "I made this for... because..."
  3. Draw a heart

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Share Creations — Show what you made
  2. Delivery Plan — When/how will we give these?
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for the chance to bless others. Help us always look for ways to share your love. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Expressed personal gratitude

  • Participated in design process

  • Created item with care

  • Connected service to faith

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-folded card ready to decorate

  • Focus on drawing over writing

  • Work alongside teacher

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Write longer personal messages

  • Create multiple items

  • Help others with spelling/ideas

docs.title: SAFETY / recipient consent / evidence
docs.text: Teacher confirms recipient/organization wishes and delivery restrictions before promising a project; no required purchases/donations. Use paper/crayon cards, no food, loose glitter or student contact details. Grade 1 dictates a kind message; Grade 2 explains a purposeful communication choice. Do not claim tested engineering from a decorated card. Technology: None primary path; school photo permissions apply to any optional documentation. Last 3 making minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; an oral thank-you costs nothing)
docs.text: Family Activity: As a family, do a service project! Ideas: rake leaves for a neighbor, deliver cookies, write cards to relatives, donate toys or food. Talk about how it feels to help others.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Arrange delivery to nursing home or recipients

  • Take photos of students with creations

  • Follow up with recipient responses if possible

  • This embodies Catholic Social Teaching: care for others

Previous: Session 05 — Nature Exploration Next: Session 07 — Light in Darkness

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 7 of 17

Students explore the science of light during Advent, connecting Jesus as the "Light of the World" to scientific understanding of light and darkness.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand that light travels and can be blocked (shadows)

  • Explore how light helps us see

  • Connect Advent waiting to Jesus as Light

  • Create a light-themed project

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Flashlights

  • 📦 Prisms or CDs

  • 🎨 Star shapes, yellow/gold paper

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🕯️ LED tea light candles (safe)

  • 📦 Various objects for shadow-making

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching devotional details
docs.text: Mary, Star of the Sea — Mary guides us to Jesus, the true Light, just as stars guide sailors home.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: John 8:12; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced. Light language is religious imagery, not a measured property of Jesus.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear Jesus, in this Advent season, we wait for you—the Light of the World. Help us shine your light to everyone we meet. Come, Lord Jesus! Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Create Atmosphere — Dim lights, use LED candles
  2. Advent Connection — "We're waiting for Christmas! For Jesus to come!"
  3. Jesus = Light — "Jesus called himself the Light of the World"
  4. Science + Faith — "Today we'll learn about light AND think about Jesus!"
  5. Wonder Question — "Why do we need light?"

docs.title: Main Activity: Light Exploration (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Light Investigation (7 minutes)

  • Flashlight experiments:
  • Shine through paper (dim)
  • Shine through glass/plastic (bright)

  • Blocked by solid objects (shadow!)

  • "Light travels in straight lines until something stops it"

  • Make shadow puppets on wall

Part 2: Rainbow Discovery (5 minutes)

  • Use prism or CD to split light

  • Find rainbows on walls

  • "White light has ALL colors hiding inside!"

  • "God made light full of beautiful colors"

Part 3: Advent Star Creation (7 minutes)

  • Create an Advent star

  • Star of Bethlehem guided the Wise Men to Jesus

  • Decorate with gold, glitter, or sequins

  • Add: "Jesus is our Light"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw one light experiment
  2. Draw your Advent star
  3. Write: "Jesus is the light because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Light Connection — "How can WE be lights?" (Being kind, helping others)
  2. Star Display — Show stars, announce where they'll be displayed
  3. Closing Prayer — "Jesus, Light of the World, shine through us. Help us spread your light this Advent season. Come, Lord Jesus! Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Participated in light experiments

  • Understood light and shadow concepts

  • Connected Jesus to light imagery

  • Created Advent star

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-cut star shape to decorate

  • Focus on one light concept

  • Work with light partner

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Explain why some things cast shadows

  • Create complex star design

  • Write about light and faith connection

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence / cleanup
docs.text: Low-power flashlights, plastic safety prism/transparent objects, enclosed LED lights only; no glass, lasers, real flames, sun viewing, glow-stick opening or beams at eyes. Keep aisles visible and children seated if dimming. Replace glitter/sequins with crayon/foil. Grade 1 shows a blocked versus transmitted beam orally; Grade 2 explains one changed material/position using observations. Technology: None primary path. Reserve final 3 creation minutes for cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; flashlight play indoors or picture discussion)
docs.text: Family Activity: Look for lights during Advent! Christmas lights, candles, stars. Talk about how Jesus is the Light of the World. Make shadow puppets together using a flashlight.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Coordinate with Advent wreath lighting in school

  • Display stars in hallway or church

  • Great connection to religion class Advent lessons

  • Consider using glow sticks as alternative

Previous: Session 06 — Thanksgiving Service Next: Session 08 — Coding Basics

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 8 of 17

Students learn foundational coding concepts using ScratchJr, creating simple animated stories and programs.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand that coding is giving instructions to computers

  • Navigate the ScratchJr interface

  • Create a simple program with motion blocks

  • Debug (fix) programs when they don't work

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📱 Tablets with ScratchJr app installed

  • 📋 ScratchJr quick reference cards

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📺 Display for demonstration (optional)

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Saint Carlo Acutis, canonized September 7, 2025: Vatican source. Specific computing/website biography is VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: John 1:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: read from the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced. The divine Word is not computer code; omit the creation/programming equivalence.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for creative minds. Help us use technology responsibly in service of others. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. What is Coding? — "Giving step-by-step instructions to a computer"
  2. Connection to Robots — "Remember Dash? Same idea!"
  3. ScratchJr — "This app lets us code stories and games"
  4. Saint Carlo Acutis — Optional verified biography; responsible technology use is the assessed connection.
  5. Today's Goal — "Make a character move!"

docs.title: Main Activity: ScratchJr Exploration (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: App Tour (4 minutes)

  • Open ScratchJr

  • Explore interface:

  • Character (Cat)
  • Stage (background)
  • Blocks (instructions)

  • Green flag (start)

  • "The blocks are like puzzle pieces that tell the character what to do"

Part 2: First Program (8 minutes)

  • Guided tutorial:
  • Add "Start on Green Flag" block
  • Add "Move Right" block
  • Tap green flag—watch cat move!
  • Add more move blocks

  • Try: Up, down, left

  • Challenge: Make cat walk across the screen

Part 3: Personalize (5 minutes)

  • Change background

  • Try different character

  • Add sounds or speech bubbles

  • Free creation time

Part 4: Share (2 minutes)

  • Show neighbor what you made

  • "You just wrote a computer program!"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw the ScratchJr character you used
  2. Write or draw the instructions you gave
  3. Circle: Easy 😊 or Tricky 🔧

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Celebration — "You are now CODERS!"
  2. Next Time — "We'll learn more coding tricks!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for the gift of learning. Help us use coding and technology for good things. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Opened ScratchJr and explored

  • Created program with motion

  • Used green flag to run program

  • Showed willingness to try

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-made starter project to modify

  • Partner with experienced peer

  • Focus on one block type (motion)

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Add loops (repeat blocks)

  • Create multi-scene story

  • Help classmates who are stuck

docs.title: Technology / privacy / individual evidence
docs.text: Required primary path: school-approved ScratchJr tablets for executed motion code. Grade 1 points to/orders green-flag and two movement blocks, personally runs them and corrects one deliberate wrong direction; Grade 2 predicts/explains the changed output. No devices: cards/token sequence/debug only, not app/executed-program mastery. Do not publish names/photos/voice externally. Use final 3 personalization minutes for save/return/cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; oral token directions need no tablet)
docs.text: Family Activity: If you have a tablet, try ScratchJr at home! (Free app) Create a story together. No tablet? Play "programmer"—give family members step-by-step instructions to do something!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• ScratchJr is free for iPad and Android

  • Pre-install and test app before session

  • Consider projecting tablet for demonstrations

  • Common issue: Blocks not snapping together—show how to connect

Previous: Session 07 — Light in Darkness Next: Session 09 — Catholic Inventors

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 9 of 17

Students celebrate Catholic Schools Week by learning about Catholic scientists and inventors who changed the world while serving God.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Learn about Catholic scientists and inventors

  • Understand that faith and science work together

  • Celebrate being in a Catholic school

  • Create a project honoring Catholic scientists

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📸 Pictures of Catholic scientists

  • 📄 Short biographies (age-appropriate)

  • 🎨 Art supplies for poster/project

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📋 "My Catholic School" activity sheet

docs.title: Scientist connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text:
Multiple Catholic Scientists:

  • Gregor Mendel — Monk who discovered genetics

  • Louis Pasteur — Studied microorganisms and heating processes; specific religious-affiliation claims are unverified and omitted.

  • Fr. Georges Lemaître — Priest who proposed the Big Bang theory

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Psalm 19:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for our Catholic school where we learn about you AND about your world. Thank you for Catholic scientists who loved you and loved learning. Help us follow their example. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Catholic Schools Week! — "We're celebrating our school!"
  2. Faith + Science — "At Catholic schools, we learn that God made science!"
  3. Catholic Scientists — Introduce heroes:
  4. Gregor Mendel: Monk who grew pea plants and discovered how traits pass from parents to children (genetics)
  5. Louis Pasteur: Heating can reduce harmful microorganisms; pasteurization does not make every milk sample automatically safe and is not a classroom milk experiment.
  6. Fr. Georges Lemaître: Priest who figured out the universe is expanding (Big Bang)
  7. Key Message — "Loving God and loving science go together!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Catholic Scientist Celebration (18 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Meet a Scientist (6 minutes)

  • Focus on ONE scientist in depth (Gregor Mendel recommended for 1-2)

  • "Brother Mendel was a monk—he prayed every day"

  • "He was curious about God's creation"

  • "He grew thousands of pea plants!"

  • "He discovered that children look like their parents because of tiny instructions (genes)"

  • Discussion: "What made him a good scientist AND a good Catholic?"

Part 2: Create a Tribute (10 minutes)

  • Option A: Scientist Poster
  • Draw the scientist
  • Write one fact

  • Add: "Catholic Scientist!"

  • Option B: Pea Plant Activity (Mendel connection)

  • Sort items by traits (like Mendel did)
  • Big/small, green/yellow

  • Connect to Mendel's work

  • Option C: Thank You to Teachers

  • Create cards for school teachers
  • "Thank you for teaching us about God and science!"

Part 3: Share (2 minutes)

  • Show creations

  • Say one thing learned about Catholic scientists

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your favorite Catholic scientist
  2. Write: "I learned that..."
  3. Write: "I'm thankful for my Catholic school because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. School Pride — "What's special about our Catholic school?"
  2. Future Scientists — "You can be a Catholic scientist too!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for faith and science together. Thank you for our Catholic school. Help us love learning and love you. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Learned about at least one Catholic scientist

  • Understood faith-science connection

  • Participated in celebration activity

  • Expressed gratitude for Catholic school

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focus on one scientist's story

  • Simple drawing activity

  • Work alongside teacher or buddy

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Research additional scientists

  • Write a short report

  • Present to the class

docs.title: Source gate / low-tech evidence
docs.text: If verified biographies are unavailable, replace the six-minute scientist story with sorting large paper pea-picture cards by two visible traits. Grade 1 names a grouping rule orally; Grade 2 separates an observed trait from an untested inheritance explanation. Do not infer genetic rules from color-sorting crafts. Technology: None primary path. Teacher checks safe large supplies, no food/tasting; last 3 tribute minutes are cleanup. Additional Church/history claims require approved sources; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; discuss the class observations without internet)
docs.text: Optional family activity: Ask what students observed or learned from a teacher-verified biography. No research device or purchase is needed; do not assign unverified religious affiliations.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Coordinate with school-wide Catholic Schools Week activities

  • Consider inviting a scientist from the parish

  • Display student work in hallway

  • See Resources/Catholic_Scientists_Heritage.md for more scientists

Previous: Session 08 — Coding Basics Next: Session 10 — Weather Watchers

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 10 of 17

Students become meteorologists, observing and recording weather data and building simple weather instruments.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Identify different types of weather

  • Record weather observations systematically

  • Build a simple weather tool

  • Understand that scientists study God's patterns in weather

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📋 Weather chart/calendar

  • 🌡️ Outdoor thermometer

  • 🎐 Windsock materials (paper, string, streamers)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📸 Pictures of weather types

  • ☁️ Cloud chart

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching legends/biographies
docs.text: St. Scholastica — According to legend, she prayed and God sent a storm so she could keep talking with her brother (St. Benedict) about faith!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Psalm 135:7; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced. A devotional story is not meteorological evidence.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you control the weather—the sun, rain, snow, and wind. Thank you for the patterns you built into nature. Help us learn about your amazing world. Keep us safe in all weather. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Today's Weather — Look outside. "What's the weather today?"
  2. Weather Types:
  3. ☀️ Sunny
  4. ☁️ Cloudy
  5. 🌧️ Rainy
  6. ❄️ Snowy
  7. 💨 Windy
  8. Meteorologists — Scientists who study weather
  9. God's Patterns — Weather follows patterns God designed
  10. Today's Goal — "We're going to be weather scientists!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Weather Station (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Weather Observation (5 minutes)

  • Go outside or observe from window

  • Record on chart:

  • Temperature (read thermometer together)
  • Cloud cover (sunny, partly cloudy, cloudy)
  • Wind (calm, breezy, windy)

  • Precipitation (none, rain, snow)

  • "Scientists record what they observe!"

Part 2: Cloud Study (4 minutes)

  • Look at clouds

  • Cloud types (simplified):

  • Describe visible cloud shapes/color without treating them as guaranteed forecasts.

  • A single classroom observation cannot establish a weather pattern; a prediction remains a guess to check later.

  • Draw the clouds you see

Part 3: Build a Windsock (8 minutes)

  • Materials: Paper tube/cup, streamers, string

  • Steps:

  • Attach streamers to one end of tube
  • Add string for hanging

  • Decorate!

  • "This tool shows us wind direction!"

  • Test by window or briefly outside

Part 4: Weather Prediction (2 minutes)

  • Based on observations: "What do you think weather will be like tomorrow?"

  • "Scientists make predictions based on patterns!"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw today's weather
  2. Record temperature
  3. Draw your windsock
  4. Predict tomorrow's weather

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Weather Wonder — "What amazes you about weather?"
  2. God's Care — "God sends rain for plants and sunshine for warmth"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for weather that waters the earth and gives us seasons. Help us appreciate every kind of day you give us. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified weather conditions

  • Recorded observations

  • Built windsock

  • Made weather prediction

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focus on three weather types

  • Pre-made windsock base

  • Partner observation

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Record multiple data points

  • Compare to weather forecast

  • Research cloud types

docs.title: SAFETY / indoor weather route / evidence
docs.text: Default: observe from a closed window and read a teacher-provided outdoor temperature; use a non-glass thermometer and follow placement instructions, not indoor heat against a sunny window. Never go outside in extreme cold/storms or fly streamers near traffic/electrical lines; teacher controls strings, no neck loops. Test windsock indoors with a teacher gently moving air using cardboard; no shared mouth blowing. Grade 1 draws two observed weather details; Grade 2 records temperature/date and names prediction uncertainty. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 building minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; one spoken window observation is enough)
docs.text: Family Activity: Start a family weather journal! Record the weather each day for a week. Hang your windsock outside and watch it. Compare your observations to the weather forecast—how accurate were you?

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Start ongoing classroom weather tracking if possible

  • Windsocks can be hung in classroom or sent home

  • Connect to daily calendar weather activities

  • Great springboard for water cycle discussions

Previous: Session 09 — Catholic Inventors Next: Session 11 — Lenten Engineers

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 11 of 17

Students design and create something to help others during Lent, connecting engineering skills to the Lenten practices of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand Lenten practices (prayer, fasting, almsgiving)

  • Design something to serve others

  • Create a service-focused project

  • Connect engineering to Catholic social teaching

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Craft supplies (paper, markers, cardboard)

  • 📦 Recycled materials

  • 💜 Purple paper/decorations (Lent color)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📋 Service planning sheet

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Katherine Drexel — She gave away her fortune to serve others, especially building schools for children who didn't have them.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Matthew 25:40; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear Jesus, during Lent we remember your sacrifice for us. Help us give up something to help others. Show us how to use our hands and minds to serve. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Lent Season — "What is Lent?"
  2. 40 days preparing for Easter
  3. Time to grow closer to Jesus
  4. Three Practices:
  5. 🙏 Prayer — Talking to God more
  6. 🍞 Fasting — Giving up something
  7. 💝 Almsgiving — Giving to others
  8. Engineers for Others — "How can our building skills help people?"
  9. Today's Mission — "Design something that helps others!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Service Design Project (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Identify Needs (3 minutes)

  • "Who could use our help?"
  • Elderly neighbors
  • Children without toys
  • Hungry families

  • Lonely people

  • "What could we MAKE to help?"

Part 2: Design & Create (14 minutes)

Option A: Kindness Coupons Holder

  • Build a small box or folder

  • Fill with kindness coupons:

  • "I can offer a kind word" (physical contact is never owed)
  • "I'll clean up"

  • "I'll share with you"

  • Give to family members

Option B: Caring Cards

  • Design cards for nursing home residents

  • Include cheerful drawings

  • Message: "God loves you!"

Option C: Collection Box

  • Build a box for collecting items

  • Rice Bowl / food shelf donations

  • Coins for charity

  • Decorate with Lenten symbols

Part 3: Reflection (2 minutes)

  • "How will this help others?"

  • "How does giving make YOU feel?"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw what you designed/made
  2. Write: "This will help... by..."
  3. Draw a cross or Lenten symbol

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Sharing — Show your service project
  2. Lenten Commitment — "What will you give this Lent?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Jesus, help us give like St. Katherine Drexel. May our work bring joy to others and glory to you. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Understood Lenten practices

  • Participated in service design

  • Created project with intention

  • Connected work to serving others

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-made project template

  • Focus on decorating

  • Work with partner

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Plan larger service project

  • Write detailed messages

  • Design multiple items

docs.title: SAFETY / Lent access / evidence
docs.text: Do not assign food fasting to young children; school-approved age-appropriate generosity can mean sharing time, not giving up needed food or spending family money. No forced hugs, glass coin jars, loose small coins or sharp recycled items. Default cardstock kindness folder holds three paper coupons without spilling; child tests and revises a fold. Grade 1 tells/draws how it helps; Grade 2 explains a test-based revision. Recipient delivery requires consent. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 making minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; no-cost kindness conversation equally valid)
docs.text: Family Activity: As a family, choose a Lenten service project! Ideas: donate to food shelf, visit someone lonely, do extra chores, save money to give away. Make a family Lent calendar.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Coordinate with school-wide Lenten initiatives (Rice Bowl, food drives)

  • Consider delivering cards to nursing home

  • Connect to religion class Lenten lessons

  • Purple is the liturgical color of Lent

Previous: Session 10 — Weather Watchers Next: Session 12 — Life Cycles

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 12 of 17

Students explore plant and animal life cycles, discovering God's pattern of growth, change, and renewal in living things.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand that living things have life cycles

  • Sequence stages of plant and/or butterfly life cycles

  • Create a life cycle model

  • Connect life cycles to God's pattern of renewal

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Seeds and small pots (optional)

  • 📸 Life cycle pictures (plant, butterfly, frog)

  • 🎨 Paper plates for cycle craft

  • 📦 Pasta shapes (life cycle materials)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🦋 Butterfly kit (if available)

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Thérèse of Lisieux (The Little Flower) — She compared spiritual growth to a flower blooming. Growth takes time and trust in God.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: John 12:24; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible. This is religious imagery: a viable seed does not need to die biologically to germinate.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you made everything with cycles of growth and change. Thank you for seeds that become plants and caterpillars that become butterflies. Help us grow closer to you every day. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Growth Question — "Have YOU changed since you were a baby?"
  2. Life Cycles — "Living things go through stages called a life cycle"
  3. Examples:
  4. Plants: seed → sprout → plant → flower → seed again
  5. Butterfly: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly
  6. You: baby → child → teenager → adult
  7. God's Pattern — "God built change and growth into creation!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Life Cycle Exploration (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Learn the Cycles (5 minutes)

  • Show plant life cycle:
  • 🌰 Seed (planted in soil)
  • 🌱 Sprout (pushes through)
  • 🌿 Plant (grows leaves)
  • 🌸 Flower (blooms)

  • 🌰 Seeds (makes new seeds!)

  • Show butterfly life cycle:

  • 🥚 Egg (on a leaf)
  • 🐛 Caterpillar (eats and grows)
  • 🛖 Chrysalis (transforms inside)
  • 🦋 Butterfly (emerges!)

Part 2: Life Cycle Craft (12 minutes)

  • Paper plate divided into 4 sections

  • Choose plant OR butterfly cycle

  • Create each stage:

  • Draw pictures

  • OR use pasta: orzo=egg/seed, rotini=caterpillar/sprout, shell=chrysalis/bud, bow tie=butterfly/flower

  • Add arrows showing cycle direction

  • Label stages

Part 3: Connection (2 minutes)

  • A butterfly remains alive through its stages; a new generation begins with eggs laid by an adult.
  • Easter is a faith claim, not a repeating biological death/resurrection cycle. Teacher symbols must not replace the science.

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw the life cycle you learned
  2. Label the stages
  3. Write: "God makes things grow by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Share — Show life cycle crafts
  2. Easter Preview — "Easter celebrates the greatest new life—Jesus rising!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for life cycles. Thank you that you can make all things new—even us! Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified stages of life cycle

  • Sequenced stages correctly

  • Created life cycle model

  • Connected to faith themes

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focus on one life cycle

  • Pre-drawn stages to color

  • Fewer stages (3 instead of 4-5)

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Create both plant AND butterfly cycles

  • Add frog or human life cycle

  • Write about each stage

docs.title: SAFETY / model accuracy / evidence
docs.text: Use drawn paper stages rather than loose pasta/food. No wild collecting or unapproved live butterfly release; teacher photos/models are the default. Grade 1 points to four ordered butterfly stages and tells a change; Grade 2 explains the new-generation arrow and a model limitation. Reducing to three pictures is support toward, not mastery of, four stages. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 model minutes are cleanup; no routine homework or purchased live kits.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; discuss a book/picture instead of planting)
docs.text: Family Activity: Plant a seed and watch it grow! Bean seeds grow quickly. Take photos at each stage. Look for caterpillars, butterflies, or tadpoles in nature. Talk about how things change and grow.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Consider raising butterflies (kits available)

  • Great spring activity as plants and insects emerge

  • Strong connection to Easter resurrection themes

  • John 12:24 is particularly relevant

Previous: Session 11 — Lenten Engineers Next: Session 13 — Easter Innovation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 13 of 17

Students celebrate Easter's message of new life and new beginnings through a creative innovation project.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Connect Easter to themes of new life and hope

  • Design something representing new beginnings

  • Create an Easter-themed innovation

  • Express Easter joy through creativity

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 🎨 Art supplies (paper, markers, crayons)

  • 📦 Craft materials (pipe cleaners, tissue paper, cups)

  • 🌷 Flower/butterfly supplies

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📸 Pictures of spring new life

docs.title: Catholic connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: The Risen Jesus — Easter celebrates the greatest new beginning: Jesus rising from the dead!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Revelation 21:5; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Alleluia! Jesus is risen! Dear God, thank you for Easter and the gift of new life. Help us celebrate your love today and every day. Alleluia! Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Easter Joy! — "Alleluia! What are we celebrating?"
  2. New Life Everywhere:
  3. Jesus rose from the dead
  4. Spring flowers blooming
  5. Baby animals being born
  6. New beginnings all around!
  7. Innovation Connection — "Today we'll CREATE something new!"
  8. Design Challenge — "Make something that shows NEW LIFE!"

docs.title: Main Activity: New Life Creation (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Inspiration (3 minutes)

  • Show pictures:
  • Empty tomb → resurrection!
  • Butterfly emerging → transformation!
  • Flower blooming → new life!

  • Sunrise → new day!

  • "Pick one idea that inspires you"

Part 2: Design & Create (14 minutes)

Option A: Paper Flowers

  • Tissue paper flowers that "bloom"

  • Represent resurrection and spring

  • Add stem and leaves

Option B: Butterfly Mobile

  • Coffee filter butterflies

  • Hanging display

  • Symbol of transformation

Option C: Easter Garden Scene

  • Cup or small box garden

  • Include tomb, stone rolled away

  • Add flowers, grass

  • "He is risen!"

Option D: Free Innovation

  • Student chooses what to create

  • Must represent "new life"

  • Any available materials

Part 3: Celebration (2 minutes)

  • "Gallery walk" to see all creations

  • Say "Alleluia!" together!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw what you created
  2. Write: "New life means..."
  3. Draw the empty tomb or a butterfly
  4. Write: "Alleluia!"

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Share — One thing your creation represents
  2. Easter Message — "Jesus makes ALL things new—including us!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Alleluia, Jesus is alive! Thank you for the gift of new life. Help us live as Easter people, full of joy and hope. Alleluia! Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Connected Easter to new life themes

  • Designed creative project

  • Expressed Easter meaning

  • Participated in celebration

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-cut flower/butterfly pieces

  • Choose from two options

  • Work with partner

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Create multiple items

  • Write Easter poem or story

  • Explain symbolism in detail

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence / cleanup
docs.text: Paper flowers/cards are the safe default; no real eggs, glass, sharp wire ends, wild collecting or strings around necks. Grade 1 orally explains one chosen symbol; Grade 2 revises one visual feature to communicate meaning to a partner. This is artistic/faith communication, not assessed engineering or a scientific resurrection demonstration. Technology: None primary path; indoor pictures work in winter. Last 3 creation minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; indoor picture discussion equally valid)
docs.text: Family Activity: Go on an "Easter new life hunt"! Look for signs of new life: flowers, baby animals, birds, buds on trees. Attend Easter Mass together and celebrate the resurrection!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Perfect timing for Easter week celebration

  • Display creations prominently

  • Coordinate with Easter celebrations in religion class

  • Consider creating class "Alleluia" banner

Previous: Session 12 — Life Cycles Next: Session 14 — Sound Engineering

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 14 of 17

Students explore the science of sound and engineer their own musical instruments to praise God.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand that sound is made by vibrations

  • Experiment with pitch (high/low) and volume (loud/soft)

  • Design and build a simple instrument

  • Connect music to praising God

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Rubber bands (various sizes)

  • 📦 Boxes, containers, cardboard tubes

  • 📦 Rice, beans (for shakers)

  • 📦 Paper, plastic cups

  • 🎵 Simple instruments for demonstration

  • 📓 Engineering journals

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies/traditions
docs.text: St. Cecilia — Patron saint of music! She sang to God even in difficult times.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Psalm 150:3-4; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for the gift of sound and music. Help us use music to praise you! Like St. Cecilia, may our songs bring joy to heaven. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Sound Investigation — "What IS sound?"
  2. Vibration Demo:
  3. Pluck rubber band — see it shake!
  4. Touch throat while humming — feel vibration!
  5. "Sound happens when things VIBRATE"
  6. High/Low: — Different vibration speeds = different pitches
  7. Loud/Soft: — Big vibrations = loud; small = soft
  8. Today's Goal — "Build an instrument to praise God!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Instrument Engineering (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Sound Exploration (4 minutes)

  • Try different sound makers:
  • Pluck rubber bands of different sizes
  • Shake containers with different contents

  • Observe a teacher plucking a short secured rubber band; no shared mouth instruments.

  • "What do you notice?"

  • Compare pitches and volumes

Part 2: Design & Build (12 minutes)

Option A: Rubber Band Guitar

  • Stretch rubber bands around a box

  • Try different band sizes

  • Pluck to make music

Option B: Shaker

  • Put rice/beans in container

  • Seal securely

  • Decorate!

Option C: Drum Use a closed cardboard box and fingertip tapping, not balloons, cans or rigid striking sticks.

Option D: Rhythmic card Tap a drawn two-beat/four-beat pattern on the desk with fingertips. This explores rhythm; it does not replace vibration/pitch evidence unless separately demonstrated.

  • All students: Test and improve your instrument

Part 3: Praise Band (3 minutes)

  • All play instruments together

  • Follow teacher's conducting (loud, soft, fast, slow)

  • Sing a simple praise song while playing

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your instrument
  2. Label the parts
  3. Write: "Sound is made by..."
  4. Write: "I praise God by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Sound Science — "What makes sound?"
  2. Praise Connection — "God loves when we make joyful noise!"
  3. Closing Prayer + Music — Play instruments while praying: "Thank you, God, for sound and music! Alleluia! Amen!"

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Understood vibration creates sound

  • Built a working instrument

  • Experimented with pitch/volume

  • Connected music to praising God

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-made instrument to decorate

  • Focus on one instrument type

  • Partner building

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Build multiple instruments

  • Explain the science behind their design

  • Create a band with different sounds

docs.title: SAFETY / sound evidence / cleanup
docs.text: No latex balloons, shared mouthpieces, glass bottles, sharp cans or open rice/beans. Teacher permanently seals/counts shakers; if leakage occurs remove and use claps. Short secured bands only, away from faces; omit bands if latex clearance fails. Keep volume comfortable; quiet/visual vibration alternative by choice. Grade 1 points to vibration and contrasts soft/loud; Grade 2 changes one safe vibration feature and describes result. Pre-made decoration alone is not sound mastery. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 building minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; gentle clapping needs no materials)
docs.text: Family Activity: Make instruments at home using household items! Experiment with pots and pans, rubber bands and boxes, containers with different fillings. Have a family praise concert!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Consider keeping instruments for future use

  • Great connection to music class

  • Psalm 150 lists many instruments—explore together

  • Digital music connection: simple music apps (GarageBand, Chrome Music Lab)

Previous: Session 13 — Easter Innovation Next: Session 15 — Robot Challenge

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 15 of 17

Students use their Dash Robot skills from earlier to complete mission challenges, demonstrating growth in programming concepts.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Apply programming skills to solve challenges

  • Program a sequence of movements

  • Problem-solve when code doesn't work (debugging)

  • Collaborate on robot missions

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Dash Robots (from CSCOE library)

  • 📱 Tablets with Go/Wonder app

  • 📋 Mission challenge cards

  • 🚧 Obstacle materials (cups, blocks, tape)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🏁 Tape for start/finish lines

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED
docs.text: Thomas Aquinas biography requires a vetted source. The attributed "Logic is God's gift!" quotation is unverified and removed. Use children's own reasoning, not an invented saying.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Philippians 4:13; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced or guarantee of coding success.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for giving us problem-solving minds. When things don't work, help us try again. Give us patience and creativity as we work with our robot friends today. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Robot Review — "We are learning specific skills; show the short sequence you can run."
  2. Challenge Day — "Today you'll complete MISSIONS!"
  3. Programming Review:
  4. Robots follow our instructions exactly
  5. We can drive OR we can program sequences
  6. Growth Mindset — "If it doesn't work, that's a learning chance!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Robot Mission Challenges (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Mission Setup: Create course with tape lines and obstacles

Part 1: Review & Practice (3 minutes)

  • Quick refresh of Dash controls

  • Practice driving forward and turning

  • Use preflighted Blockly for stored forward-distance/turn sequences, as in revised Session 04; app labels must match installed help.

Part 2: Mission Challenges (15 minutes)

Mission 1: Straight Shot (3 min)

  • Program Dash to drive from START to FINISH line

  • No driving—must use programming!

  • Goal: Accurate straight line

Mission 2: Turn Around (4 min)

  • Program Dash to go forward, turn around, come back

  • Requires forward, turn 180°, forward

Mission 3: Obstacle Course (5 min)

  • Navigate around cups or blocks

  • Requires turns and distance planning

  • Teams collaborate to solve

Mission 4: Creative Challenge (3 min)

  • "Program Dash to do something cool!"

  • Add sounds, lights

  • Share with class

Part 3: Celebration (2 minutes)

  • Teams share favorite accomplishments

  • Discuss: "What was tricky? How did you solve it?"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw one mission you completed
  2. Write: "The hardest part was..."
  3. Write: "I solved it by..."
  4. Rate your programming: Beginner → Expert!

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Growth Celebration — "Look how much you've learned!"
  2. Problem-Solving — "What did you do when it didn't work?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for letting us solve problems and learn new things. Help us use technology wisely. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Completed at least two missions

  • Used programming (not just driving)

  • Problem-solved when stuck

  • Collaborated with team

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Simplified missions (shorter distances)

  • Partner with experienced programmer

  • Focus on driving with some programming

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Create own mission course

  • Use Wonder app for complex programs

  • Mentor other students

docs.title: Technology / SAFETY / measurable limit
docs.text: Required primary path: Dash/tablet/Blockly for physical stored code, not just Go driving. Preflight compatibility/charge; low-speed dry marked bays, no chasing, teacher-only cords. Narrow to one forward-turn-return mission and a debug rerun within the same time block. Each Grade 1 child points to/orders and runs two actions; Grade 2 runs three and explains one changed distance/turn result. Driving-only support is practice, not programming mastery. No devices: arrow/token debug, not real robot programming/operation credit. Reserve final 4 mission minutes for cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; oral directions without devices)
docs.text: Family Activity: Talk about robots at home! Where do we see robots? (Vacuums, car factories, space exploration) If you have a tablet, try ScratchJr to practice programming. Give family members "robot" commands to follow!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Reserve Dash Robots 2 weeks ahead

  • Charge all robots night before

  • Have backup activities if tech fails

  • This session shows growth from Session 4

Previous: Session 14 — Sound Engineering Next: Session 16 — Community Helpers

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 16 of 17

Students design solutions to help their community, applying engineering skills to serve others.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Identify needs in their community

  • Design a solution to help someone

  • Build or plan a service project

  • Connect engineering to Catholic social teaching

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Building materials (cardboard, craft sticks, tape)

  • 🎨 Art supplies

  • 📋 "Community Needs" brainstorm sheet

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📸 Pictures of community helpers

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Vincent de Paul — He organized help for the poor, creating systems to serve those in need.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Galatians 5:13; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you call us to love our neighbors. Help us see what our community needs. Give us creative ideas to help others. Bless the work of our hands. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Community Helpers — "Who helps in our community?"
  2. Police, firefighters, nurses, teachers
  3. Mail carriers, trash collectors, store workers
  4. Parents, volunteers, neighbors
  5. Everyone Can Help — "YOU can be a community helper too!"
  6. Engineering for Good — "We can use our design skills to help people!"
  7. Today's Mission — "Design something that helps our community!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Service Design Project (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Identify Needs (4 minutes)

  • Brainstorm community needs:
  • Elderly neighbors need help with tasks
  • Homeless need warm clothes
  • Animals need shelter
  • Environment needs care (litter cleanup)

  • Lonely people need friendship

  • Pick one need to address

Part 2: Design & Build (13 minutes)

Option A: Bird Feeder for Creation Care

  • Simple design from recyclables

  • Helps birds, beautifies community

  • Build and take home

Option B: Kindness Kit Design

  • Design a "kit" for someone in need

  • What would go inside?

  • Draw and label items

  • Plan to assemble real ones

Option C: Thank You Signs

  • Create signs for community helpers

  • "Thank you, mail carrier!"

  • Display in windows or deliver

Option D: Free Design

  • Student identifies need and solution

  • Build prototype or detailed plan

  • Present to class

Part 3: Share Plans (2 minutes)

  • Groups share what they designed

  • "How will this help?"

docs.title: Engineering Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your design
  2. Write: "This helps... by..."
  3. Write: "One thing I can do this week to help someone is..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Service Summary — "How can engineers help communities?"
  2. Challenge — "This week, be a community helper!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, help us be your hands and feet. Show us how to serve others every day. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified community need

  • Designed thoughtful solution

  • Connected design to service

  • Committed to action

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Join group with clear role

  • Focus on one simple project

  • Teacher-guided brainstorming

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Create detailed implementation plan

  • Design multiple solutions

  • Lead group discussion

docs.title: SAFETY / recipient choice / evidence
docs.text: Default a paper/cardboard organizer model for a classroom helper who states a need. No actual bird-feeder deployment without teacher hygiene/species/location plan, no unsafe litter picking, food deliveries or required donations. Teacher screens recyclables and confirms recipient consent. Grade 1 explains user need orally; Grade 2 checks one agreed criterion and revises. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 making minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; thank someone orally at no cost)
docs.text: Family Activity: Do a family service project! Ideas: Make bird feeders, pick up litter, bake treats for neighbors, donate toys, write thank you notes to community helpers. Talk about how it feels to help.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Follow through on any service projects planned

  • Connect to school/parish service initiatives

  • Consider class "Day of Service"

  • Embodies Catholic Social Teaching: dignity of workers, care for community

Previous: Session 15 — Robot Challenge Next: Session 17 — Year Exhibition

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 17 of 17

Students celebrate their year of C-STREAM learning, sharing portfolios and demonstrating growth in engineering, coding, and faith integration.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Reflect on their year of learning

  • Share accomplishments with others

  • Demonstrate growth in C-STREAM skills

  • Celebrate faith and reason together

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📓 Engineering journals (from all year)

  • 📸 Photos from C-STREAM sessions

  • 🏆 Certificates (optional)

  • 🎨 Display materials

  • 📋 "I Learned..." reflection sheet

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before recalling biographies
docs.text: Recall only vetted accounts actually taught. Carlo Acutis is Saint, canonized September 7, 2025: Vatican source.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Philippians 1:3; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for an amazing year of discovery! Thank you for letting us learn about your wonderful world. Thank you for our teachers and friends. Bless us as we continue to grow. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Celebration! — "We've completed a whole year of C-STREAM!"
  2. Memory Lane — Show photos from throughout the year
  3. Count Our Learning:
  4. 17 sessions of exploring!
  5. Bridges, robots, coding, instruments, and more!
  6. Saints Remembered — Quick mention of saints we met
  7. Today's Celebration — "Share what you've learned!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Exhibition (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Portfolio Review (5 minutes)

  • Students look through their engineering journals

  • Mark favorite pages with sticky notes

  • Identify: "My best work" and "My biggest growth"

Part 2: Partner Sharing (6 minutes)

  • Share with a partner:
  • One saved bridge/design: its criterion, test result and one change, shown orally or with drawings
  • Something that was hard but you figured out

  • Your favorite saint we learned about

  • Partners encourage each other

Part 3: Class Gallery (5 minutes)

  • Display journals and projects

  • Gallery walk to see everyone's work

  • Positive comments only!

Part 4: Awards & Recognition (3 minutes)

  • Optional certificates:
  • "Wonder Champion"
  • "Master Builder"
  • "Code Creator"
  • "Service Star"

  • "Faith & Reason Explorer"

  • Recognize every student's growth

docs.title: Reflection & Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. In journal, write/draw:
  2. My favorite C-STREAM memory
  3. Something I learned about God's world
  4. What I want to learn next year

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude Round — Each student: "I'm thankful for..."
  2. Future Engineers — "You're ready for more adventures!"
  3. Final Blessing & Prayer:

Dear God, Thank you for this year of wonder. Thank you for curious minds and creative hands. Thank you for showing us that faith and science are friends. Bless these young engineers as they grow. Help them always use their gifts for good. In Jesus' name, Amen.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
End-of-Year Reflection:

  • Can identify learning growth

  • Expresses pride in accomplishments

  • Connects C-STREAM to faith

  • Shows enthusiasm for future learning

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-select journal highlights

  • Partner with supportive peer

  • Focus on verbal sharing

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Present to the class

  • Create "tips" for next year's students

  • Write reflection letter

docs.title: Technology / SAFETY / assessment limit
docs.text: Optional primary path: school-permitted teacher photos; paper journals suffice. No food/latex decorations or compulsory family attendance. Grade 1 tells/shows one earlier test; Grade 2 explains before/after evidence. Portfolio enthusiasm/certificates are not robotics mastery. Last 3 gallery minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional)
docs.text:
Summer Challenge: Keep being a C-STREAM explorer all summer!

  • Build with whatever you find

  • Ask "I wonder..." questions

  • Look for God's patterns in nature

  • Use technology for good

  • Help others with your skills

  • Never stop wondering!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Prepare certificates in advance

  • Invite parents/families if possible

  • Take lots of photos

  • Send journals home as keepsakes

  • Celebrate each child's unique growth

docs.title: 🎊 Congratulations, C-STREAM Engineers! 🎊
docs.text:
You've completed Grades 1-2 Year A C-STREAM!

This year you:

  • ✅ Built bridges and towers

  • Explored Dash input/output; claim programmed stored sequences only for children with saved individual device evidence.

  • ✅ Created code with ScratchJr

  • ✅ Explored God's patterns

  • ✅ Engineered instruments

  • ✅ Served your community

  • ✅ Connected faith and reason

You are engineers, scientists, and children of God!

Keep building. Keep wondering. Keep praising God.

Previous: Session 16 — Community Helpers

End of Grades 1-2 Year A Bi-Weekly C-STREAM Curriculum

docs.title: 🌟 Grades 1-2 Year B Bi-Weekly C-STREAM
docs.text:
17 Sessions | 30 Minutes Each | Every Other Week

This folder contains the condensed Grades 1-2 Year B C-STREAM curriculum for schools with bi-weekly STREAM classes. Year B features different projects, saints, and contexts than Year A while building the same foundational skills.

docs.title: Audit and entry conditions
docs.text:
See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. This track has 17 actual meetings/17 files = 510 minutes; weekly has 32 meetings/960 minutes. Fewer contacts mean fewer independent device turns and science observations, not equivalent mastery.

Year A is not a prerequisite. Teach safe handling, observation and picture sequences before challenges. Grade 1 can point, draw or respond orally without reading; Grade 2 should justify a feature/measurement and revise using evidence. Session 14 rechecks Session 03 stored-code start/stop rather than declaring students experts.

Meet Sphero and Garden Engineers are fully rebuilt; remaining files have targeted corrections but unresolved readiness work. Historical/doctrinal details and official benchmarks marked VERIFICATION REQUIRED must be verified before teaching; no universal substitute-readiness claim is made.

docs.title: 📋 Session Overview
docs.text: Session Title Theme Key Activity Session 01 Design Detectives Introduction Everyday design Session 02 Tower Power Engineering Tower challenges Session 03 Meet Sphero Technology Sphero basics Session 04 Animal Adaptations Science Animal design Session 05 Garden Engineers Life Science Garden design Session 06 Gratitude Gifts Thanksgiving Gift creation Session 07 Star Makers Advent Star engineering Session 08 Digital Art Technology Digital creation Session 09 Faith Scientists Catholic Schools Women in STEM Session 10 Magnets & Motion Science Magnetism Session 11 Lenten Love Service Service project Session 12 Butterfly Wonder Life Cycles Metamorphosis Session 13 Easter Joy Resurrection New life celebration Session 14 Sphero Challenge Technology Robot missions Session 15 Simple Machines Engineering Levers and pulleys Session 16 Earth Care Environment Creation care Session 17 Year Celebration Exhibition Portfolio showcase

docs.title: 🎯 Year B Learning Goals
docs.text:
Target outcomes, demonstrated individually where actually taught:

  • ✅ Apply design thinking to new challenges

  • Predict/run/debug a short stored Sphero program; manual driving alone is not programming evidence.

  • Communicate/revise an artistic idea with paper or an approved drawing app; paper does not establish digital-tool operation.

  • ✅ Explore animal adaptations and life cycles

  • ✅ Connect faith to environmental stewardship

  • ✅ Serve others through engineering projects

docs.title: From CSCOE Library
docs.text:
Possible loans only: confirm actual availability, booking terms, model/app compatibility and charge; no guaranteed class set.

  • Sphero Robots & Tablets

  • KEVA Planks

  • Simple Machines Kit

  • Magnet exploration kit

  • Butterfly/Life cycle materials

docs.title: Technology
docs.text:
• Sphero Edu app

  • Drawing/art apps on tablets

docs.title: Classroom Supplies
docs.text:
• Craft materials for building

  • Garden supplies

Plant care stays at school with a named adult checking moisture; no automatic daily watering, outdoor growth requirement or compulsory home care. Photos/models replace live butterflies unless species/care/ecological plans are approved; purchased animals are not released simply because weather is warm. Digital art is Recommended, not device-essential; actual robot execution has a Required primary path with an honest algorithm-only fallback. Home activities are optional with no routine homework, purchases or required donations.

  • Construction paper

docs.title: 🔄 Year A / Year B Rotation
docs.text:
Year B focuses on:

  • 🏰 Tower building and habitats

  • 🤖 Sphero robot programming

  • 🦋 Butterflies and animal adaptations

  • 🎨 Digital art creation

  • 🌍 Environmental stewardship

Year A (alternate year) focuses on:

  • 🌉 Bridge building

  • 🤖 Dash Robot programming

  • 🌱 Plant life cycles

  • 🎵 Sound and instruments

  • 👥 Community helpers

Grades 1-2 Year B Bi-Weekly — New challenges, same wonder!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 1 of 17

Students become Design Detectives, distinguishing human-made objects designed for a purpose from naturally occurring things.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Recognize that objects are designed with purpose

  • Identify problems that designs solve

  • Begin thinking like designers

  • Connect human creativity to God-given gifts

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Collection of everyday objects (scissors, cup, shoe, pencil, backpack)

  • 📓 Design Detective journals

  • 🔍 Magnifying glasses

  • 🖍️ Crayons/pencils

  • 📋 "Design Detective" badges (paper)

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: Blessed Fra Angelico — A Dominican friar who used his artistic talents to design beautiful paintings for God's glory.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: James 1:17; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for giving people creative minds to design things that help us. Help us be good designers who think about others. Bless our discovering today. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Detective Mission — "Today we become DESIGN DETECTIVES!"
  2. Human-made or natural? Compare a pencil with a washed stone: someone designed the pencil for a purpose; the stone formed naturally. Catholic belief about creation is distinct from identifying human manufacture.
  3. Design Questions:
  4. WHO designed this?
  5. WHY did they make it?
  6. What PROBLEM does it solve?
  7. God's Gift — "God gave people creativity to design helpful things"
  8. Badge Distribution — Hand out Design Detective badges!

docs.title: Main Activity: Design Investigation (18 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Object Investigation (8 minutes)

  • Small groups receive everyday objects

  • Detective questions for each:

  • What is it?
  • What is it made of?
  • What problem does it solve?

  • How could it be better?

  • Record observations

Part 2: Class Share (4 minutes)

  • Each group presents one object

  • "This [object] was designed to..."

  • Class discusses: "What would life be without it?"

Part 3: Your Turn! (6 minutes)

  • Think of a problem you have

  • Draw a design that could solve it

  • Examples: Homework holder, snack carrier, toy organizer

  • Share with a partner

docs.title: Design Detective Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw one object you investigated
  2. Write: "It was designed to..."
  3. Draw YOUR design idea

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Detective Discovery — "What surprised you about design?"
  2. Year Ahead — "We'll design and build all year!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for creative minds. Help us design things that help others. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified purpose of designed objects

  • Asked thoughtful questions

  • Created original design idea

  • Recorded in journal

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focus on 2-3 familiar objects

  • Partner investigation

  • Draw-only journal entry

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Investigate more complex objects

  • Write about design features

  • Create detailed design plans

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence / cleanup
docs.text: Use blunt scissors only as a closed teacher-held example; no unsupervised cutting/sharp tools in mystery collections. Grade 1 names one human-made object/purpose orally; Grade 2 distinguishes natural from designed and sketches a user-centered improvement. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 investigation minutes are cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; orally discuss one familiar object)
docs.text: Family Activity: Be Design Detectives at home! Pick 5 objects and figure out what problems they solve. What objects could be designed better? Draw your improvement ideas!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Save Design Detective badges for year-long use

  • Start collecting interesting objects for future sessions

  • Journals will be used throughout the year

  • Connect to inventions and inventors

Next Session: Session 02 — Tower Power

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 1-2 | Duration: 30 minutes | Session: 2 of 17

Students explore what makes structures stable, designing and building towers that are tall AND strong.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand that wide bases provide stability

  • Build towers using various materials

  • Test structures for height and strength

  • Practice iteration (trying again to improve)

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 KEVA Planks (from CSCOE library)

  • 📦 Cups (paper or plastic)

  • 📦 Index cards

  • 📏 Measuring stick or tape measure

  • 📓 Design Detective journals

  • 📸 Pictures of famous towers

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies/patronage
docs.text: St. Barbara — Patron saint of architects and builders. She's remembered for her faith that was strong like a tower!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 18:10; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced. The tower is religious imagery, not a guarantee of structural stability.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you are our strong tower! Help us build towers today that are strong and stable. When we face challenges, remind us that you are our strength. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Famous Towers — Show pictures:
  2. Eiffel Tower
  3. Leaning Tower of Pisa
  4. Church bell towers
  5. What Makes Towers Strong?
  6. Wide base
  7. Balanced weight
  8. Strong materials
  9. Today's Challenge — "Build the TALLEST tower that can stand for 10 seconds!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Tower Engineering (19 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Quick Challenge - Cup Towers (6 minutes)

  • Partners receive 10 cups

  • Challenge: Build as tall as possible

  • Test: Does it stand for 10 seconds?

  • Observe: What patterns make towers stable?

Part 2: KEVA Plank Towers (10 minutes)

  • Switch to KEVA Planks

  • Challenge: Build to a 20 cm comparison mark while staying below the 30 cm safety limit.

  • Design considerations:

  • Start with wide base
  • Build symmetrically

  • Test as you build

  • Measure final heights

Part 3: Improvement Round (3 minutes)

  • "What would make your tower stronger?"

  • One more try to improve!

  • Compare: Better? What changed?

docs.title: Design Detective Journal (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your tallest tower
  2. Label: Base, middle, top
  3. Write: "My tower was ___ inches tall"
  4. Write: "Strong towers need..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (2 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Tower Secrets — "What makes towers stable?"
  2. Faith Connection — "God is our strong tower!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for being our strong tower. Help us build strong structures and strong faith. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Built towers using multiple materials

  • Identified features of stable structures

  • Measured and compared heights

  • Improved designs through iteration

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focus on cup stacking only

  • Lower height goal (6 inches)

  • Build alongside teacher

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Support one soft eraser within a tabletop height limit of 30 cm; never place a book/heavy object on a tall tower.

  • Try multiple tower designs

  • Record data systematically

docs.title: SAFETY / Grade 1 / evidence
docs.text: Maximum tabletop tower height 30 cm, hands/faces clear during collapse, no furniture climbing or heavy loads. Grade 1 points to base and compares two heights orally; Grade 2 records same-unit height and 10-second test before/after one revision. Technology: None primary path. Last 3 building minutes are plank/cup count and cleanup; no routine homework.

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠 (optional; avoid food-can/heavy tower loads)
docs.text: Family Activity: Build towers at home with blocks, cups, cards, or food cans. Have a family tower competition! What made the winning tower special? Visit or look up pictures of the Eiffel Tower.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Reserve KEVA Planks from CSCOE 2 weeks ahead

  • Save tower measurement data for comparison

  • Take photos of successful designs

  • Connect to architecture and construction careers

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Meet Sphero Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 3 of 17 / C, T Big idea Code is stored input; rolling and light are observable output. Student objective "I can run two stored instructions, predict output, and change one block." Why Responsible programmers test short understandable sequences before complex paths. Catholic connection Fair turns and careful shared resources; teacher application of CCC 2407/2415. Standards Local CST-C3: equipment care; CST-T1: input/output and start/stop; CST-T2: sequence and one debug. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Required primary path: compatible charged Sphero/tablet with Sphero Edu for physical stored-code execution. Token fallback assesses algorithms, not robot mastery. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first model/app preflight plus charging; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Confirm real inventory/loan and school permissions. Check the exact model supports chosen blocks; do not assume Mini/BOLT features identical.
  2. In Blocks test light-color -> roll at heading 0 for 0.5-1 second at low speed -> stop; write model-specific working settings on board. Aim heading 0 away from children.
  3. Mark dry 1 m floor bays; prepare light/roll/stop picture cards, tabletop tokens and safe stop signal.
  4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, individual roster check.
  5. Per team of 2-3: one robot/tablet kit and picture cards/token.
  6. Class: floor tape, timer, board, storage trays.
  7. Teacher-only: chargers, installed help and model screening. No attached pens.
Students Teams / simultaneous kits Papers 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

If only three kits exist, at 25 supervise one station with three 4-minute waves of three teams; off-device teams predict cards. With one kit, record unobserved individual runs and repeat assessment later. Do not infer mastery from watching another child's robot.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; input/output = code/result; aim = set direction reference; debug = fix a mismatch. Manual Drive mode is remote control. A connected stored sequence that executes hands-off is programming. Floor, charge and aim influence travel. Misconception: every rolling robot run matches an exact path. Observe before promising accuracy. If asked "Are we experts now?" We are beginning programmers; evidence shows specific skills, not expertise.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show robot, purpose and care/turn rule. Optional original prayer asks for wise tool use.
  2. 4-7: Children predict color then forward movement using cards/token, orally or by pointing.
  3. 7-11: Teacher contrasts Drive with a stored Blocks sequence; demonstrate aim, Run and Stop.
  4. 11-23: Each child predicts and executes starter, changes a color or roll duration and reruns. Roles rotate after each run; teacher records each child's observed actions.
  5. 23-26: Individual exit: point to two ordered actions, name an output and one change; identify safe equipment care.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / measurable evidence
docs.text: What is stored before Run? Why aim again? What changed after your edit? How did you protect shared equipment? Grade 1: order two action cards, personally Run/Stop under supervision and point to changed output. Grade 2: assemble at least two stored actions, predict, change a block and explain mismatch or change. Record not observed / prompted / independent for each criterion; care assessed through an action, not a saint fact.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Connection failure: check selected robot/charge once, switch after two minutes. Token alternative: arrange two cards, have partner follow, fix one intentionally wrong card. Record algorithm/debug evidence only; no real robot operation/programming mastery. Mis-aim: stop/re-aim/shorten movement. All work indoors, no winter/outdoor condition.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Low-speed marked bays; stop if out of area; no chasing/racing or holding running robots. Teacher handles chargers and small removable model components. Dry floor only, no art paint/markers attached to ball. Support: picture starter, narration, large cards, adult scribing and accessible tabletop token; Grade 1 needs no independent reading. Challenge: Grade 2 adds light/wait action or compares two durations, not expert mazes.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text:
Stop/power down according to model guide, count kits, return trays, remove lesson tape; teacher handles charging. We contrasted driving with stored programs and tested one changed instruction. Catholic connection: stewardship and fair access. Ask: "What changed in your program?" Optional: give two directions to a paper token; no robot/tablet/purchase or routine homework. Sphero official education site, installed help requires preflight; CCC 2407/2415. Acutis biography/title: VERIFICATION REQUIRED before optional use, not needed for this lesson.
