docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 3 of 17

Students explore bridge engineering principles and build bridges using KEVA planks, testing their structures for strength.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Identify different bridge types and their features

  • Understand how triangles add strength

  • Build and test a bridge structure

  • Apply the engineering design process

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 KEVA Planks (from CSCOE library)

  • 📸 Bridge type pictures

  • 🪙 Weights for testing (coins, washers)

  • 📏 Rulers for measuring span

  • 📓 Engineering journals

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Patrick — Built "bridges" between people and faith in Ireland. He connected communities!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!" — Romans 10:15 (Bridges help spread good news!)

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you connect heaven and earth. Like St. Patrick who built bridges of faith, help us build structures that connect and serve others. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Bridge Purpose — "Bridges connect people and places!"
  2. Bridge Types:
  3. Beam — Simple, flat across supports
  4. Arch — Curved, pushes weight outward
  5. Truss — Uses triangles for strength
  6. Suspension — Hangs from cables
  7. Support and joints — A joined triangle can resist changing shape; loose KEVA planks need stable overlap/support, not a promise that any triangle is strong
  8. St. Patrick — Connected communities through faith

docs.title: Main Activity: Bridge Building Challenge (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: The Challenge (3 minutes)

  • Build a bridge that:
  • Spans at least 8 inches (between two books)
  • Can hold weight

  • Uses only KEVA planks

  • Test up to 10 identical plastic counters; record last held count or "at least 10." No unlimited loading.

Part 2: Design & Build (18 minutes)

IMAGINE (3 min):

  • Sketch your bridge design

  • Label: supports, deck, special features

  • Which bridge type will you use?

PLAN (2 min):

  • Estimate planks needed

  • Decide where to start building

CREATE (11 min):

  • Build your bridge!

  • Check the deck's support and stable overlapping contact; unjoined planks are not a rigid truss

  • Test balance before adding weight

TEST (2 min):

  • Add weights one at a time

  • Count held counters and stop at 10; never load with heavy weights

  • Record your results

Part 3: Analysis (5 minutes)

  • Which bridges held the most weight?

  • What designs worked best? Why?

  • How could you improve?

  • Class discussion of findings

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Sketch your bridge design (before and after building)
  2. Record: "My bridge held ___ weights"
  3. Write: "Our support arrangement helped by..."
  4. Write: "Next time I would..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Celebrate Successes — Recognize strong bridges
  2. Real Bridges — Where do you see bridges in our community?
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, help us be bridge builders—connecting people with love and service. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified bridge types

  • Created design before building

  • Built stable bridge structure

  • Tested and recorded results

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Provide starter bridge base

  • Work with partner

  • Simplified span requirement

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Longer span requirement

  • Design constraints (limited planks)

  • Research famous bridges

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Find bridges in your community! What type are they? Why were they designed that way? Build a bridge at home using blocks, straws, or popsicle sticks. Test with toy cars!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Reserve KEVA planks from CSCOE library

  • Clear large floor/table space

  • Use books for stable supports

  • Take photos for portfolio

  • Connect to local bridge examples

Previous: Session 2 — Dash & Code Next: Session 4 — Animal Habitats

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Use low fixed books and a tray, no metal weights, load above 10 counters, climbing or hands beneath a loaded deck. Do not require all teams to collapse their bridge. Have each child state one kept-same test condition; supplied planks and scalable quantities still require teacher kit preparation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 4 of 17

Students explore how animals are designed for their habitats and create habitat models demonstrating this connection.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Define habitat and identify its components

  • Explain how animals are adapted to their habitats

  • Design and build a habitat model

  • Connect habitat design to God's providence

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📸 Pictures of various habitats/animals

  • 📦 Habitat model materials (boxes, craft supplies)

  • 🌿 Natural materials (if available)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📋 Habitat component checklist

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Francis of Assisi — Patron saint of animals and ecology! He saw all creatures as brothers and sisters.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Look at the birds of the air; they do not sow or reap or store away in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them." — Matthew 6:26

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, help us appreciate living things and protect their habitats. Give us careful eyes and caring hands. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. What is a Habitat?
  2. "A habitat is an animal's HOME—where it finds everything it needs"
  3. Habitat Components (Four Things Needed):
  4. 🍽️ Food — What does it eat?
  5. 💧 Water — How does it get water?
  6. 🏠 Shelter — Where does it hide/sleep?
  7. 🌡️ Space — Room to move and live
  8. Adaptations — Features can help survival in particular conditions; no animal is guaranteed perfectly suited to every changing habitat
  9. St. Francis — Loved all creatures

docs.title: Main Activity: Habitat Design Challenge (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Habitat Exploration (6 minutes)

  • Explore habitat types:
  • 🌲 Forest — Trees, seasons, varied animals
  • 🏜️ Desert — Dry; deserts can be hot or cold
  • 🌊 Ocean — Saltwater; some animals breathe air, others obtain oxygen from water
  • 🧊 Arctic — Cold, ice, thick fur/blubber

  • 🌿 Rainforest — Wet, layers, biodiversity

  • Pick ONE habitat to design

Part 2: Design & Build (16 minutes)

Choose Animal & Habitat (2 min):

  • Select habitat type

  • Choose animal for that habitat

  • Think: How is this animal designed for its home?

Design (3 min):

  • Sketch habitat model

  • Include all 4 components: food, water, shelter, space

  • Label adaptations

Build (11 min):

  • Create 3D habitat model in box or on paper plate

  • Show:

  • Where food comes from
  • Water source
  • Shelter/hiding spots

  • Space for movement

  • Add your animal (drawn or craft)

Part 3: Habitat Showcase (4 minutes)

  • Gallery walk to see habitats

  • Presenters explain: "My animal survives because..."

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your habitat model
  2. Label: Food, Water, Shelter, Space
  3. Write: "My animal is designed for its habitat because..."
  4. Write: "God shows care for animals by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Design Appreciation — "What amazed you about animal adaptations?"
  2. Stewardship — "How can we protect habitats?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for living things. Help us protect habitats and be responsible stewards. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Identified habitat components

  • Connected animal adaptations to habitat

  • Created habitat model with all 4 components

  • Explained animal's survival design

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Habitat template with labeled sections

  • Partner work

  • Focus on familiar animals

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Research specific adaptations

  • Compare two animals in same habitat

  • Include food chain in model

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: What's YOUR habitat? List the food, water, shelter, and space in your home! Watch nature documentaries about different habitats. Visit a zoo and observe how exhibits recreate natural habitats.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Connect to standards on habitats and adaptations

  • Consider outdoor observation of local habitat

  • Coordinate with science curriculum

  • Habitats can be displayed for parents

Previous: Session 3 — Bridge Engineering Next: Session 5 — Scratch Intro

docs.title: Evidence / SAFETY
docs.text: Use verified animal food/water/shelter cards (VERIFICATION REQUIRED for species-specific claims), not invented diet relationships. Models are explanatory, not engineered homes for live animals. No handling wild animals, unknown plants, mold or sharp natural objects; window/photos replace outdoor work in unsafe weather. Each child labels needs and supports one adaptation explanation with the provided source card.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 5 of 17

Students are introduced to Scratch programming, learning how block-based coding works and creating their first animated project.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Navigate the Scratch interface

  • Understand how code blocks connect to create programs

  • Create a simple animated character

  • Use sequences and loops in programming

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 💻 Computers/Chromebooks with Scratch

  • 📋 Scratch quick reference cards

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🖥️ Projector for demonstration

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Creativity and responsibility — Programming is a human tool; "God as programmer" is only a metaphor, not a scientific description of creation or human freedom.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "In the beginning was the Word... Through him all things were made." — John 1:1,3

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you created the universe with perfect order and logic. As we learn to program, help us appreciate your incredible design. Guide our creativity today! Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. What is Scratch?
  2. "A programming language where you connect blocks like puzzle pieces!"
  3. Created at MIT for learning to code
  4. Used by millions of kids worldwide
  5. Programming = Giving Instructions
  6. Computers do EXACTLY what we tell them
  7. We need to be precise and logical
  8. Faith reflection — Use our creativity responsibly; we are not discovering literal divine computer code

docs.title: Main Activity: Scratch Exploration (27 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Interface Tour (5 minutes)

  • Stage — Where the action happens

  • Sprites — Characters and objects

  • Code Blocks — Instructions that snap together

  • Categories:

  • 🎬 Motion — Move and turn
  • 👀 Looks — Appearance and speech
  • 🔊 Sound — Sounds and music
  • 🎮 Events — Triggers (when clicked, etc.)
  • 🔁 Control — Loops and waits

Part 2: Guided Activity: Make the Cat Dance! (12 minutes)

Step 1: Basic Motion (3 min)

  • Find "move 10 steps" block

  • Snap under "when green flag clicked"

  • Click green flag to test

  • Try different numbers!

Step 2: Add Turning (3 min)

  • Add "turn 15 degrees"

  • See what happens

  • Create a spinning cat!

Step 3: Loops & Waiting (3 min)

  • Find "forever" block (in Control)

  • Put motion blocks INSIDE the loop

  • Add "wait 0.5 seconds"

  • The cat dances forever!

Step 4: Add Speech (3 min)

  • Find "say Hello for 2 seconds"

  • What should your cat say?

  • Add sound blocks if time

Part 3: Free Creation (8 minutes)

  • Customize YOUR cat:
  • Change costume (Looks: next costume)
  • Add more movements
  • Make it say something meaningful

  • Add sounds

  • Explore other sprites if time

Part 4: Demo Showcase (2 minutes)

  • Volunteers show their dancing cats

  • Celebrate creativity!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw the Scratch interface (Stage, Sprites, Blocks)
  2. List 3 block types you used
  3. Write: "Programming is like..."
  4. Write: "I want to create a program that..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Share Discoveries — "What cool thing did your cat do?"
  2. Logic Appreciation — "God's creation follows logic too!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for minds that can create and problem-solve. Bless our coding adventures! Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Navigated Scratch interface

  • Connected code blocks successfully

  • Created working animation

  • Used at least one loop

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Paired with experienced peer

  • Step-by-step visual guide

  • Focus on basic motion only

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Add multiple sprites

  • Create sprite interaction

  • Explore variables

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Optional family activity: Scratch is free at scratch.mit.edu; an account or home device is not required. Describe or draw the sequence for a family member. No homework.

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Use guest/offline projects and private local saves; no shared pupil credentials or compulsory accounts

  • Pre-load Scratch on all devices

  • Bookmark Scratch website

  • Students will use Scratch again in Session 8

  • Consider Scratch offline if internet unreliable

Previous: Session 4 — Animal Habitats Next: Session 6 — Gratitude Tech

docs.title: Technology / individual evidence
docs.text: Primary Required for executable Scratch. Without devices, trace motion/turn/repeat cards with a token and identify a bug; record CT only, not Scratch operation. Every child predicts what the loop repeats and explains one edit; log who actually edits/runs code. Reserve 5 minutes of exploration for saving/stopping/device return.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 6 of 17

Students use technology to create digital gratitude projects, expressing thankfulness to God and others.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Connect gratitude to faith

  • Use technology to express thankfulness

  • Create a digital or tech-enhanced gratitude project

  • Share appreciation with others

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 💻 Computers with Scratch or presentation software

  • 📱 Tablets (optional)

  • 🎨 Digital creation tools

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📝 Gratitude planning sheets

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Paul — Wrote letters of gratitude to churches. Many Bible books are his "thank you notes"!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus." — 1 Thessalonians 5:18

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for the abundance of blessings in our lives. Help us use our skills to express gratitude to you and to the people who help us. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude & Thanksgiving:
  2. "Thanksgiving is about saying THANK YOU"
  3. Who do we thank? God, family, friends, teachers, community
  4. St. Paul's Letters:
  5. He couldn't be with people, so he WROTE to them
  6. Technology helps us connect with gratitude too!
  7. Today's Challenge — "Create a digital gratitude project!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Digital Gratitude Creation (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Gratitude Brainstorm (4 minutes)

  • List people you're thankful for

  • List things you're thankful for

  • Choose who/what to focus on

Part 2: Digital Creation (18 minutes)

Option A: Scratch Gratitude Animation

  • Create animated "thank you" in Scratch

  • Show what you're thankful for

  • Add speech, movement, backgrounds

Option B: Digital Slideshow

  • Create presentation of thankfulness

  • Include images, words, reasons

  • 4-6 slides minimum

Option C: Gratitude Podcast/Recording

  • Record audio thank-you message

  • Include specific reasons

  • Could send to recipient!

Option D: Tech-Enhanced Card

  • Design digital card

  • Print to give to someone

  • Add QR code to special message (if able)

Part 3: Sharing (4 minutes)

  • Volunteers share projects

  • Discuss: How does sharing gratitude feel?

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Write: "I'm thankful for... because..."
  2. Draw/describe your gratitude project
  3. Write: "Technology helped me express gratitude by..."
  4. Write: "I will share this with..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude Circle — Each person shares one thanks
  2. Reflection — "How did creating gratitude feel?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for everything! Help us be people who always say thank you. Bless our families this Thanksgiving. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Communicated a specific respectful thank-you; personal emotions are not scored

  • Used technology creatively

  • Completed digital project

  • Planned to share with others

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Partner work

  • Template provided

  • Simple slideshow option

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Multiple project formats

  • Add music/advanced features

  • Create for multiple recipients

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Share your gratitude project with family! Create a family gratitude list. Write thank-you notes together. At Thanksgiving dinner, each person says what they're thankful for!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Time lesson before Thanksgiving break

  • Help deliver digital projects to recipients

  • Connect to school gratitude initiatives

  • Print cards if needed for those without tech

Previous: Session 5 — Scratch Intro Next: Session 7 — Light & Circuits

docs.title: Privacy / fallback
docs.text: Teacher approves delivery and recipient consent; no pupil identifying photos/voices, public QR links or uploads without school permission. If devices fail, make a paper message and revise it with peer feedback; this is art/communication evidence, not digital-tool operation or computer programming. Home sharing is optional, no homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit Grades 3-4 / Circuits / Light & Circuits Time One 40-minute meeting, including 5-minute cleanup Domains Catholic audience care, science systems, technology tools, artistic communication Big idea / objective "I can trace and test an open/closed light circuit, then communicate what the light means." Why Safe testing helps us understand everyday tools. Catholic connection Advent light symbolizes hope in Christ (John 8:12); electricity does not prove Christ's divinity. Use the school's approved Scripture translation and design a respectful message without judging the reader's circumstances. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (respectful message), CST-S3 (circuit model), CST-T1 (test/repair), CST-A3 (message feedback/revision). Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for actual operation; paper is a model, not circuit mastery. Prerequisites No prior circuit lesson or Year B assumed Prep / cleanup First kit inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 5 minutes included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text: Complete the OLP Snap Circuits guide preflight for the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project. Leave the approved diagram and counted station list ready for a substitute. Do not assume holder protection, a two-AA allocation or LED current limiting.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
• Per pupil: pencil, evidence half-sheet, art/message half-sheet.
  • Per team: diagram sheet, shared marker, dry work area.
  • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with only project parts, grid and tray. Battery type/count and checked reserves follow the guide.
  • Teacher/class: approved instructions, setup card, board, timer, roster, dry storage and adult-controlled cells; demo uses a station kit.
Pupils Teams / diagram sheets Kits / trays Waves Student half-sheets / pencils 10 4 4 1 20 / 10 15 5 5 1 30 / 15 20 7 7 1 40 / 20 25 9 5 2 50 / 25

Reuse the same hardware for Year B Christmas Circuits; no second kit purchase.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and safety
docs.text:
Circuit: complete conducting path, including return. Open: interrupted. Closed: complete. Switch: opens/closes the path. Current: charge flow. The battery supplies energy; light symbolism is not an electrical explanation of faith or human dignity. A lamp project does not establish LED polarity mastery.

Misconception: touching any two conductors makes a safe circuit. If asked: "Why is it off?" Trace the approved path while power is isolated; ask the adult to check contacts/cells. Never short the supply.

SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/school gate, adult source isolation before snap changes and adult inspection before power is restored. No pupil battery access, coin cells, mains/USB power, extra loads, fan blades, live shorts, bare LED substitutions or take-home circuits. Warm/smelly/leaking/damaged: stop/report, adult isolates and marks OUT OF SERVICE.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose/symbol. Prayer: "Jesus, help us share hope and care for one another." Explain symbol versus physical explanation and the real-turn rule.
  2. 4-8: Model safely. Teacher traces the approved full path, demonstrates OFF/ON and models source isolation/inspection.
  3. 8-10: Predict individually. Each child traces battery -> switch -> light -> return and predicts both states.
  4. 10-22: Wave A. Follow the guide's isolated team build, adult checks, each child's two OFF/ON cycles and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Waiting teams draw diagrams and draft an Advent message with a named reader.
  5. 22-23: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 23-35: Wave B / communicate. Remaining teams get the identical hardware routine; finished teams peer-check and revise one message detail, record repair evidence and answer individual path/state questions. At smaller enrollment all teams use this window for retests/feedback. Ask: "Where is the gap? What showed the repair worked? What does your message mean?"
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Isolate/count/return parts and cells, store dry kits and collect sheets. Record any missing physical turns explicitly.

docs.title: Success, support and alternatives
docs.text:
Each child traces a full path, predicts and operates both states twice, explains a repair using observed evidence and revises a respectful message. Record physical contribution/test observed / prompted / not yet separately from reasoning/art. Score 1 decoration only; 2 prompted path; 3 independent path/state/repair and message evidence; 4 explains a model limitation or two possible open-path faults without unsafe live testing.

  • Grade 3/support: traced diagram, large words/symbols, oral responses, motor help for snaps; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 4/challenge: compare two drawn faults; no extra branches or loads.
  • 25 pupils: nine pairs/trios, five stations, two 12-minute waves. Each child must have an observed turn; defer unfinished evidence rather than rush inspection. No four-person hardware groups.
  • No working kit: isolate/report, use a checked reserve or the guide's verified protected-AA route. Never connect Snap parts to that supply.
  • Paper route: use identical times with drawn paths and an on/off token. Record circuit reasoning/art only; electrical operation not observed. A demonstration alone does not prove each child's assembly/testing.

docs.text:

Describe the actual hardware or paper route. Ask: "Where is the gap when the light is off?" Only paper goes home; no electrical homework or purchases.

docs.text:

Part 2: Build Weather Instruments (16 minutes)

Choose ONE to build:

Option A: Rain Gauge

  • Straight-sided flat-bottomed clear plastic cup, uncut; mark zero at the inside bottom with a ruler

  • Mark measurements on side

  • Practice water depth in mm; only a properly placed straight-sided collector measures rainfall, not snow depth

  • Place outside to track rainfall

Option B: Airflow Indicator

  • Tape a 20 cm tissue strip to a cardboard handle; no pins
  • Gently move a card to create air movement; note the strip's response
  • This is not a calibrated wind-direction/speed instrument

Option C: Teacher photo of an anemometer

  • Discuss what a calibrated instrument measures; no pin assembly or claim that spin counts equal a wind speed

Option D: Teacher photo of a barometer

  • Read a labeled sample scale; do not build a latex/glass model or use it to guarantee a storm

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Life inquiry / Plants & Growth Time One 40-minute meeting, including cleanup; real germination takes days Domains Catholic truth/stewardship, life science, investigation, measurement Big idea A living seed needs suitable conditions to germinate; observing takes time. Student objective "I can observe a seed, plan a one-change test, and compare labeled practice data." Why Gardeners and scientists separate predictions from observations and plan reliable care. Catholic connection John 12:24 uses a seed image to teach about Jesus' self-giving; it is a theological metaphor, not a claim that a seed must die to germinate. Care for living things and tell the truth about evidence. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C1 (distinguish metaphor/evidence); CST-S1 (observations); CST-S2 (one variable/controls); CST-M1 (length/count comparisons). Technology None; photos optional, not required Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; compare whole millimeters and identify one changed condition. No Year A/Year B prior sequence required. Prep / cleanup 15 minutes for dry kit/data; 5 minutes cleanup. Optional actual sprout samples need days of advance growth, not concealed in prep estimate.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Check school seed/legume allergy guidance; substitute paper seed drawings if needed. No seed tasting or sending loose seeds to younger children.
  2. Pair pupils, final trio if needed. Give each team two clear cups labeled moist and dry, two folded paper towels, and four untreated bean seeds (two per cup).
  3. Board the practice table below, labeled SIMULATED DATA; NOT OUR OBSERVATIONS. Draw lines 4 mm and 9 mm long for ruler practice.
  4. Decide whether a regular teacher has accepted daily care for a real optional test. Write caretaker name and check dates. If no caretaker, leave seeds dry and assess the plan/data today; do not start an unattended living experiment.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth kit is spare. The water budget includes those spare cups and is a maximum.

  • Per student: pencil, evidence half-sheet.
  • Per team: 4 untreated bean seeds, 2 clear plastic cups, 2 paper towels, 2 labels, 1 ruler, 2 recording sheets.
  • Class: jug with 100 mL maximum water; 1 teacher measuring spoon; 1 tray/bin to hold all cups; board/timer.
  • Teacher only: water dispensing, optional live sample and care calendar. No soil, fertilizers or grow lights needed.
Students Teams Seeds Cups / towels / labels Rulers Team paper Slips / pencils 10 5 20 10 each 5 10 sheets 10 each 15 8 32 16 each 8 16 sheets 15 each 20 10 40 20 each 10 20 sheets 20 each 25 13 52 26 each 13 26 sheets 25 each

Use 5 mL water per moist cup initially only if care is arranged: 25/40/50/65 mL for the four class sizes, from the 100 mL supply. Damp, not pooled. Cups/rulers/bin reusable; seeds/towels/labels/paper consumable.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background, misconception and answer
docs.text:
Seed: contains a living embryo and stored resources. Germinate: begin growth from a viable seed. Variable: condition intentionally changed. Control conditions: things kept the same. Prediction: expected result, not data.

Beans need water, oxygen and suitable temperature for germination; they can germinate on a damp towel without soil/burial. Many germinating seeds use stored food before leaves develop; growing green plants need light and nutrients. Needs vary by species; do not claim every seed has identical light needs.

Misconception: "The seed dies or must be buried to sprout." A viable embryo remains alive while growing. If asked: "Will it grow today?" Answer: "Not visibly during our class. Today we observe, plan and practice measuring; actual changes must be checked over days."

docs.title: Practice data: two seeds per condition
docs.text:
Condition / seed Day 0 root length (mm) Day 3 (mm) Day 5 (mm) Moist / 1 0 4 9 Moist / 2 0 3 8 Dry / 1 0 0 0 Dry / 2 0 0 0

Invented instructional values, not guaranteed bean growth or observed evidence. They illustrate comparison; two seeds do not prove a universal rule. Keep seed type, cup/towel, location, temperature and observation time the same; vary added water only. Do not test several variables at once.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No eating seeds, rubbing eyes, handling mold or using chemicals. Teacher pours water. Keep cups open to air; no tight bags around faces. Wash hands after contact; wipe spills. Adult discards moldy samples without student handling. No outdoor requirement or classroom heat equipment.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-5: Observe. Short original prayer: "God, help us care for living things and speak truthfully." Show a dry bean. "What can you actually see? What are you guessing is inside?"
  2. 5-10: Explain life and metaphor. Draw embryo/stored food/coat. Clarify that an alive seed grows; John 12:24 is not a botany rule. "Could a dead embryo grow?"
  3. 10-17: Plan a test. Each team states question: "How does added water affect these seeds?" Write prediction; circle changed condition and list two controls. Ask: "Why use the same kind of seed in both cups?"
  4. 17-23: Set up model. Place towels and two seeds in each labeled cup. If care is arranged, teacher adds 5 mL to moist cup; otherwise all remain dry and are labeled planned setup only. Every child sketches both conditions. No growth result claimed.
  5. 23-29: Read practice evidence. Teacher labels simulated table. Pupils compare day 5 moist and dry counts/lengths, and measure the drawn 4/9 mm lines. "Did our class grow these roots? What would real observations need?"
  6. 29-34: Individual evidence. Child records one observation, the variable/two controls, and a correct whole-number comparison: 9 mm versus 0 mm, difference 9 mm. Grade 4 also compares the two moist seeds (1 mm difference) and names a reason more seeds could help.
  7. 34-35: Check success. Teacher asks two children: "What do we know today, and what remains a prediction?"
  8. 35-40: Cleanup. Store any cared-for cups in adult-approved spot with caretaker/date card; otherwise return dry seeds to teacher storage. Collect rulers, wipe cups/desks and wash hands. Collect slips.

docs.title: Success, trouble, support, challenge and indoor alternative
docs.text:
Success: each child distinguishes observation from prediction/simulated data, identifies water as one variable and two kept-same conditions, and reads/compares whole-mm values. Growth itself is not today's assessment. Score 1 unsupported growth claim; 2 identifies water with prompts; 3 observation/variable/controls/comparison correct; 4 adds replication or species/model limitation.

  • No seed supplies or allergy restriction: sketch two labeled cups with seed drawings; the same timed planning/data work remains. Record direct seed observation as unavailable.
  • No care between bi-weekly meetings: use dry planning setup and supplied simulated data; no failed forgotten plants or required home care.
  • No sprout appears later: log "no visible root"; check water/temperature/viability without inventing a result.
  • Support / Grade 3: oral explanations, pre-drawn cups, adult ruler placement and tally/whole-number comparison.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: propose more seeds per condition and a consistent check schedule; no multi-variable "challenge" that ruins the fair test.
  • Indoor alternative / winter: the primary plan is entirely indoor and includes data now. No spring weather or greenhouse needed.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We observed seeds, planned a fair water test and compared clearly labeled practice data. We learned that germination is growth of a living embryo, not a resurrection experiment. Our Catholic connection was honest inquiry and care for life. Ask: "Which condition changed, and which stayed the same?" Optional at home: notice a growing plant with an adult. No planting supplies, daily log or homework required.

docs.text:

Students explore all six simple machines, understanding how they make work easier and building working examples.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Identify all six simple machines

  • Explain how each machine makes work easier

docs.title: Materials Needed

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Joseph the Worker — As a carpenter, he used simple machines every day to build and create. Feast day: May 1st!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord." — Colossians 3:23

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, like St. Joseph who worked with his hands, help us appreciate the tools that make work easier. Thank you for simple machines that multiply our effort. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. What is Work?
  2. For a constant force along the motion, work is force times distance; no formal formula calculation required here
  3. Moving something takes energy/effort
  4. Simple Machines:
  5. Tools that make work EASIER
  6. They don't reduce work, they change HOW we do it
  7. The Six Simple Machines:
  8. 🪜 Inclined Plane — Ramp
  9. 🪵 Wedge — Ax, knife
  10. 🔩 Screw — Spiral inclined plane
  11. ⚖️ Lever — Seesaw, crowbar
  12. 🛞 Wheel & Axle — Doorknob, car
  13. 🪢 Pulley — Flagpole, blinds

docs.title: Main Activity: Simple Machine Stations (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Station Rotation (18 minutes) Set up 3 stations, rotate every 6 minutes:

Station 1: Lever Experiments

  • Build levers with different fulcrum positions

  • Test: Where is it easiest to lift a weight?

  • Test moving a lever's fulcrum closer to the load, leaving a longer effort arm; identify both arms. "Closer" without saying to what is misleading.

  • Identify lever classes (1st, 2nd, 3rd)

Station 2: Inclined Plane & Wedge

  • Test ramps at different angles

  • Measure effort to push objects up

  • Discover: Longer ramp = less effort

  • See how wedge splits/cuts

Station 3: Wheel/Axle & Pulley

  • Test wheel and axle advantage

  • Use simple pulley to lift weight

  • Discover: Pulley changes direction of force

  • Compare lifting with and without machines

Part 2: Find Simple Machines (5 minutes)

  • Identify simple machines in classroom

  • Scissors = lever + wedge

  • Doorknob = wheel and axle

  • List as many as possible!

Part 3: Design Challenge (3 minutes)

  • Quick sketch: Design a machine using 2+ simple machines

  • Share ideas!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw and label all 6 simple machines
  2. Write: "Simple machines make work easier by..."
  3. List 5 simple machines you found in the classroom
  4. Sketch your machine design idea

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Discovery Share — "Which simple machine surprised you most?"
  2. St. Joseph Connection — "What machines would he have used?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, thank you for tools that help us work. Like St. Joseph, may we work with joy and skill. Amen."

docs.text:

  • Identified real-world examples

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Simple machine scavenger hunt at home! How many can you find? Identify the simple machines in tools, toys, and household items. Try building a simple machine to solve a problem!

docs.text:

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence
docs.text: Use low tabletop levers/ramps and teacher-selected loads capped at 10 plastic counters. No knives, axes, exposed cutting wedges, crushing/pinch tests or suspended heavy loads. Pulleys stay low with short string kept off bodies. Machines trade force/distance/direction and do not create energy; friction may increase work input. Effort described by feeling is qualitative, not a measured force unless a calibrated spring scale is provided. Each child labels load/effort/fulcrum and compares one observed change.

docs.text:

  • Buzzer
  • Motor
  • LED

Part 2: Sensor Exploration (8 minutes)

  • Try different inputs:
  • Light sensor
  • Sound sensor

  • Dimmer

  • Create "if-then" circuits:

  • IF dark, THEN light on

  • IF sound, THEN motor spins

  • How could these help people?

Part 3: Invention Challenge (10 minutes)

Challenge: Design something useful or joyful!

Ideas:

  • Night light (light sensor + LED)

  • Doorbell (button + buzzer)

  • Greeting card with sound

  • Spinning display

Steps: 1. Choose your purpose 2. Select components 3. Build and test 4. Improve! 5. Mount on craft material if desired

docs.title: SAFETY / compatibility gate
docs.text: Teacher inventories manufacturer-approved modules and closed battery holders; no wall power, loose magnets/batteries, exposed spinning blades or improvised connections. Off before edits; warm/leaking/damaged parts mean stop/off/report and adult isolation. VERIFICATION REQUIRED: actual light-sensor dark mode and available sound/dimmer modules; use the button/LED path if unsupported. No automatic dark-light claim without testing. Primary electronics Required; paper input/output diagrams are models, not working devices. Hardware stays at school; reserve 5 minutes of invention for cleanup. Each child predicts input/output and explains an observed test.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grade Band: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes per session | Sessions: 17 over the school year | Rotation Year: B

This bi-weekly schedule alternates contexts for combined classrooms. It revisits skills but does not establish identical coverage or mastery to Year A or the weekly curriculum.

docs.title: Audit status and availability
docs.text:
17 represented meetings / 680 minutes in 17 files. Read the Grades 3-4 review and lesson audit. Ozobot Coding and Christmas Circuits are rebuilt; other sessions still have varied preparation/assessment needs. No entire-track substitute certification.

Year B can be a first rotation: do not require prior Year A circuits or Scratch. Grade 3 uses supported counts and labeled models; Grade 4 adds test comparisons, limits and justified revisions. Scratch Games needs a novice bridge; it is not four weekly meetings' work in forty minutes.

No guaranteed CSCOE loans or installed software. Verify hardware models/stock, official code chart, voltage/current limits, batteries and approved connection methods in advance. Ozobot paper fallbacks are CT, not actual color-code/sensor operation. Christmas Circuits uses secured AA holders/current-limited modules; paper models are not electrical operation and no loose coin-cell gift goes home.

All biographies, quotations, scripture translation/verse numbering, current roles and patronage not backed by a verified source are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before fact-card use. Life-cycle learning distinguishes living metamorphosis from Easter symbolism. Home extensions/materials are optional, never homework prerequisites.

docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand the design thinking process

  • Practice empathy in problem-solving

  • Complete a user-focused design challenge

  • Connect design thinking to serving others

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📋 Design thinking process poster

  • 📦 Challenge materials (paper, tape, misc supplies)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📝 User interview cards

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Isidore of Seville — Associated with organizing knowledge. Do not present a proposed/popular internet patronage as an official declaration; exact patronage and biography are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.text: "So in everything, do to others what you would have them do to you." — Matthew 7:12

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, help us see the world through others' eyes. Give us compassion to understand what people need and creativity to design solutions that truly help. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Design Thinking:
  2. "Starts with understanding PEOPLE, not just problems"
  3. Used by top companies like Apple, Google, IDEO
  4. The Five Steps:
  5. 💗 EMPATHIZE — Understand the user
  6. 🎯 DEFINE — State the problem clearly
  7. 💡 IDEATE — Brainstorm many solutions
  8. 🔧 PROTOTYPE — Build quick models
  9. 🧪 TEST — Get feedback, improve
  10. St. Isidore — Organized information to help people learn
  11. Golden Rule — Design for others as you'd want!

docs.title: Main Activity: Design Challenge (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Empathize & Define (8 minutes)

Challenge: Design something to help a classmate!

Interview Your Partner (4 min):

  • What's something difficult in your day?

  • What frustrates you at school?

  • What would make your life easier?

  • What do you wish you had?

Define the Problem (4 min):

  • Write a problem statement:

  • "[Name] needs a way to [do something] because [reason]"

  • Example: "Maria needs a way to keep her desk organized because she loses her pencils"

Part 2: Ideate (5 minutes)

  • Sketch 3+ different solution ideas

  • Wild ideas welcome!

  • Don't judge yet—just generate!

  • Share ideas with partner

Part 3: Prototype (10 minutes)

  • Choose your best idea

  • Build a quick model using available materials

  • Doesn't need to be perfect—just enough to show the idea

  • Label important features

Part 4: Test & Feedback (3 minutes)

  • Show prototype to your partner

  • Get feedback:

  • What works?
  • What could be better?
  • Does it solve their problem?

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Write your partner's problem statement
  2. Sketch your solution idea
  3. Write: "Design thinking starts with..."
  4. Write: "The feedback I received was..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Empathy Reflection — "What did you learn about your partner?"
  2. Serving Others — "How does understanding people help us serve?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, thank you for helping us see others' needs. May we always design with love. Amen."

  • Simplified prototype

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Post design thinking process in classroom

  • This framework is used throughout the year

  • Encourage genuine empathy in interviews

  • Prototypes should be rough—that's the point!

Next: Session 2 — Ozobot Coding

docs.title: Interview boundaries
docs.text: Use a simple optional classroom organization problem, never demand disclosure of family hardship, disability or private frustration. The user can decline. A model's appearance is not proof of usefulness; each child records one actual user comment and proposed revision.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Computing / Ozobot Coding Time One 40-minute meeting, including cleanup Domains Catholic truthfulness, technology/computing Big idea A sensor reads a physical input; a command only works when its representation and hardware are compatible. Student objective "I can predict, test and debug one verified command on a line route." Why A reliable programmer checks documentation and actual output, rather than guessing commands. Catholic connection Honest claims and patient shared testing respect other people. St. Carlo Acutis is an example of service with technology; use the verified 2025 Vatican canonization homily, not a fabricated quotation. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C1 (record verified versus unverified claims); CST-T1 (optical input/output/troubleshooting); CST-T2 (command sequence/debugging). Technology Required primary: 2 charged Ozobots, a model-matched official color-code chart, markers. Tablets/OzoBlockly not required. Paper fallback assesses CT, not sensor calibration, color-code operation or real robot programming. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; no Year A, OzoBlockly or prior Ozobot experience assumed Prep / cleanup 20 minutes with charged kits and chart already obtained; charging and first model verification are advance work. 5 minutes in class.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Confirm model and loan; do not assume CSCOE inventory. Obtain its official chart from the kit or Ozobot color-code resources (also keep the existing family resource ozobot.com).
  2. VERIFICATION REQUIRED: code order, entry direction, line/segment widths and calibration procedure for the actual model. The previous unsourced U-turn/spin/turbo color list has been removed. Do not replace it with guessed colors.
  3. Choose one speed-change command from that chart, copy its exact colors/label to the board and record model / chart title / command / teacher observed output. Test it twice. Choose a slow setting, not a race/turbo challenge. If chart/testing unavailable, announce line-following observation only; command programming not observed, or use the paper pathway.
  4. Draw one smooth, unbranched black line on white paper, roughly 30 cm long, with rounded bends and clear start/end. Start around 5 mm width, then adjust to the model's instructions. Prepare a second line with the verified code on a straight portion. Follow the model guide for calibration; do not guess power-button timing.
  5. Pair pupils, final trio if odd. Two desk testing trays; assign seven one-minute rounds at most for thirteen teams.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth kit is spare. Seven two-robot rounds are an upper capacity bound.

  • Per student: pencil, evidence half-sheet.
  • Per team: 2 white paper sheets, paper robot token, 1 ruler, 4 markers (black/red/blue/green), 6 hand-drawn command/condition cards on team paper.
  • Class: 2 Ozobots, 2 chargers, 2 shallow testing trays, 1 official model chart, 2 teacher-demo paper sheets, timer/board.
  • Teacher: charging/calibration access and model guide. No tablet or internet during teaching.
Students Teams / rulers / tokens Team paper + 2 demo Markers (4 per team) Cards Slips / pencils Robots / chargers / trays 10 5 each 12 sheets 20 30 10 each 2 each 15 8 each 18 sheets 32 48 15 each 2 each 20 10 each 22 sheets 40 60 20 each 2 each 25 13 each 28 sheets 52 78 25 each 2 each

Share marker sets between adjacent teams if needed; it does not require shared robots to be increased. Robots/markers/rulers/cards/trays reusable; paper consumable.

docs.title: Vocabulary and teacher background
docs.text:
Sensor: hardware detecting information. Input: sensed line/color. Output: movement/light response. Command: instruction represented by a verified color pattern. Calibration: adjusting sensing for the surface. Debug: compare expected and actual, change one thing and retest.

Ozobot does not "think" like a person; onboard programs respond to sensor readings. A line-following demonstration is not proof that a pupil programmed it. A pupil-created, tested, compatible color command is additional programming evidence. Branch choices are not guaranteed without verified instructions.

Misconception: "Any colorful stripe is code." The model expects particular patterns and spacing. If asked: "Why didn't it obey?" Answer: "Check the model chart, entry direction, colors, spacing and calibration one at a time. An invented command cannot be fixed by trying harder."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Use only desk trays; prevent falls at table edges. Teacher handles charging and calibration controls; dry paper/clean hands. Keep robots/small parts out of mouths and away from younger children. No racing, stairs, liquids or marker ink on the robot. Cap markers during tests; stop motion before retrieval.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose. Original prayer: "God, help us be truthful and patient with one another." Ask: "What does a sensor detect? Does a robot understand kindness the way a person does?"
  2. 4-10: Model input/output. Teacher shows baseline line-following, then the preverified speed-change command. Point to model chart. "What input changed? What output did we actually see?" If not verified, explicitly teach only observed line following.
  3. 10-15: Paper prediction. Partners trace a line with a token and sequence cards: follow route, read named command, change speed. Use "slow" as a paper rule, not a claim about an unverified color combination. Swap reader/executor.
  4. 15-27: Draw/test slots. Teams draw a smooth line and the exact verified code, with correct entry direction from the chart. In one-minute slots across two trays, one child places/starts, another observes output, then swap on a retest. Trio adds chart checker. Teacher logs each child's real operation/command evidence; waiting teams trace and label route.
  5. 27-32: Debug one thing. Teacher chooses a failed line or code. Change line width, segment spacing or calibration one at a time, per guide. Retest. "Which change is supported by the result?"
  6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Child names input/output, points to the documentation used, and explains one expected/actual difference. Paper-only children identify a sequence bug; do not claim real color decoding.
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Teacher switches off/stores robots and counts kits; pupils cap markers, collect paper/tokens/rulers, clear trays and hand in slips.

docs.title: Unplugged / indoor alternative
docs.text: Use the same sequence/time windows. Teacher follows named paper rule cards with a token; partners insert a wrong instruction, find the first mismatch, replace it and retest. No invented color chart. Label CT sequencing/debugging observed; sensor/robot programming not observed. All pathways are indoor, independent of winter and internet.

docs.title: Success, troubleshooting, support and challenge
docs.text:
Success: child predicts a sequence, identifies input/output and documentation, and explains one debug change. Actual robot programming additionally requires that child's verified command construction/test, not simply watching line following. Score 1 guess; 2 trace with help; 3 independent prediction/debug/evidence distinction; 4 explains a hardware/model limitation.

  • No chart / unexpected response: stop the color-code claim; use observed line following or paper sequence and report missing programming evidence.
  • Leaves line: smooth solid width, plain white surface, gentle curves, calibration per model. No guessed "connect Ozobot" tablet requirement.
  • Support / Grade 3: pre-drawn route and adult marker assistance; child chooses/checks command and predicts.
  • Challenge / Grade 4: compare two trials, explain why successful sensing differs from successful paper execution; OzoBlockly is a later optional extension with separate setup.
  • 25 pupils: thirteen stationary teams, two trays, seven rounds; no multi-mission race. With one robot, use a teacher demonstration and log who actually tests.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We checked a robot's documentation, predicted a route and debugged one input. Paper tracing shows computational thinking, not actual robot sensing. Our Catholic connection was honest evidence and respectful shared work. Ask: "What did you verify before calling it a command?" Optional at home: create and test three named paper rules with a token; ozobot.com has optional resources. No robot purchase or homework.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 3 of 17

Students explore structural engineering by building tall towers using KEVA planks, testing height and stability.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand principles of tall structure stability

  • Apply engineering concepts: base, center of gravity

  • Build and test tower structures

  • Iterate and improve designs

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 KEVA Planks (from CSCOE library)

  • 📏 Measuring tape

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 📸 Camera for documentation

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Tower of Babel Reflection — The Bible story reminds us that our building should glorify God, not ourselves. We build to SERVE!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain." — Psalm 127:1

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you are the master architect of creation. Help us build structures that serve others and give glory to you. Guide our engineering today. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Tall Structures:
  2. "Why do people build tall?"
  3. Examples: Burj Khalifa, Empire State Building, church spires
  4. Engineering Principles:
  5. Wide Base — Distributes weight
  6. Center of Gravity — Keep it balanced
  7. Symmetry — Equal on all sides
  8. Triangles — Add strength
  9. Tower of Babel:
  10. Built for pride, not service
  11. Our towers serve people and honor God
  12. Challenge — "Build the tallest stable tower!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Tower Engineering (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: The Challenge (3 minutes)

  • Build the tallest FREESTANDING tower

  • Must stand for 10 seconds

  • Only KEVA planks—no tape, glue, etc.

  • Work in pairs

Part 2: Design & Build (18 minutes)

Design Phase (3 min):

  • Sketch tower design

  • Think: How will it be stable?

  • Plan base structure

Build Phase (12 min):

  • Start building!

  • Remember: Wide base, balanced design

  • Test stability as you go

  • If it falls—learn and rebuild!

Measurement (3 min):

  • Final measurement (must stand 10 seconds)

  • Record heights

  • Document what worked

Part 3: Analysis (5 minutes)

  • Compare towers:
  • What design features do the tallest share?

  • What caused towers to fall?

  • Class discussion: Design principles discovered

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your tower design (before and after)
  2. Record: "My tower reached ___ inches/cm"
  3. Write: "The most important design principle is..."
  4. Write: "If I did this again, I would..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Height Records — Celebrate tallest and most creative!
  2. Service Focus — "How do tall buildings serve people?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, may everything we build serve others and give glory to you. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Applied stability principles

  • Built freestanding structure

  • Iterated after failures

  • Analyzed successful designs

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Starter base structure

  • Partner with experienced builder

  • Lower height goal

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Height + weight-bearing challenge

  • Limited plank count

  • Design constraints (specific base size)

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Build towers at home with playing cards, blocks, or other materials! Research the tallest buildings in the world. What makes them stable? Visit a tall building or church steeple!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Reserve KEVA planks from CSCOE

  • Clear large floor/table space

  • Document with photos

  • Consider class tower record board

  • Great for collaboration skills

Previous: Session 2 — Ozobot Coding Next: Session 4 — Ecosystems

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence limits
docs.text: Cap towers at 60 cm on low stable surfaces; no climbing, standing beneath structures or dropping planks. Teacher-selected counter loads only for an optional test, at most 10. A wide base/symmetry may help but do not guarantee stability. Each pupil compares a measured height and one test-driven change; plank quantities and cleanup kit remain P1 preparation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 4 of 17

Students explore ecosystems and food webs, understanding how all living things are connected in God's design.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Define ecosystem, food chain, and food web

  • Identify producers, consumers, and decomposers

  • Create a food web for a local ecosystem

  • Appreciate the interconnection of all creation

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📸 Ecosystem pictures

  • 🧶 Yarn for food web activity

  • 📋 Organism cards

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🎨 Food web poster materials

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Kateri Tekakwitha — Study her faith with a verified biography; do not infer ecological beliefs/practices from Indigenous ancestry. Specific biography claims are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "For in him all things hold together." — Colossians 1:17

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you created an amazing world where everything is connected. Help us see your wisdom in ecosystems and be good stewards of your creation. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Ecosystem Definition:
  2. "A community of living things interacting with their environment"
  3. All living + non-living things work together
  4. Key Vocabulary:
  5. Producer — Makes own food (plants)
  6. Consumer — Eats others for energy
  7. Decomposer — Breaks down dead things
  8. Food Chain vs Web:
  9. Chain: Single path of energy (grass → rabbit → fox)
  10. Web: Multiple connected chains (more realistic!)
  11. St. Kateri — Saw God's design in nature

docs.title: Main Activity: Food Web Exploration (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Food Chain Building (6 minutes)

  • Start simple: sun → producer → consumer → decomposer

  • Minnesota examples:

  • Sun → grass → deer → wolf → bacteria

  • Sun → algae → minnow → bass → eagle

  • These examples begin with sunlight; some ecosystems have producers using chemical energy. Arrows show food/source -> eater, not the reverse.

Part 2: Food Web Game (10 minutes)

  • Students receive organism cards (plants, animals, decomposers)

  • Place organism cards on desks or the floor while seated; lay short yarn pieces between cards

  • Pass yarn to show connections:

  • "I am a plant, I'm eaten by..." → pass yarn

  • Continue building web

  • Observe connections without winding yarn around bodies or pulling it.

  • Remove one card; identify links no longer represented. This model does not prove the size or certainty of a real ecological cascade.

Part 3: Create Food Web Poster (8 minutes)

  • Choose ecosystem: forest, prairie, wetland, pond

  • Draw food web showing:

  • At least 3 producers
  • At least 4 consumers
  • At least 2 decomposers

  • Arrows showing energy flow

  • Label: Producer, Consumer, Decomposer

Part 4: Share & Discuss (2 minutes)

  • Show webs

  • "What happens if _____ disappears?"

  • Everything is connected!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw a simple food chain (4 organisms)
  2. Label: Producer, Consumer, Decomposer
  3. Write: "Everything is connected because..."
  4. Write: "We should protect ecosystems because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Connection Appreciation — "What surprised you about food webs?"
  2. Stewardship — "How can we protect ecosystems?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, your creation is beautifully connected. Help us protect the web of life you designed. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Defined ecosystem vocabulary

  • Participated in food web game

  • Created accurate food web

  • Understood interconnection

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-made organism cards with labels

  • Simplified food web

  • Partner work

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Research specific ecosystem

  • Include energy percentages

  • Create disruption scenario analysis

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Create a food web for your backyard or local park! What plants grow there? What animals live there? Research what eats what. Watch nature documentaries about ecosystems!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Food web yarn activity is powerful visual

  • Remove a card/link to discuss possible effects; no pulling on pupils

  • Connect to environmental stewardship

  • Consider outdoor observation if possible

Previous: Session 3 — Tower Challenge Next: Session 5 — Scratch Games

docs.title: SAFETY / scale / individual evidence
docs.text: No body yarn webs, knots around fingers/necks, tugging, live animal contact or unknown natural specimens. Indoor photos/cards replace outdoor work in unsafe weather. Start with one producer, two consumers and a decomposer, using source-checked diet cards; nine organisms in eight minutes is optional extension, not minimum. Each pupil draws a correctly directed food-to-eater arrow and states one evidence-supported relationship. Species diets remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED until cards are prepared.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 5 of 17

Students create interactive games in Scratch, learning about user input, variables, and game logic.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand game mechanics (input, feedback, scoring)

  • Program keyboard/mouse controls

  • Use variables for scorekeeping

  • Create a playable mini-game

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 💻 Computers with Scratch

  • 📋 Game planning templates

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🖥️ Projector for demo

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: God the Creator — God gave us creativity! Games bring joy and connection, reflecting God's gift of play.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "A cheerful heart is good medicine." — Proverbs 17:22

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for the gift of play and creativity. Help us create games that bring joy and connect people. Guide our programming today! Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Why Games?
  2. Games bring joy and connection
  3. Exercise minds and teach skills
  4. Combine art, logic, and creativity
  5. Game Elements:
  6. Input — How players control (keys, mouse)
  7. Feedback — What players see/hear
  8. Goals — What players try to achieve
  9. Score — How progress is measured
  10. Creativity as Gift — "God creates—so can we!"

docs.title: Main Activity: Game Creation (27 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Game Mechanics Demo (5 minutes)

  • Demo simple game:
  • Sprite moves with arrow keys
  • Catches/avoids other sprites

  • Score increases

  • Show key blocks:

  • "when [key] pressed"
  • "change x by 10"
  • "if touching [sprite]"
  • "change [score] by 1"

Part 2: Build Your Game (18 minutes)

Primary novice path (2 min): Use the bounded three-point click game in Weekly Year B Game Design Studio, specifically its two-stack starter. Create Score, reset to 0 on green flag, add 1 on click only if Score < 3. Trace four clicks as 0,1,2,3,3. This session uses that starter, not all four meetings. The game choices below are extensions for pupils already able to code.

Optional game types:

  • Maze navigator

  • Catching game

  • Avoid obstacles

  • Chase game

Build Step-by-Step (16 min):

  1. Player Controls (4 min)
  2. Add sprite for player

  3. Program arrow key movement:

    • Up: change y by 10
    • Down: change y by -10
    • Left: change x by -10
    • Right: change x by 10

  4. Game Elements (4 min)

  5. Add sprite to catch/avoid
  6. Make it move (glide randomly or bounce)

  7. Or create walls/obstacles

  8. Scoring (4 min)

  9. Create variable called "Score"
  10. Use a discrete click or wait for separation after contact; unguarded continuous touching can score every program cycle

  11. Display score on stage

  12. Polish (4 min)

  13. Add sounds for events
  14. Add instructions
  15. Test and debug!

Part 3: Playtest (4 minutes)

  • Swap with a partner

  • Play each other's games

  • Give feedback: What's fun? What's confusing?

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your game screen
  2. List the controls in your game
  3. Write: "The hardest part was..."
  4. Write: "Games bring joy by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Play Showcase — Quick demos of games
  2. Joy of Creating — "How did making this feel?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for creativity and play. Help us use games to bring people together. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Created working player controls

  • Implemented game logic

  • Used variable for scoring

  • Tested and improved

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Remix starter project

  • Simpler game (just movement)

  • Partner work

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Multiple levels

  • Timer feature

  • Two-player mode

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Share your game with family! Explore other Scratch games for inspiration. Discuss: What makes a game fun? Create games that the whole family can play together!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Scratch games are highly engaging

  • Allow time to play each other's games

  • Use private guest/offline local files; no public studio without school approval

  • Games can be continued/improved later

Previous: Session 4 — Ecosystems Next: Session 6 — Thanksgiving Design

docs.title: Scope and honest evidence
docs.text: Primary technology Required for executable Scratch. Paper token/score traces are a no-device CT path, not device operation. Every child predicts the fourth-input score and explains the guard/restart; log actual edit/run separately. Grade 3 uses counts 0-3; Grade 4 explains boundary behavior. Reserve 5 minutes of the build/polish block for saving/cleanup. Complete novice pacing and a local starter-file kit still need P1 work; home coding is optional.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes | Session: 6 of 17

Students design and create projects that express gratitude, combining engineering skills with thankfulness.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Reflect on gratitude and blessings

  • Apply design thinking to express thanks

  • Create a gratitude-focused project

  • Share appreciation with others

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📦 Various making materials

  • 📝 Gratitude planning sheets

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🎨 Art supplies

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Paul — His letters overflow with thanksgiving! "I thank my God every time I remember you." (Philippians 1:3)

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his love endures forever." — Psalm 107:1

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you have given us so many blessings! Help us have grateful hearts and creative minds to express our thanks to you and to others. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Thanksgiving Season:
  2. Time to pause and give thanks
  3. Not just food—gratitude for everything!
  4. St. Paul's Example:
  5. Started letters with THANKS
  6. Gratitude even in prison!
  7. Design Challenge:
  8. Use creativity to EXPRESS gratitude
  9. Create something that shows thanks

docs.title: Main Activity: Gratitude Design Sprint (26 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Gratitude Reflection (5 minutes)

  • List 10 things you're grateful for

  • Circle the 3 most important

  • Who do you want to thank?

  • What would make them feel appreciated?

Part 2: Design & Create (17 minutes)

Choose a Project:

Option A: Gratitude Machine

  • Build a mechanical card

  • Pull tab reveals message

  • Moving parts express thanks

Option B: Thank You Engineering

  • Design something useful for recipient

  • Phone holder, pencil organizer, bookmark

  • Personalized for them!

Option C: Gratitude Display

  • Create 3D representation of blessings

  • Show what you're thankful for

  • Interactive elements

Option D: Appreciation Invention

  • Design something NEW to help someone

  • Show gratitude through service

  • Prototype your idea

Build Process: 1. Sketch design (3 min) 2. Gather materials (2 min) 3. Build/create (10 min) 4. Add personal touches (2 min)

Part 3: Sharing Circle (4 minutes)

  • Share creations

  • Explain: Who is this for? What does it express?

  • Receive appreciation!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw your gratitude project
  2. Write: "I made this for... because..."
  3. List 5 things you're thankful for
  4. Write: "Gratitude is important because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Delivery Plan — "How will you give your project?"
  2. Gratitude as Practice — "How can we be grateful every day?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for every blessing! Help us always have grateful hearts. Bless our families this Thanksgiving. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Observation Checklist:

  • Reflected on blessings

  • Applied design process

  • Created meaningful project

  • Plans to share with recipient

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Focused project options

  • Partner support

  • Template provided

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Complex mechanisms

  • Multiple recipients

  • Written gratitude letter included

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Share your project with the recipient! Create a family gratitude list. Write thank you notes together. Start a gratitude practice: each day, name something new you're thankful for!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Time before Thanksgiving break

  • Help ensure projects reach recipients

  • Gratitude journaling builds positive mindset

  • Connect to school Thanksgiving activities

Previous: Session 5 — Scratch Games Next: Session 7 — Christmas Circuits

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit Grades 3-4 / Circuits / Christmas Circuits Time One 40-minute meeting, including 5-minute cleanup Domains Catholic audience care, science systems, technology tools, artistic communication Big idea / objective "I can identify a circuit gap, test a repair and design a clear Nativity message." Why Electricians troubleshoot safely; designers communicate for a reader. Catholic connection John 1:5 offers light imagery; the Nativity celebrates the Incarnation. Use the school's approved text; a lamp is a symbol, not a simulation of a miracle. Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (reader/roles), CST-S3 (path model), CST-T1 (test/repair), CST-A3 (message critique/revision). Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved hardware is required for real electrical evidence; paper is not circuit mastery. Prerequisites No Year A assumed; introduce open/closed now, not blinking or series/parallel. Prep / cleanup First inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 5 minutes included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text: Complete the OLP Snap Circuits guide preflight. Retrieve the same eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135) used in Year A, not a second electronics purchase. Use the matching manufacturer's battery/slide-switch/lamp project and counted parts. Place paper artwork beside the grid, not around electrical parts; never cover contacts or heat-producing parts.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
• Per pupil: pencil, evidence half-sheet and paper Nativity/message half-sheet.
  • Per team: one cardstock backing, diagram sheet and shared marker. No powered paper card or glued-in hardware; no mounting tape required.
  • Per station: approved kit, project parts/grid and dry tray. Battery type/count and checked reserves follow the guide, not an assumed two-AA count.
  • Teacher/class: instructions/setup card, board, timer, roster, dry storage and adult-controlled cells. Demo uses a station kit.
Pupils Teams / cardstock / diagrams Kits / trays Waves Student half-sheets / pencils 10 4 each 4 1 20 / 10 15 5 each 5 1 30 / 15 20 7 each 7 1 40 / 20 25 9 each 5 2 50 / 25

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and safety
docs.text:
Open/closed: interrupted/complete conducting path. Output: light response. Troubleshoot: isolate a fault, make one approved correction and retest. The battery supplies energy; current is charge flow. A resistor alone does not make a light blink. This lesson claims neither blinking nor series/parallel. Lamp results do not establish LED polarity understanding.

Misconception: extra lights can always be attached to the same supply. If asked: "Is our light the Bethlehem star?" No; it is an artistic symbol. The electrical test cannot reconstruct or prove the religious event.

SAFETY: obey the guide's model/age/holder gate. Adult isolates the battery holder before snap changes and checks before reconnecting. No pupil cell access, coin cells, household/USB power, live shorts, bare LEDs, extra branches, motors, fan blades or take-home circuits. Warm/smelly/leaking/damaged -> stop/report, adult isolates, OUT OF SERVICE. Keep paper beside, not over, the circuit.

docs.title: Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Audience/meaning. Prayer: "Jesus, help us share hope with care." Ask how a message can include a reader who cannot distinguish colors.
  2. 4-8: Teach from the beginning. Trace the approved return path; teacher tests OFF/ON and models isolation/inspection.
  3. 8-10: Predict. Each child draws the path and predicts both states; identify a gap in a drawn fault, not a live short.
  4. 10-22: Wave A. Follow the guide's isolated build, inspection, each child's two OFF/ON cycles and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Waiting teams draw a readable Nativity message labeled "light as a symbol of hope."
  5. 22-23: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 23-35: Wave B / revise. Remaining teams get the identical hardware routine. Finished teams explain the repair, peer-check their scene/message and revise one detail; at smaller enrollment use the window for retesting and individual checks. Ask each child: "Where was the gap? What did the retest show? What change helped your reader?"
  7. 35-40: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store all parts and cells, collect evidence and paper artwork. Note any physical turns still outstanding.

docs.title: Success, support and alternatives
docs.text:
Each child contributes to the isolated team build, operates both states twice, explains the full return path and observed repair, and revises a purposeful message. Record physical evidence separately as observed / prompted / not yet. Score 1 scene only; 2 prompted path; 3 independent path/repair and message evidence; 4 explains two possible open-path faults or model limits.

  • Grade 3/support: labeled diagram, words/symbols not color alone, oral record and motor assistance; keep each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 4/challenge: compare drawn faults one at a time; no additional loads.
  • 25 pupils: nine pairs/trios, five stations, two 12-minute waves. Inspection/access overruns mean deferred physical evidence, not rushed checks.
  • Failed kit: isolate/report, use a checked reserve or the guide's separate verified protected-AA route. Never mix the two systems' supplies.
  • Paper route: same timed windows using drawn paths/on-off tokens, modeled repair and message revision. Record circuit reasoning/art only; electrical assembly/operation not observed. All work is dry/indoors.

docs.title: Family snippet
docs.text:
We predicted and repaired a switched light, then revised a Nativity message. The light is a religious symbol, not evidence about a miracle. Name the actual hardware or paper route. Ask: "What broke the path, and what showed the repair worked?" Paper only goes home; no electrical homework or purchases.

docs.text:
