docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Investigation B / Forensic Science Time One 45-minute meeting Domains C, S, M; observational diagrams support reasoning Big idea Evidence can support a limited explanation without proving identity, motive, or guilt. Student objective I can compare paper observations, support a routing hypothesis, and state what I cannot conclude. Why Investigators and citizens must avoid accusations based on weak or incomplete evidence. Catholic connection Truthfulness, dignity, and protection of reputation; Catechism 2476-2479, paraphrased. Local standards / evidence CST-S1: individual observation/inference table; CST-M1: individual comparison of three stripe/tab counts; CST-C1: evidence-limited conclusion; CST-C2: explain why no person may be accused. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local codes, not official forensic standards. Technology None. Magnifier optional and not necessary. Difficulty / prerequisites Low-moderate; count to three, compare letters, distinguish "saw" from "think." No previous rotation required. Prep / cleanup First packet 15 minutes; repeat 5-10 minutes; cleanup 4 included. No staged crime or mystery supplies.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Use ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three. Keep teams seated with all four paper cards; no station crowding.
  2. Copy the four cards below exactly, one packet/team. The entire mystery, evidence, limitations, and teacher key are supplied. Board-copy works if printing unavailable.
  3. Say: "This is a fictional museum shipping puzzle, not a crime. No real student, teacher, or community member is a suspect."
  4. Prepare each student's four-row log: card / observation / inference / uncertainty. Do not collect fingerprints, handwriting, DNA, personal statements, or photos.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text:
Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Individual four-row log/exit, double-sided 1 sheet/student 10 15 20 25 Four evidence cards on 2 sheets 1 packet/team 8 sheets 10 sheets 14 sheets 18 sheets Ruler 1/team, optional for drawings; counts sufficient 4 5 7 9 Timer; teacher key 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1 Magnifier, optional 1/team 4 5 7 9

No liquids, chemicals, powders, food, biological material, props, or real personal evidence.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Observation: directly recorded feature. Inference: explanation based on evidence. Hypothesis: possible explanation to check. Compatible: could fit, not necessarily unique. Uncertainty: what evidence cannot settle. Dignity: every person's inherent worth, independent of an accusation or mistake.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
This is an introductory evidence-comparison model, not professional identification. Pattern similarity does not uniquely identify a source, and a routing record is not proof of who physically moved an object. Teach incomplete/conflicting evidence instead of a dramatic guilty reveal.

Common misconception: one matching clue identifies a culprit.

If asked, "Who did it?" Answer: That is not our question, and these records cannot identify a person. We ask which route is best supported and what remains unknown.

docs.title: Card 1 - the question and routing chart
docs.text:
At the fictional Paper Museum, a paper star display was packed for storage at 09:05. Its location has not been confirmed. Which bay was it most likely routed toward, based on this practice packet?

Bay Printed routing label Number of vertical stripes Tab letter A R17 2 A B R17 3 B C R17 3 C

All three bays share label R17: a label alone cannot decide the route.

docs.title: Card 2 - packing drawing
docs.text:
An invented diagram, not a scene photo, records:

Display: paper star
Label: R17
Stripes: | | |       (three, not to scale)
Tab: B
Drawing time: 09:05

This diagram describes the package, not a person. A drawing could contain an error.

docs.title: Card 3 - duplicate shipping log
docs.text:
09:05 package R17 recorded for Bay B
Log copied from the packing drawing by the museum's fictional system
09:10 automatic status: "location confirmation unavailable"

The log and drawing share a source: they are not two independent confirmations. The log does not confirm arrival.

docs.title: Card 4 - incomplete viewing record
docs.text:
09:12 fictional observer recorded a box near the A/B corridor.
The tab was hidden; the stripes were not visible.
Observer could not read the label.
No location-confirmation record is supplied.

This may describe a different box. It cannot prove or disprove Bay B routing.

docs.title: Teacher answer key - disclose only after analysis
docs.text: Best-supported routing hypothesis: Bay B. Card 2 matches its three stripes and B tab; Card 3 agrees but is copied, not independent. R17 alone also fits A/C; three stripes alone fit B/C. Card 4 is inconclusive. Arrival, handler identity, motive, misconduct, and guilt are not established. A student who correctly argues "B routing is supported, but actual location remains unknown" gives a stronger answer than "It is definitely in B." No chemical/fingerprint station or secret missing clue is needed.

docs.title: EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce fictional non-crime puzzle and Catholic truth/dignity boundary. Model observation versus accusation.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Read Card 1; everyone counts stripes/tabs and identifies why R17 alone is insufficient.
  3. 12-20 (8 min): Analyze Cards 2 and 3 for four minutes each. Each student records observation, inference, and uncertainty; point out shared source without giving final answer.
  4. 20-30 (10 min): Read Card 4 (4 min); compare three bay hypotheses (6 min). Team recorder collects evidence, but each student keeps a personal log.
  5. 30-38 (8 min): Neighboring teams exchange a 60-second explanation each; revise conclusion, then compare to teacher key. With nine teams, one three-team exchange uses the same time. No suspect vote.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: best-supported route with two features, one uncertainty, and why accusing a person would violate truth/dignity.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Collect logs, store packets, tidy.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: What did you actually observe? Which feature separates B from C? Are two copied records two independent witnesses? What would confirm arrival? How could an exaggerated conclusion harm a person's reputation?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student correctly compares all three stripe counts, identifies the B tab, cites two features supporting B routing, names unavailable arrival confirmation, and rejects identity/guilt claims. Grade 5 distinguishes observation/inference in two rows. Grade 6 additionally explains dependent sources and one alternative consistent with missing confirmation. Assessment values honest uncertainty, not guessing the teacher's "culprit."

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Students accuse a classmate: stop and restate fictional routing question; no role-play accusation. Teams disagree: ask which recorded feature supports each claim, not majority vote. Missing printing: draw chart and cards on board. Too easy: remove Card 3 and discuss how confidence changes; do not invent a person or powder test.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Inert paper evidence only. No unknown powders or substances, real student fingerprints, handwriting identification, profiling, real suspects, or biological samples. No touching/tasting/sniffing "evidence," crime-scene enactment, frightening media, or forensic-TV homework. No inference about character, race, disability, gender, faith, or honesty from a pattern. Protect truth and dignity explicitly.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: read cards aloud; use "I observed / I infer / I don't know" frames and enlarged symbols. Challenge: explain why three stripes do not uniquely select B. Grade 6: same cards; challenge identify shared-source dependence and design a nonpersonal confirmation record. Accept oral/drawn individual exits with identical evidence requirements.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: Primary lesson is wholly indoors and device-free; no weather, laboratory, or staged-scene dependency.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Return/count the two-sheet packets and rulers; keep individual logs. Recycle duplicates; there is no chemical or biometric storage.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text:
Explored: careful evidence reasoning. Did: compared fictional paper routing records, not crimes or people. Learned: a supported route is not proof of arrival or guilt. Catholic connection: truth and every person's dignity/reputation. Ask: "Which part of the puzzle remained uncertain?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Recreation and Leisure — Catholic tradition values healthy recreation! St. John Bosco used games and play to reach young people. Good games can build community and skills!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "A cheerful heart is good medicine." — Proverbs 17:22

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for the gift of play and creativity. Help us design games that bring joy, build skills, and respect the player. May our creativity honor you. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Game Design Philosophy:
  2. Good games are intentionally designed
  3. Balance challenge and fun
  4. Consider the player experience
  5. Ethics in Gaming:
  6. Games can be positive or harmful
  7. Our responsibility as creators
  8. Design for good: skill-building, connection, joy
  9. Programming Concepts:
  10. Variables — Track score, lives, progress
  11. Conditionals — If-then decisions
  12. Loops — Repeated actions
  13. Events — Respond to player input

docs.title: Main Activity: Game Development (31 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Game Design Document (7 minutes)

Answer These Questions: 1. Game Concept: - What type of game? (Maze, catch, quiz, adventure, platform) - What's the goal? - What makes it fun?

  1. Game Mechanics:
  2. How does the player control?
  3. What are the rules?

  4. How does the player win/lose?

  5. Player Experience:

  6. Is difficulty balanced?
  7. Is it appropriate for all ages?

  8. Does it build positive skills?

  9. Technical Plan:

  10. What sprites needed?
  11. What variables needed?
  12. What events trigger actions?

Part 2: Programming (20 minutes)

Build Your Game:

Step 1: Set Up (3 min)

  • Create sprites

  • Set up backdrop

  • Initialize variables (score, lives)

Step 2: Player Control (5 min)

  • Arrow key movement

  • Click interactions

  • Responsive controls

Step 3: Game Logic (7 min)

  • Scoring system

  • Win/lose conditions

  • Obstacle/enemy behavior

  • Level progression (if time)

Step 4: Polish (5 min)

  • Sound effects

  • Visual feedback

  • Instructions

  • Game over screen

Part 3: Playtesting (4 minutes)

  • Test each other's games

  • Give constructive feedback:

  • What's fun?
  • What's confusing?
  • What could improve?

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Game concept sketch

docs.text:

If no devices, execute score/rule cards and label algorithm/game simulation, not actual Scratch programming. No public accounts, private input, chat, or uploads. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

  • Created functional game

  • Used variables and conditionals

  • Considered player experience

  • Incorporated feedback

Students use design thinking to create meaningful projects that express or spread gratitude to their community.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Apply design thinking to gratitude expression

  • Create meaningful thanksgiving projects

  • Consider how technology can spread gratitude

  • Reflect on blessings and thanksgiving

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 💻 Computers (optional)

  • 📦 Craft/making materials

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🎨 Design supplies

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Gratitude reflection: Use the school's approved Examen resource. The unsourced attributed saying is removed; detailed Ignatius history VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus." — 1 Thessalonians 5:18

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for countless blessings we often overlook. Open our eyes to see your gifts. Help us design ways to spread gratitude to others. Make us grateful hearts. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (7 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude in Faith:
  2. Thanksgiving is a Christian virtue

  4. Gratitude changes our perspective

  7. Who needs to be thanked?

docs.title: Main Activity: Gratitude Project Design (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Empathize & Define (8 minutes)

Who Needs Gratitude?

  • Brainstorm people who serve us:
  • School staff (custodians, cafeteria, office)
  • Community helpers (firefighters, etc.)
  • Family members often overlooked
  • Elderly in community
  • Those who are lonely

Select Focus:

  • Choose recipient group

  • Research: What would be meaningful to them?

  • Define: "How might we show gratitude to ___?"

Part 2: Ideate (5 minutes)

  • Many ideas for gratitude expression:
  • Technology: App, video, website, digital card
  • Physical: Cards, gifts, service acts
  • Experience: Event, visit, performance

  • Combination approaches

  • Choose best idea for your skills/resources

Part 3: Create Gratitude Project (15 minutes)

Options (choose one):

Digital Gratitude:

  • Thank-you video

  • Gratitude slideshow

  • Digital card collection

  • Scratch appreciation animation

  • Website celebrating recipients

Physical Gratitude:

  • Handmade cards

  • Thank-you posters

  • Appreciation display

  • Gift creation

  • Service planning

Hybrid:

  • QR code linked to video

  • Physical card with digital component

  • Display with interactive element

Include:

  • Specific thanks (not generic!)

  • Personal touch

  • Meaningful message

  • Quality execution

Part 4: Share Plan (2 minutes)

  • How will you deliver gratitude?

  • When will it happen?

  • What's the expected impact?

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude recipients: ___

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:

Personal gratitude lists may stay private; no compulsory disclosure, spiritual ranking, or promised emotional benefit. The short Ignatius saying is not verified; use a sourced paraphrase instead. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Saint Carlo Acutis - canonized September 7, 2025 (source). Unsupported quotation removed; detailed technology biography VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up." — Galatians 6:9

docs.title: Main Activity: App Development (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: User Research & App Concept (8 minutes)

Design Thinking for Apps:

EMPATHIZE:

  • Who will use this app?

  • What do they need?

  • What problems do they have?

DEFINE:

  • "This app will help [user] to [need] by [solution]"

App Ideas (service-focused):

Build Your App:

Step 1: Design Screen (6 min)

  • Labels (text display)
  • Buttons (user interaction)
  • TextBox (user input)

  • Image (visuals)

  • Arrange layout

  • Set properties (colors, text)

Step 2: Add Logic (8 min)

  • Switch to Blocks view

  • Program behaviors:

  • When button clicked → do something
  • Change text
  • Play sound

  • Navigate screens

  • Use emulator or device

  • Does it work as intended?

  • What needs improvement?

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 5-6 | Duration: 45 minutes | Session: 9 of 17

Students explore the complementary relationship between science and faith, examining how Catholic thinkers have contributed to both.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Articulate the relationship between faith and science

  • Research Catholic contributions to science

  • Present findings on faith-science harmony

  • Counter the myth of faith-science conflict

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 💻 Research computers

  • 📋 Research guides

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 🖥️ Presentation tools

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: Faith and reason - Fides et Ratio, opening affirms their relationship. The quotation without an original source is removed.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "For since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made." — Romans 1:20

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you are the author of all truth—in faith and in science. Help us see how both reveal your wisdom. Give us minds eager to learn and hearts open to wonder. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. The Big Question:
  2. "Do faith and science conflict?"
  3. Common myth vs. reality
  4. History tells a different story!
  5. Catholic Church & Science:
  6. Catholic institutions contributed to learning; claims about who founded the "first universities" oversimplify varied histories and require verified sources.
  7. Monks preserved ancient knowledge
  8. Priests made major discoveries
  9. Vatican Observatory (active today!)
  10. Key Concepts:
  11. Faith = Trusting revelation from God
  12. Reason = Using our minds to discover
  13. Both seek TRUTH — They complement each other!
  14. Science asks "How?" Faith asks "Why?"

docs.title: Main Activity: Faith-Science Exploration (28 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Research Investigation (15 minutes)

Research Options:

Option A: Catholic Scientists

  • Fr. Georges Lemaître — Big Bang Theory

  • Gregor Mendel — Genetics

  • Bl. Nicolas Steno — Geology founder

  • Maria Gaetana Agnesi — Mathematics

  • Br. Guy Consolmagno — Current Vatican astronomer

  • Jérôme Lejeune — Genetics

Option B: Church & Science History

  • Medieval monasteries preserving knowledge

  • Cathedral schools → Universities

  • Vatican Observatory history

  • Pontifical Academy of Sciences

  • Church support for hospitals and science

Option C: Philosophy of Science & Faith

  • How do they relate?

  • What questions does each answer?

  • Famous quotes on harmony

  • Modern Catholic scientists' views

Research Questions: 1. What did you discover? 2. What does the source support, and what historical tensions or limits must we acknowledge? 3. What surprised you most? 4. How can you share this truth?

Part 2: Create Presentation (10 minutes)

  • Choose format:
  • Poster/infographic
  • Digital presentation
  • Video script

  • Essay outline

  • Include evidence and sources

  • Prepare to present

Part 3: Share Findings (3 minutes)

  • Quick presentations

  • Key insights

  • Discussion

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Topic researched: ___
  2. Key findings: ___
  3. Evidence that surprised you: ___
  4. Write: "Faith and science relate by..."
  5. Write: "I can share this truth by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Key Insight — "What changed your thinking?"
  2. Sharing Truth — "How will you correct the myth if you hear it?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "God, thank you for minds that can explore your creation. Help us share the truth that faith and science work together. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Local standards (not official): CST-C1 - individual's claim with verified source and limitation; CST-T3 - evaluate source provenance; CST-A3 - communicate findings accurately. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Do not require predetermined historical conclusions; biographies and institutional/current-role claims VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching. Use preselected printed sources when devices unavailable. Observation Checklist:

  • Researched effectively

  • Found compelling evidence

  • Articulated faith-science relationship

  • Created quality presentation

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Pre-selected resources

  • Partner research

  • Template for presentation

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Multiple sources compared

  • Philosophical depth

  • Create resource for others

docs.text:

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:

docs.title: Materials Needed

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Vatican Observatory — The Catholic Church operates an active astronomical observatory! Br. Guy Consolmagno is a Jesuit astronomer studying the universe for God's glory.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is mankind that you are mindful of them?" — Psalm 8:3-4

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, Creator of the universe, help us explore the wonders of space with awe and humility. The heavens declare your glory! Open our minds to the vastness of your creation. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Universe Scale:
  2. Earth → Solar System → Galaxy → Universe
  3. Galaxy/star counts are uncertain estimates; galaxies vary greatly in size and stellar population. Do not claim every galaxy has the same range.
  4. Vatican Observatory:
  5. Church operates real observatory
  6. Jesuit astronomers study space
  7. Faith seeks understanding of all creation
  8. Space Science Today:
  9. James Webb Space Telescope discoveries
  10. Mars exploration
  11. Searching for life
  12. Understanding our place in creation

docs.title: Main Activity: Space Exploration (28 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Universe Exploration (10 minutes)

Virtual Space Journey:

  • Use NASA resources or simulations

  • Scale of universe visualization

  • Recent discoveries from James Webb

  • Mars rover findings

Key Concepts:

  • Light years (distance, not time!)

  • Galaxy types and sizes

  • Life of stars

  • Planets beyond our solar system (exoplanets)

Wonder Questions:

  • Why did God create such a vast universe?

  • What does our small Earth tell us about God's love?

  • How does space exploration honor God?

Part 2: Space Design Challenge (15 minutes)

Choose ONE Challenge:

Challenge A: Space Mission Design

  • Design a mission to explore:
  • Mars colony
  • Europa (Jupiter's moon)
  • Asteroid mining

  • Exoplanet probe

  • Include: Objectives, vehicle design, timeline

Challenge B: Space Station Concept

  • Design future space station:
  • Purpose (research, tourism, manufacturing)
  • Life support systems

  • Transportation to/from Earth

  • Include: Layout, features, operations

Challenge C: Telescope/Observatory

  • Design next-generation observatory:
  • What will it study?
  • Where will it be located?

  • What technology needed?

  • Include: Capabilities, discoveries expected

Design Requirements:

  • Scientific accuracy (realistic)

  • Engineering considerations

  • Benefit to humanity

  • Sketch with labels

Part 3: Presentation (3 minutes)

  • Share designs

  • Explain scientific basis

  • Discuss potential discoveries

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Most amazing space fact: ___
  2. Design concept sketch
  3. Mission/design purpose: ___
  4. Write: "The universe shows God's glory because..."
  5. Write: "Space exploration matters because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Wonder — "What amazed you most about space?"
  2. Faith Connection — "How does the universe reveal God?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Creator God, the heavens declare your glory! Thank you for the wonder of space and minds to explore it. Help us always see your hand in creation. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-S3 - individual scale/model limit; CST-E1 - mission purpose, criterion, constraint; CST-C1 - distinguish evidence from reflection. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. docs.title: SAFETY

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand the Works of Mercy

  • Design solutions that serve others

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📋 Works of Mercy guides

  • 📦 Prototype materials

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 💻 Research resources

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: Works of Mercy — Traditional Catholic ways of living mercy in the world, both physical (corporal) and spiritual needs.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in." — Matthew 25:35

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear Jesus, you call us to see your face in those who suffer. During Lent, help us practice mercy in action. Guide our designs to truly serve "the least of these." Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Lenten Call:
  2. Season of preparation
  3. Prayer, fasting, almsgiving
  4. Growing in mercy and love
  5. Works of Mercy:

Corporal (Physical Needs): | Work | What It Means | |------|---------------| | Feed the hungry | Provide food for those without | | Give drink to the thirsty | Provide clean water access | | Clothe the naked | Provide clothing for those in need | | Shelter the homeless | Provide housing/shelter | | Visit the sick | Care for ill and suffering | | Visit the imprisoned | Support those in prison | | Bury the dead | Honor those who have died |

Spiritual (Soul Needs): | Work | What It Means | |------|---------------| | Counsel the doubtful | Help those struggling with decisions | | Instruct the ignorant | Teach and educate | | Admonish sinners | Lovingly correct wrongs | | Comfort the sorrowful | Be present for those grieving | | Forgive offenses | Practice forgiveness | | Bear wrongs patiently | Endure difficulties with grace | | Pray for living and dead | Intercede in prayer |

  1. Engineering for Mercy:
  2. How can design address these needs?
  3. Technology serving human dignity
  4. Our skills for God's kingdom

docs.title: Main Activity: Mercy Project Design (28 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Mercy Focus Selection (6 minutes)

Choose a Work of Mercy to Address:

  • Which work resonates with you?

  • Where do you see this need?

  • How might engineering help?

Research the Need:

  • Local examples of this need

  • Who specifically is affected?

  • What solutions exist?

  • What gaps remain?

Part 2: Solution Design (18 minutes)

Design Thinking for Mercy:

EMPATHIZE (3 min):

  • Put yourself in the position of someone experiencing this need

  • What would truly help?

  • What preserves dignity?

DEFINE (2 min):

  • "How might we [address work of mercy] for [specific group]?"

IDEATE (4 min):

  • Many possible solutions

  • Technology-enabled options

  • Low-tech options

  • Service design options

PROTOTYPE (7 min):

  • Choose best solution

  • Create detailed design or prototype:

  • Physical invention
  • App/digital solution
  • Service system

  • Awareness campaign

  • Document how it works

PLAN (2 min):

  • How could this be implemented?

  • What resources needed?

  • Who would help?

Part 3: Presentation (4 minutes)

  • Share mercy project designs

  • Explain work of mercy addressed

  • Discuss implementation possibilities

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Work of Mercy chosen: ___
  2. Need addressed: ___
  3. Solution design (sketch and explain):
  4. Write: "Mercy means..."
  5. Write: "Engineering serves mercy by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Commitment — "How will you practice mercy this Lent?"
  2. Jesus' Challenge — "Whatever you did for the least of these..."
  3. Closing Prayer — "Merciful Jesus, you showed perfect mercy. Help us practice mercy in action. Bless our designs and those they will serve. Amen."

Classroom dry model only; no patient, food-contact, safety, or clinical device. Real service implementation requires an approved adult partner and separate time; family service is optional. docs.title: Overview
docs.text:

Students investigate ecosystem dynamics and design engineering solutions that support or restore environmental balance.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand ecosystem interconnections

  • Analyze human impacts on ecosystems

  • Design solutions that restore balance

  • Apply creation care principles

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 📊 Ecosystem diagrams

  • 📦 Terrarium/model supplies (optional)

  • 📓 Engineering journals

  • 💻 Research resources

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Francis of Assisi — Patron saint of ecology! "Canticle of the Sun" celebrates all creation. Pope Francis named his environmental encyclical "Laudato Si'" after St. Francis's canticle.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it, the world, and all who live in it." — Psalm 24:1

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you created an interconnected world of amazing balance. Help us understand ecosystems and our responsibility to protect them. Make us faithful stewards of your creation. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (7 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Ecosystem Wonder:
  2. Everything is connected!
  3. Food webs, energy flow, nutrient cycles
  4. Remove one part, everything affected
  5. St. Francis & Ecology:
  6. Saw God in all creation
  7. "Brother Sun, Sister Moon"
  8. Called to care for "our common home"
  9. Human Impact:
  10. We are part of ecosystems
  11. Our choices affect everything
  12. Engineers can help restore balance

docs.title: Main Activity: Ecosystem Engineering (28 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Ecosystem Investigation (10 minutes)

Understand the System:

Choose an Ecosystem to Study:

  • Local ecosystem (your area)

  • Coral reef

  • Rainforest

  • Wetland

  • Prairie/grassland

  • Urban ecosystem

Map the Connections:

  • Producers (plants/algae)

  • Consumers (herbivores, carnivores)

  • Decomposers

  • Energy flow

  • Nutrient cycles

  • Water cycle role

Identify Threats:

  • What is harming this ecosystem?

  • Human-caused issues

  • Natural challenges

  • Cascade effects (one problem leads to others)

Part 2: Restoration Design (15 minutes)

Engineering for Ecosystem Health:

Problem Definition (3 min):

  • Specific ecosystem challenge

  • Root cause, not just symptom

  • "How might we restore/protect [specific issue]?"

Solution Design (10 min):

Categories of Solutions:

  • Habitat restoration — Rebuilding damaged areas

  • Species protection — Helping threatened organisms

  • Pollution reduction — Cleaning water, air, soil

  • Barrier systems — Protecting from invasive species

  • Monitoring technology — Sensors and tracking

  • Education/behavior — Changing human actions

Design Your Solution:

  • What exactly will it do?

  • How does it address root cause?

  • How does it work with nature, not against it?

  • What's the expected impact?

  • Sketch with explanation

Part 3: Solution Share (3 minutes)

  • Present ecosystem and solution

  • Discuss feasibility

  • Connect to local actions

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Ecosystem studied: ___
  2. Draw ecosystem web (connections)
  3. Problem addressed: ___
  4. Solution design sketch and explanation
  5. Write: "Caring for ecosystems honors God because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. St. Francis Prayer — Read excerpt from Canticle of the Sun
  2. Personal Commitment — "One thing I'll do for creation care..."
  3. Closing Prayer — "Creator God, help us be good stewards of ecosystems. Like St. Francis, may we see your beauty in all creation. Guide our hands to protect and restore. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Individual local check (not official): CST-S3 - food-web arrows from food to consumer and one perturbation; CST-A1 - labeled system model/limit; CST-C3 - stewardship tradeoff. Ecosystems change and are not guaranteed perfect balance. Primary indoor diagram only; no wild specimens, unknown water/soil, terrarium organisms, or habitat interventions. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

  • Understood ecosystem connections

  • Identified human impacts

  • Designed viable restoration solution

  • Connected to faith stewardship

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:

  • Research real restoration projects

  • Implementation planning

docs.text: "I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die." — John 11:25

Project Guidelines:

Work Time:

No public sharing/private data/home accounts; approved Scripture content VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

docs.text: Dear God, help us give our best effort in today's competition. May we honor you through excellence, celebrate others' success, and show good sportsmanship. Win or lose, may we glorify you. Amen.

docs.title: Main Activity: Robot Olympics (32 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Opening Ceremony & Setup (4 minutes)

  • Quick Sphero connection

  • Team/individual assignments

  • Rules review

Part 2: Olympic Events (24 minutes)

Event 1: Sprint Race (4 min)

  • Straight-line speed

  • First to finish line wins

  • Controlled speed at most 20; score accuracy and debug explanation, not maximum speed

  • Scoring: Gold, Silver, Bronze + participation

Event 2: Slalom Course (5 min)

  • Navigate through obstacles

  • Accuracy matters

  • Timed runs

  • Programming precision required

Event 3: Light Show (4 min)

  • Creative LED programming

  • Music/rhythm coordination (optional)

  • Judged on creativity and complexity

  • All participate, voted favorites

Event 4: Cooperative Target (4 min)

  • One robot at a time stops inside a marked target, no contact with others.
  • Teams predict, test, and correct duration at speed at most 20.
  • Score accuracy and explanation; no pushing, collisions, or tournament bracket.

Event 5: Obstacle Course (4 min)

  • Complex course with multiple challenges:
  • Speed section
  • Precision section

  • Problem-solving section

  • Most accurately explained and safely controlled route meets the criterion; no speed prize

Event 6: Innovation Freestyle (3 min)

  • Show off your best skill!

  • Any program you've created

  • Demonstrate growth since Session 2

  • Celebration of learning!

Part 3: Awards Ceremony (4 minutes)

  • Medal/certificate for each event

  • Special recognitions:

  • Best Sportsmanship
  • Most Creative
  • Most Improved
  • Team Spirit

  • Perseverance Award

  • Everyone recognized for something!

docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-T2 - individual program trace/debug; CST-E2 - evidence-based retest; CST-C2 - safe cooperative roles. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.text:
Adult checks robot/lane condition; 1 m lane per active robot plus 50 cm observer boundary. One robot/lane, short runs at most 1 second, Stop before retrieval, no collisions or shaking. At 25 students use three lanes in rounds; six events are optional, not guaranteed mastery. No-device paper grid route assesses algorithm reasoning only, not robot programming/operation. Observation Checklist:

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Grades: 5-6 | Duration: 45 minutes | Session: 15 of 17

Students explore energy transformation and simple machines, applying physics concepts to engineering challenges.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

  • Understand energy types and transformations

  • Apply simple machine principles

  • Design machines that transform energy

  • See God's design in physics

docs.title: Materials Needed
docs.text:
• 🔧 Simple machine materials

  • 🧱 KEVA Planks/construction materials

  • 📏 Measuring tools

  • 📓 Engineering journals

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Leonardo da Vinci — Catholic artist and inventor who saw no conflict between faith and science! Designed amazing machines centuries ahead of his time.

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: Ecclesiastes 3:14 is a religious reflection, not a physics statement or proof of energy conservation. Read from the school's approved Bible if desired; no scientific law is inferred from the verse.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, you created a universe of amazing order where energy transforms but is never lost. Help us understand these principles and use them to engineer solutions. Your design is perfect! Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (8 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Energy Fundamentals:
  2. Energy cannot be created or destroyed—only transformed!
  3. Types of energy:
    • Kinetic — Energy of motion
    • Potential — Stored energy (height, elastic, chemical)
    • Thermal — Heat energy
    • Electrical — Moving electrons
    • Sound — Vibration energy
    • Light — Radiant energy
  4. Simple Machines:
  5. Tools that make work easier
  6. Six types:
    • Lever — Lifts/moves with fulcrum
    • Wheel & Axle — Rotates to reduce friction
    • Pulley — Changes direction of force
    • Inclined Plane — Ramp reduces force needed
    • Wedge — Splits or separates
    • Screw — Inclined plane wrapped around cylinder
  7. Conservation:
  8. God's design: Energy conserved
  9. Nothing is lost, only transformed
  10. Physics describes conservation within specified systems; religious reflection is distinct evidence.

docs.title: Main Activity: Energy Engineering (28 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Energy Transformation Investigation (10 minutes)

Build Energy Chain:

  • Create system showing energy transformations:
  • Start: Potential energy (height)
  • Transform to: Kinetic energy (motion)
  • Transform to: Kinetic (hit something)
  • Transform to: Sound (noise)

Simple Example: Rube Goldberg Starter

  • Ball on ramp (potential → kinetic)

  • Ball hits lever (kinetic → kinetic)

  • Lever lifts something (kinetic → potential)

  • Continue the chain!

Part 2: Simple Machine Challenge (15 minutes)

Engineering Challenge: Design and build a system that:

  • Uses at least 2 different simple machines

  • Accomplishes a task (lift, move, separate, etc.)

  • Shows clear energy transformations

  • Is as efficient as possible

Design Ideas:

  • Lifting system (lever + pulley)

  • Vehicle (wheel & axle + inclined plane)

  • Nonlaunching lever that raises a light paper load; no catapult or projectile

  • Ball run with multiple energy transformations

Build & Test:

  • Construct your machine

  • Test multiple times

  • Measure/observe energy transformations

  • Improve efficiency

Part 3: Demonstration (3 minutes)

  • Show machines working

  • Explain energy transformations

  • Identify simple machines used

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Draw and label your machine
  2. Simple machines used: ___
  3. Energy transformations (chain):
  4. Write: "Energy conservation shows God's design because..."
  5. Write: "Simple machines help by..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (4 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Physics Wonder — "What amazed you about energy?"
  2. Order in Creation — "How does energy conservation reflect God's design?"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Creator God, thank you for the order and consistency in your creation. Help us use these principles to build things that serve others. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-S3 - individual energy-transfer chain including thermal/sound pathways; CST-E2 - measured before/after task test; CST-C1 - distinguish physical law from religious reflection. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Do not claim quantitative efficiency without measured input/output energy.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text:
Adult inspects low ramps/lever supports; use large soft balls inside a catching tray, at most 15 cm height and 100 g paper/packet loads. No catapults, projectiles, finger pinch traps, electrical improvisation, or body-weight testing. Classroom model stays indoors; specific historical claims about Leonardo's beliefs VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

  • Identified energy types

  • Built working machine

  • Explained transformations

  • Connected to simple machines

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Simpler machine focus

  • Partner construction

  • Guided design

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Complex Rube Goldberg

  • Efficiency calculations

  • Multiple simple machine types

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Find simple machines at home (scissors = lever, screwdriver = wheel & axle, etc.)! Track energy transformations in your day. Build a simple Rube Goldberg machine together. Research Leonardo da Vinci's inventions!

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Simple materials work great

  • Safety with moving parts

  • Energy vocabulary important

  • Great outdoor activity option

docs.title: Main Activity: Innovation Lab (31 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Problem Discovery (5 minutes)

Find a Problem Worth Solving:

  • Observe: What frustrates people around you?

  • Listen: What do people complain about?

  • Research: What needs exist?

Good Problems:

  • Affect real people

  • Haven't been perfectly solved

  • Match your skills/resources

  • You care about solving

Choose Your Focus:

  • Write problem statement

  • Who is affected?

  • Why does it matter?

Part 2: Invention Development (22 minutes)

Full Design Thinking Cycle:

1. EMPATHIZE (3 min):

  • Deep understanding of people with this problem

  • What's their experience?

  • What have they tried?

  • What would help most?

2. DEFINE (2 min):

  • Clear problem statement

  • "How might we [solve problem] for [users]?"

3. IDEATE (4 min):

  • Generate many solutions

  • Wild ideas welcome!

  • Build on possibilities

  • Select promising approach

4. PROTOTYPE (10 min):

  • Build your invention!

  • Options:

  • Physical prototype
  • App/digital solution
  • Combined approach

  • System/service design

  • Focus on demonstrating the concept

5. TEST (3 min):

  • Does it work?

  • Get quick feedback

  • Note improvements

Part 3: Pitch Preparation (4 minutes)

  • Prepare 2-minute pitch:
  • Problem you're solving
  • Who benefits
  • Your solution
  • How it works
  • Why it matters

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Invention name: ___
  2. Problem solved: ___
  3. User group: ___
  4. Solution sketch and description:
  5. Write: "I'm proud of this because..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Preview — Quick invention previews
  2. Celebration — "You are all inventors!"
  3. Closing Prayer — "Thank you, God, for creativity and the ability to solve problems. Bless these inventions and the people they will serve. Amen."

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Individual local check (not official): CST-E1 - criterion and constraint; CST-E2 - test/revision evidence; CST-C2 - respectful user decision. Use one dry cardboard/paper function, not "everything" from the year; a mockup is not a validated working device. No bodily, clinical, launching, chemical, mains, or improvised battery projects. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Observation Checklist:

  • Identified real problem

  • Applied design process

  • Created working prototype

  • Prepared presentation

docs.title: For Students Who Need Support
docs.text:
• Simpler problem focus

  • Guided prototyping

  • Partner work

docs.title: For Advanced Students
docs.text:
• Complex multi-part invention

  • User testing incorporated

  • Implementation planning

docs.title: Wonder at Home 🏠
docs.text: Family Activity: Practice your pitch for family! Get feedback to improve. Research young inventors and their stories. Discuss: What problems in our world need solving? How could you contribute?

docs.title: Teacher Notes
docs.text:
• Second-to-last session

  • Inventions ready for exhibition

  • Encourage originality

  • Consider competition or showcase

docs.text:

Students present their portfolios and inventions, celebrating two years of growth and achievement in C-STREAM.

docs.text:
By the end of this session, students will:

docs.text:

docs.title: Theme
docs.text: Celebrating Gifts — Each person has unique gifts from God. Celebrating achievements recognizes God's generosity in us!

docs.title: Scripture
docs.text: "Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Come and share your master's happiness!" — Matthew 25:23

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text: Dear God, thank you for two amazing years of learning and creating. Thank you for the unique gifts in each student. As we celebrate, help us give you glory for all we've accomplished. Amen.

docs.title: Opening Circle (6 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Year B Complete!
  2. "17 sessions of incredible work!"
  3. Review Year B highlights with photos
  4. Two-Year Journey:
  5. Year A accomplishments

  7. Total transformation!

docs.title: Main Activity: Exhibition (31 minutes)
docs.text:
Part 1: Portfolio Curation (8 minutes)

Select Your Best:

  • Review Year B engineering journal

  • Choose highlights:

  • Design thinking masterpiece
  • Best programmed project
  • Favorite engineering build
  • Proudest service moment

  • Original invention

  • Prepare exhibition display

Reflection Questions:

  • What was your biggest growth?

  • What surprised you?

  • What will you remember most?

  • How did faith connect?

Part 2: Exhibition Gallery (15 minutes)

Gallery Walk:

  • Set up displays

  • Rotate as exhibitors and visitors

  • Present your work:

  • What you created
  • Skills demonstrated
  • What you learned

  • Faith connections

  • Ask thoughtful questions

  • Appreciate peers' work

Part 3: Invention Showcase (5 minutes)

  • Innovation Lab inventions

  • 1-2 minute pitches

  • Celebrate creativity and service focus!

Part 4: Awards & Recognition (3 minutes)

Year B Certificates:

  • "Design Thinker"

  • "Code Master"

  • "Engineering Architect"

  • "Science Investigator"

  • "Innovation Champion"

  • "Faithful Creator"

  • "Service Designer"

  • Custom recognitions

Every student recognized for unique strengths!

docs.title: Engineering Journal (5 minutes)
docs.text: Final Year B Entry: 1. "This year I became..." 2. "My proudest achievement..." 3. "Faith and STREAM connect because..." 4. "I will use my gifts to..." 5. "My future innovation will be..."

docs.title: Closing Circle (3 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Gratitude Circle — Each person shares one thanks
  2. Future Vision — "What will you create/become?"
  3. Final Blessing:

Dear God, Thank you for this Year B journey of growth and discovery. Thank you for creative minds and compassionate hearts. Thank you for showing us that faith and innovation belong together. Bless these young engineers, scientists, and designers. May they continue to grow in wisdom and skill. May they use their gifts to serve you and love others. May they never stop wondering, creating, and believing. We ask this through Christ our Lord. Amen.

🎓 CONGRATULATIONS, GRADUATES! 🎓

docs.text:
Local standards (not official): CST-E3 - tested technical result and limit; CST-A3 - caption revision; CST-C3 - resource example. Year B may precede A; assess actual attended lessons. Continue Your Journey:

Year A/B may be taken in either order. Coverage is supplemental and does not certify a comprehensive subject curriculum or individual mastery.

docs.title: 🌟 Kindergarten Bi-Weekly C-STREAM
docs.text:
17 Sessions | 25 Minutes Each | Every Other Week

This folder contains 17 documents and 17 teaching meetings (425 minutes) for schools with bi-weekly C-STREAM. It is an alternative to the weekly track, not an equally deep replacement for its 32 meetings. Plant care between meetings is an adult responsibility, not an eighteenth STREAM session.

See the Kindergarten review and complete audit. All 17 documents are complete instructional references after autonomous closure. Read K routines with the selected lesson; actual kit/school checks and classroom trials remain.

Source gate: unverified inherited quotations/biographies were omitted from rewritten minimum paths. CST codes are local. The source-verified arts candidates need MDE-copy/school review; science/math identifiers and diocesan approval remain unverified.

Minimum pathway gate: use the single reference sequence and named alternative. Pictures/models do not establish live observation or device operation when those are the target. Physical help requires consent. No homework, home device, family donation or purchase is a prerequisite. All minimum pathways are indoors.

Quantity convention: for 10/15/20/25 pupils, pairs with a final trio make 5/7/10/12 active teams. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment; all supply totals include that reserve.

docs.title: 📋 Session Overview
docs.text: Session Title Theme Key Activity Session 01 Welcome to Wonder Introduction Safe Indoor Detail/Question Session 02 God's Amazing World Creation Nature exploration Session 03 Building Basics Engineering Block towers Session 04 Colors & Light Science Light exploration Session 05 Simple Machines Engineering Ramps & rolling Session 06 Thanksgiving Wonder Gratitude Thankful collage Session 07 Advent Light Wonder Star & light activities Session 08 Winter Science Seasons Ice & snow exploration Session 09 Our Catholic School Community Respectful Message/Privacy Choice Session 10 Weather Wonder Science Two Labeled Weather Records Session 11 Growing Things Life Science Planting seeds Session 12 Animal Homes Engineering Habitat building Session 13 Easter New Life Renewal Butterfly life cycle Session 14 Sound & Music Arts Vibration/Four-Beat Phrase Session 15 Helping Others Service/Computing Respectful Message/Tested Algorithm Session 16 Water Wonder Science Sink/float exploration Session 17 Year Celebration Exhibition Portfolio sharing

docs.title: 🎯 Learning Goals
docs.text:
By the end of the year, Kindergarten students will:

  • ✅ Approach the world with wonder and curiosity

  • ✅ Observe with safe senses and ask questions; never taste nature materials

  • ✅ Build simple structures and compare tests; act out and correct a two-command picture algorithm in Session 15

  • ✅ Understand that faith and discovery go together

  • ✅ Show kindness and care for others and creation

  • ✅ Share what they've learned with others

docs.title: Optional library additions; availability not assumed
docs.text:
• KEVA or ordinary wooden blocks; 100/160/200/260 for 10/15/20/25 students

  • Pattern Blocks

docs.text:
• Construction paper

  • Craft sticks

  • Playdough

  • Crayons/markers

  • Large adult-drawn nature pictures or inspected clean specimens; no collecting prerequisite

docs.title: 👨‍👩‍👧 Family Connection
docs.text:
Family activities are optional invitations, never homework or required materials. Copy the unit snippets in the review; do not imply that every lesson used hardware or that attendance proves grade-one readiness. Consider:

  • Sending home a bi-weekly Wonder Journal page

  • Creating a classroom photo book families can check out

  • Hosting a Family Wonder Night in spring

Kindergarten Bi-Weekly C-STREAM — Where wonder meets discovery!

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Wonder / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, A; careful observations can become questions Objective / why "I can show a detail, ask a question and care for shared materials." Inquiry begins with noticing. Catholic connection Wonder and stewardship are actions, not simply an opening prayer. Local standards CST-C3: material care; CST-S1: detail/question; CST-A1: observation drawing. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Draw three large nature cards per kit: a leaf with lines, a tree with branches, and a flower with petals. Drawings can be ordinary paper, no printing. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active pair/trio teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: three large cards 15 24 30 39 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and demonstration from one kit. No journal purchase required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Observe = notice a detail; question = something to find out; model = picture, not the living thing; stewardship = careful care. Misconception: a guessed feature is an observation. Ask the child to point to it. If asked whether the drawing grows, explain it represents a living thing. Paper primary: no tasting, unknown specimens, close smelling, small rocks, sharp shells or required outdoor collection. Tactile drawings/read-aloud support access.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Introduce noticing and care; original school prayer optional.
  2. 4-8: Model a visible line and "I wonder what it does"; distinguish picture observation from a claim about a real specimen.
  3. 8-17: Partners choose cards, notice details and each draw/indicate one. Swap chooser/reporter roles; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Each child shows an actual detail, asks/selects one question and demonstrates care by returning a shared card intact.
  5. 21-25: Date/retain drawings, count three cards per kit, return crayons, clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Assess detail, question, representation and material care, not enthusiasm or handwriting. Ask "What did you see? What do you wonder?" Support: two pictured choices and scribing. Challenge: compare two details. No prepared cards: teacher draws the three examples on the board; keep the same individual checks. All work is indoors, device-free and no home collection.

Family: We noticed and represented a detail and asked a question. Ask, "What could you point to?" Optional conversation only.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Observation and sorting / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, M; a sorting rule uses a feature we can check Objective / why "I can sort pictures, show the rule and represent two groups." Organizing evidence makes comparisons possible. Catholic connection Care for creation and reusable classroom resources. Local standards CST-C3: care/reuse; CST-S1: visible feature; CST-M2: grouped representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 10 minutes first cards / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Draw six >=5 cm cards: three leaves with visible lines, three smooth oval stone pictures without lines. The rule is lines/no lines in these pictures, not a universal claim about all leaves/stones. Two paper sorting mats per kit. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: six cards 30 48 60 78 Kit: two mats 10 16 20 26 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and demonstration from a kit. No natural specimens required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Sort = group by a rule; feature = visible detail; represent = show grouped information; reuse = use again. Different defensible rules are possible. Misconception: there is no need for evidence because every answer is right. If asked where a difficult card belongs, inspect the chosen feature or revise the rule, rather than guessing an unseen biological property. No food, acorns, feathers, unknown rocks or nature collection; large paper only.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall careful noticing and conserving shared materials.
  2. 4-8: Model lines/no lines on two mats; intentionally misplace a card and correct it using its visible feature.
  3. 8-17: Each child sorts at least three of the six cards in a full turn, points to the rule, then draws/indicates two groups. Begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child explains a card's placement, represents a group and shows a care/reuse action. Ask "What feature supports this group?"
  5. 21-25: Save dated records, count six cards/two mats per kit, clear.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and family copy
docs.text:
Check visible rule, correct placement and grouped representation separately. Support: two cards first, tactile line/no-line drawings and scribing. Challenge: choose a second visible rule and explain changed group membership. Mixed rules: name one rule and restart, not a competition. No cards: draw six forms on the board and let children indicate groups individually. Entire pathway is indoors; no collections, purchases or donations.

Family: We sorted by a visible rule and showed two groups. Ask, "What made your pictures belong together?" No routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Structures / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, E, M; a changed base can affect stability Objective / why "I can test, change and retest a tower using the same blocks." Evidence supports improvement. Catholic connection Care for shared blocks and respect a partner's work. Local standards CST-C3: care; CST-E2: retest; CST-M1: count/compare common measure. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and quantities
docs.text:
Read K routines. Inspect/pretest a low six-block tower. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits for active 5/7/10/12 teams; no brand/loan required. Mark a 10 cm comparison on each ruler.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: 20 large blocks 100 160 200 260 Kit: tray; ruler 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and one kit for demonstration, returned before practice.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Base = bottom supports; stable = unaided standing; retest = repeat the same check; compare = identify a difference. Criterion is ten seconds, not tallest. Misconception: a fall means the child failed. It is information about this model. If asked about height, use the same marked ruler next to both attempts; no untaught centimeter reading is required. Seated low structures; no throwing, shaking, tall competition, splintered pieces or standing on furniture.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Name careful sharing and the ten-second unaided criterion.
  2. 4-8: Count six blocks, demonstrate a low base and common measuring reference.
  3. 8-17: Partners test, change only base arrangement and retest with the same six blocks/time. Swap builder/tester turns; begin individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child counts the selected blocks, points to a tested change, compares stability and above/below the same 10 cm reference. Save two results.
  5. 21-25: Return/count all 20 blocks, retain evidence, collect rulers and clear.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and family copy
docs.text: Record count/common comparison and actual redesign result, not participation. Ask "What changed? What stayed the same?" Support: adult-started three-block structure and pointing; record reduced task. Challenge: repeat to check consistency. Both fall: try flat pieces on a broader base; preserve earlier results. Few kits: groups <=3 with full turns, same test. No safe blocks: defer construction evidence rather than call a drawing a tested tower. All work indoors. Family: We compared two fair tower tests. Ask, "What did your base change do?" No homework or purchase.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Shadows / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea S, T, A; a shadow changes when an object changes position relative to light Objective / why "I can predict a shadow change, test it and show the result." A fair comparison needs a kept-same condition. Catholic connection Honest observation and care; no spectrum/color-mixing mastery is claimed. Local standards CST-S2: comparison; CST-T1: light control/input-output; CST-A1: result representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None for digital devices / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Inspect secure flashlight covers; adults handle cells. Set lamp and white screen 30 cm apart; mark cutout positions 10 and 20 cm from the lamp. Pretest visible shadows, then keep the lamp/screen positions fixed. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: flashlight; screen; >=8 cm cutout; ruler 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Student: result half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster; demonstrate with one budgeted kit.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Source = makes light; shadow = area receiving less light because an object blocks it; predict = expectation; evidence = result observed. Misconception: a prism always produces a visible rainbow. No prism, broken CD or filter activity is required or scored. If asked why shadows change, point to the light paths/model positions; compare actual size rather than promise every setup yields a particular result. No beams at eyes, Sun viewing, dark walking room, lasers, glass or student battery access.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Identify lamp control and ask what happens behind the cutout.
  2. 4-8: Model one position, then change only cutout distance. Look at screen.
  3. 8-17: Partners predict/test both marked positions, swap roles, and each draw/point to a result. Teacher begins individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child shows changed/kept-same conditions, actual outcome and flashlight input/output; accepts an unchanged or unclear result honestly.
  5. 21-25: Date/save drawings, switch off/count lights and shapes, clear.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and family copy
docs.text: Check comparison, control and communicated observation, not rainbow colors. Ask "What moved? What stayed still? What did you see?" Support: adult handles lamp under child's direction; large tactile cutout and scribed report. Challenge: repeat the same positions. No shadow: teacher adjusts lamp/screen setup before pupils test and records the adjustment; no unsafe darkening. Missing safe lights: demonstration/model only, student operation deferred. All primary work is indoors. Family: We compared shadows with one changed condition. Ask, "What moved in your test?" No homework or Sun observation.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Ramps / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, E, M; shape and ramp slope affect observed movement Objective / why "I can compare the same object on two low ramps and report roll, slide or stay." Fair tests help us understand useful tools. Catholic connection Accessible routes serve people; a toy ramp is not approved for a person. Local standards CST-C2: access need; CST-S2: fair comparison; CST-E1: contained low-ramp criterion; CST-M1: compare rise. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Adult pretests a smooth 30 cm ramp into a catch tray at rises 5 and 10 cm. Stabilize supports; mark the same release point. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12. Ball is >=5 cm, blocks have no loose parts.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: ramp; tray; ball; large test block; ruler 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Kit: two stable low supports 10 16 20 26 Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster, adult-only setup scissors, one budgeted demo kit.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Ramp = inclined surface; roll = turn while moving; slide = move without rolling; stay = no visible movement. Gravity does not become stronger at the taller classroom ramp. Do not infer speed from travel distance or guarantee every block stays. If asked which is a wheelchair ramp, explain our desk model does not meet real construction/accessibility standards. No launches, races, marbles, body ramps, heights above 10 cm or floor traffic. Teacher changes supports; keep hands away from the contained descending object.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Explain accessible-route purpose and contained tabletop criterion.
  2. 4-8: Compare marked rises; model release without pushing and three outcome words.
  3. 8-17: Children predict/test ball and block; teacher resets rise, children repeat the same object from the same point. Swap turns; begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child names actual motion, indicates changed rise/kept-same object and uses ruler/reference to compare gentle versus steeper.
  5. 21-25: Save records, remove elevated boards safely, count pieces and clear.

docs.title: Success, access, troubleshooting and family copy
docs.text: Check actual outcome, fair comparison, low-ramp constraint and a service reason. Ask "Was it rolling, sliding or staying? What changed?" Support: adult releases under child's direction; two pictured outcomes first. Challenge: repeat to check agreement, never change several variables at once. Object escapes tray: stop, contain/stabilize before resuming. No safe ramp: teach a labeled drawing and defer movement evidence. Indoors; no home test needed. Family: We compared the same object at two low ramp rises. Ask, "Did it roll, slide or stay?" No purchases or routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Gratitude communication / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A; a picture can express a specific appreciative message Objective / why "I can show thanks, explain my picture and make its meaning clearer." Art communicates to people. Catholic connection Gratitude with dignity; no required private family/religious disclosure. Local standards CST-C2: respectful recipient; CST-A3: communication/feedback/revision. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Offer a school helper or trusted recipient; children can instead appreciate a safe familiar aspect of creation. No assumptions about household resources. Model a simple school-helper picture; use the same materials budget.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: message sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and classroom envelope. No mural-size paper, treats, nature collection or glue required. Pair children; final trio rotates listening.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Gratitude = appreciation; recipient = whom a message is for; feedback = helpful response; revise = make meaning clearer. Misconception: a finished picture automatically communicated its intent. Ask a listener what it means. If asked about artistic quality, judge the message, not realism. School-approved crayons/paper, no acorns, food, sharp specimens or private images.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Invite a brief original prayer/thanks and a specific appreciative idea.
  2. 4-8: Model a picture a partner cannot yet interpret; add a detail explaining it.
  3. 8-17: Each child draws/points/directs a grateful picture. Partner describes its meaning; child revises a mark or explanation. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child identifies recipient/idea and explains the actual change; accept speech, pointing or dictated meaning.
  5. 21-25: Share concurrently, retain dated communication evidence, return crayons and clear. No 25-child gratitude queue.

docs.title: Success, support, challenge and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check respectful intent and clearer communication, not prayer participation. Ask "What do you want someone to understand? What helped them understand?" Support: two picture choices and scribing. Challenge: convey the idea with fewer marks but a clear reason. No class-display area: retain individual sheets. Child declines private topic: offer a classroom object/helper or creation care. Fully indoors; no school-event date or home contribution required.

Family: We communicated appreciation and revised a message after feedback. Ask, "How did you make your idea clearer?" Optional conversation, no homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Purposeful symbol art / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A, M; a chosen symbol communicates meaning but is not a light source Objective / why "I can count star points and choose a design that communicates kindness." Visual choices can serve an audience. Catholic connection Advent, when applicable, invites preparation and kindness; the classroom star is a chosen symbol, not a scientific explanation. Local standards CST-C2: kind recipient/action; CST-A2: purposeful design; CST-M1: point count. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes first shapes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and exact materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Use the actual school calendar; this lesson also works as kindness art outside Advent. Precut five large five-point paper stars per child. No tiny decorations.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Student: five >=5 cm paper stars 50 75 100 125 Kit: glue stick, pairs/final trio plus reserve 5 8 10 13

Teacher timer/roster and a paper sample from the student budget. No flashlight, candle, dark-room setup, photograph or device required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and SAFETY
docs.text: Point = corner of this paper symbol; purpose = intended meaning; source = makes light; symbol = represents an idea. Paper reflects available light; real stars make light and do not physically have five paper points. Misconception: shiny paper makes its own light. If asked about a Bible story, use only an approved school reading; no unverified quote/history is necessary. No glitter, sequins, flame, button-cell candle, Sun viewing or dark movement.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Ask how a kind action can include a person; original prayer optional.
  2. 4-8: Count five points on a paper star, distinguish symbol/source, and model choosing placement/size for a visible meaning.
  3. 8-17: Each child chooses star placement and explains a kind message; partner interprets it, then child revises a visual choice. Begin checks.
  4. 17-21: Child counts three to five chosen points accurately, explains placement and identifies a recipient/action without stereotyping.
  5. 21-25: Save dated evidence, count unused stars, cap glue and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access and troubleshooting
docs.text: Check count, purposeful choice and respectful meaning; no spiritual-maturity score. Ask "What should someone notice first? Does paper make light?" Support: larger/tactile star, adult positioning directed by child. Challenge: make two arrangements and explain preference. No precut stars/glue: teacher draws a five-point symbol; pupils count/represent with crayons, same objective. Indoors; no night visit or household supply. Family: We counted a symbol's points and chose how it communicates kindness. Ask, "Why did you put that shape there?" No routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Water changes / Winter Science Time / domains 25 minutes / C, S, A Big idea / objective Ice is solid water; in a warmer room it can melt. "I can show before/after evidence of water changing." Why Observing icy conditions helps us make safe decisions in Minnesota. Catholic connection Care for people and avoid wasting materials; stewardship of resources, CCC 2402, paraphrase. Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-S3, CST-A1; local, not official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty None / Beginner Prep / cleanup Light: 10 minutes plus freezing overnight / 4 minutes in class

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Freeze plain tap water in standard ice trays. No toys, salt, sugar, dyes or food experiment.
  2. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 children (pairs/final trio). Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment; totals include it. Put one transparent 240 mL cup on a tray per team. Place one cube in each active cup just before class; no handling by pupils.
  3. Start one teacher demonstration cube 10-15 minutes early at room temperature so there is likely some visible meltwater. Label "started earlier." Do not claim it melted during student observation.
  4. Fold individual paper into two boxes: draw an eye above BEFORE and AFTER, spoken aloud. Prepare teacher sketches of an ice cube and a puddle as a clearly labeled model if no freezer is available.

docs.title: Exact supplies
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: transparent cup; tray; 20 mL ice cube 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each Per team: two paper-towel sheets 10 16 20 26 Teacher: demonstration cup/cube; reserve cubes (two) 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

Total cubes including one demonstration and two reserves: 8/11/13/16. Water to freeze: 160/220/260/320 mL. Teacher/class any size: one ice tray with at least 16 cells accepting 20 mL each (or two smaller trays), one pair adult-only tongs, one marker, timer, roster and a clean stable collection container of at least 1 L. The shared K 5 L collector also works. Only adults transfer/empty water, following the actual school hygiene plan. No warm/hot water required.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Solid: keeps its own shape, like the cube. Liquid: flows and takes the container's shape. Melt: change from solid to liquid. Evidence: what we can point to that supports our account.

Ice receives energy from warmer surroundings and melts. This lesson observes a change; it does not rank melting methods or prove a controlled-variable result. Water may collect from melting and a little from condensation outside the cup; point to liquid inside for the intended evidence.

Misconception: "Ice disappears." It becomes water; keep it in the cup to see where it went.

If asked, "Do all winter animals sleep?" "No. Some migrate, some remain active, and some reduce activity. Different animals have different strategies." Animal adaptation is optional discussion, not this meeting's assessed science target. The former rescue-dog saint story is removed rather than presented as verified history.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No touching ice against skin, tasting, freezing small toys, hot water, salt experiments or icicle hunting. Adult uses tongs. Use trays on seated tables; stop and wipe spills immediately. No outdoor exposure at -10 F. Keep all cups below table-edge risk and out of mouths. Offer drawings when sensory needs make ice observation uncomfortable.

docs.title: Numbered steps: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief prayer for wise care of resources; show the ice cup and ask what pupils notice.
  2. 3-6 (3 min): Model solid/liquid with fresh cube and labeled earlier cup. Explain no touching/tasting and how to point to evidence.
  3. 6-12 (6 min): Teams observe their cup, alternate describing and draw/dictate BEFORE details. Adult points out any water starting to form.
  4. 12-17 (5 min): Reobserve and make AFTER detail. Compare with BEFORE. If little changes, record "little/no visible change" and compare labeled earlier sample. Teacher starts individual solid/liquid/comparison checks.
  5. 17-21 (4 min): Finish remaining checks: each child points to solid and liquid or selects pictures, describes actual change/no change and names one safe action around ice. Teacher marks roster without a 25-child exit line.
  6. 21-25 (4 min): Adult collects cups/water into pitcher; pupils wipe dry trays and return crayons. Adult empties pitcher at sink and stores dry cups/trays.

docs.title: Evidence and what success looks like
docs.text: Record solid/liquid distinction and one before/after comparison as independent / prompted / not yet. A child who truthfully sees no change in their own cup may use the labeled earlier sample to identify melted water. Never require all cubes to melt in 25 minutes or judge drawing beauty.

docs.title: Questions, support, challenge, troubleshooting and indoor option
docs.text:
• "Where did the ice go? Can you point to the liquid? Did every cup change equally?"
  • Support: two large picture choices, oral response, adult sketch from dictated detail; no writing required.
  • Challenge: predict whether ice kept in a freezer would look the same; identify that a prediction is not today's observation.
  • Cube too large/no visible melting: use earlier labeled cup; do not increase heat or invent a successful result.
  • No freezer: compare teacher BEFORE/AFTER sketches, explicitly a model; evidence demonstrates the concept, not a live investigation.
  • 25 students: twelve active trays and one reserve kit; no water station line or whole-class sharing round.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: indoor melting is primary. Use a window only if it adds safe evidence; no walk needed.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text:
We observed solid ice and liquid water and used before/after evidence. Ask: "What happened to the ice, and how did you know?" No home freezing activity, homework or donation.
