docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus E (Engineering), A (Art), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Design and create a functional gift item 2. Follow step-by-step construction process 3. Apply fine motor skills in assembly 4. Consider recipient's needs in design

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect gift-giving to God's gifts to us 2. Understand the joy of giving over receiving 3. Practice the virtue of generosity

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Gift of Self — The best gifts come from our hearts and hands. When we make something for someone, we give them our time and love. God gave us the greatest gift — His Son, Jesus.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: 2 Corinthians 9:7; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check numbering/translation in the school's approved Bible. No quotation is reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching historical details
docs.text: The Magi (Wise Men) — They traveled far to bring gifts to baby Jesus. Their gifts showed their love and worship. We give gifts to show our love too.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Craft materials (paper, cardboard, decorations)

  • Scissors and glue

  • Markers/crayons

  • Gift project templates (bookmarks, card holders, or ornaments)

  • "Who Will You Give To" planning sheet

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Generous God, You give us so many gifts! Help us be cheerful givers today as we make gifts for people we love. Amen."

Discuss:

  • "Why do we give gifts?"

  • "How does it feel to give something you made?"

  • "Who would you like to make a gift for?"

docs.title: Gift Planning (4 min)
docs.text:
Planning sheet:

  • Who is this gift for?

  • What do they like?

  • Which gift will you make?

Gift options: 1. Bookmark — For someone who likes to read 2. Card Holder — For someone's desk 3. Paper Ornament — For decoration

docs.title: Gift Creation (18 min)
docs.text:
Demonstrate steps for chosen gift project.

Student creation time:

  • Follow construction steps

  • Personalize with colors and decorations

  • Think about the person receiving it

Teacher support:

  • "Who are you making this for?"

  • "What will they like about it?"

  • "What message do you want to share?"

Quality encouragement:

  • Take your time

  • Make it with love

  • It's special because YOU made it

docs.title: Closing Reflection (4 min)
docs.text:
Share: Students show gifts and tell who they're for.

Faith Connection: "When you give something you made, you're giving part of yourself! That's what God did when He sent Jesus — He gave us the most precious gift. Your handmade gifts show love just like God's love for us."

Closing Prayer: "Thank you, God, for the joy of giving. Bless these gifts and the people who will receive them. Help us always be cheerful givers. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Completed a gift with care and intention

  • Could explain who the gift is for

  • Demonstrated understanding of giving as love

docs.title: SAFETY and workable default
docs.text: Use a cardstock bookmark: teacher precuts a 5 x 15 cm strip; child chooses a recipient, draws a useful visible pattern/message and tests whether it marks a closed book without protruding dangerously. No beads, staples or hot glue. Grade 1 dictates a message; Grade 2 explains a design choice. Use final 3 minutes of creation to return tools/recycle scraps. Handmade and purchased gifts can both express care; do not grade family resources.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We made gifts today! Your child has a special handmade gift for someone. Ask them to tell you about who they made it for and why. Talk about how making gifts shows love — just like God shows His love for us!"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus All STREAM Areas

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Reflect on and articulate learning from the semester 2. Demonstrate skills learned through activities 3. Work cooperatively in celebration stations 4. Celebrate growth and achievement

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Express gratitude for learning opportunities 2. Recognize God's gifts of curiosity and creativity 3. Celebrate community and cooperation

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Celebration of Gifts — God gives each of us unique gifts and talents. When we celebrate our learning, we thank God for the gift of our minds and the joy of discovery.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: James 1:17; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check numbering/translation in the school's approved Bible. No quotation is reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching historical details
docs.text: All the Saints — We celebrate the saints because they used their gifts to serve God. Today we celebrate how we've used our gifts to learn and grow!

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Station materials (see station descriptions)

  • Celebration certificates

  • Student portfolios/work samples

  • Festive decorations

  • Reflection sheets

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Thank You, God, for our STREAM journey this semester! Thank You for curious minds, creative hands, and friends to learn with. We celebrate Your gifts today! Amen."

Introduction: "Today we celebrate all we've learned! We'll visit fun stations that let us remember and show our skills."

docs.title: Celebration Stations (20 min)
docs.text:
Students rotate through 4 stations (5 minutes each):

Station 1: Sphero Speed Challenge

  • Quick coding challenge

  • Navigate a simple maze

  • Each child explains one input and resulting movement/output on a supervised replay. This checks tool input/output, not new stored-code mastery.

Station 2: KEVA Quick Build

  • 3-minute building challenge

  • Build the tallest tower

  • Celebrate engineering

Station 3: Memory Sharing

  • Look at work from the semester

  • Share favorite memories with a partner

  • "My favorite STREAM activity was..."

Station 4: Thank You Cards

  • Write/draw thank you to someone who helped you learn

  • Could be teacher, classmate, family member

  • Express gratitude

docs.title: Closing Celebration (6 min)
docs.text:
Circle gathering:

  • Each student shares ONE thing they learned this semester

  • "This semester I learned..."

  • "I'm thankful for..."

Certificate presentation: Distribute fall semester certificates.

Faith Connection: "Look how much you've grown! God gave you curiosity and you used it! God gave you creativity and you created! God gave you friends and you worked together! That's worth celebrating!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for an amazing semester of STREAM learning. Thank You for our wonderful class community. Bless us as we rest and play over break. Help us come back ready to learn even more! Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Participated in celebration stations

  • Shared a learning memory or accomplishment

  • Expressed gratitude

docs.title: Technology / SAFETY / evidence limit
docs.text: Recommended primary path: charged robot/tablet for a supervised replay, not a speed race. No devices: predict a path with cards; do not award robot mastery. Towers below 30 cm, no heavy loads. Use one supervised device station or table portfolios when staffing is limited. Photos only under school permissions. Reserve 3 station minutes for cleanup; certificates recognize participation/growth, not unobserved domain mastery.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We celebrated our STREAM learning today! Ask your child: 'What was your favorite thing you learned?' 'What are you proud of?' 'What do you want to learn next?' Thank you for supporting our STREAM journey!"

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) STREAM Focus S (Science), R (Religion), A (Art)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Identify light sources (natural and artificial) 2. Explain how shadows are formed 3. Explore reflection with mirrors 4. Conduct simple light experiments

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect Jesus as "Light of the World" to physical light 2. Understand Advent as waiting for the Light 3. Recognize how we can be light to others

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Jesus is the Light — Just as physical light helps us see, Jesus helps us see what is good and true. During Advent, we prepare for the Light of Christ to enter the world at Christmas.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: John 8:12; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: check numbering/translation in the school's approved Bible. No quotation is reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED
docs.text: Lucy traditions and feast date require an approved source. The cave/food story is devotional tradition, not established historical evidence; omit it unless clearly labeled and verified. The investigation needs no biography.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Flashlights (1 per group)

  • Small mirrors

  • White paper

  • Colored objects

  • Cardboard for shadow puppets

  • Prisms (optional)

  • Darkened area in classroom

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Advent Prayer: "Lord Jesus, You are the Light of the World. As we learn about light today, help us see Your light in our lives. Come, Lord Jesus! Amen."

Light discussion:

  • "Where does light come from?" (Sun, lamps, candles, screens)

  • "What happens when there's no light?" (Darkness, can't see)

  • "Why is light important?"

docs.title: Light Sources Exploration (8 min)
docs.text:
Natural vs. artificial light:

  • Natural: Sun and other stars; human-lit fires/candles are artificial sources. Do not classify all fire by one origin.

  • Artificial: Lamps, flashlights, screens

Faith Connection: Genesis 1 is a theological creation account, not the measured chronology of this light investigation. The Sun is our nearest star, not the largest star or light source. Jesus as Light is religious imagery, not physical brightness.

docs.title: Shadow Investigation (12 min)
docs.text:
Shadow stations (rotate in groups):

Station 1: Shadow Making

  • Use flashlight and objects

  • Make shadows bigger and smaller (move closer/farther)

  • Draw around shadows

Station 2: Shadow Puppets

  • Use cardboard cutouts

  • Create shadow puppet show

  • Tell a simple story

Station 3: No Shadow Challenge

  • Can you make the shadow disappear?

  • What happens with light from all sides?

docs.title: Closing Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Discussion:

  • "How do shadows form?"

  • "What makes shadows bigger or smaller?"

Faith Connection: "Shadows happen when something blocks light. Sin is like a shadow — it blocks God's light in our lives. But Jesus's light is so powerful, no shadow can overcome it!"

Closing Prayer: "Jesus, Light of the World, shine in our hearts. Push away the shadows. Help us walk in Your light. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Review (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, help us reflect Your light to others today. Make us mirrors of Your love. Amen."

Review: "What did we learn about shadows?"

docs.title: Mirror Exploration (10 min)
docs.text:
Mirror activities:

  • Look in mirror — what do you see?

  • Use mirror to see around corners

  • Use mirror to redirect flashlight beam

Guided discovery:

  • "What happens to light when it hits a mirror?"

  • "Can you bounce light from one place to another?"

Challenge: Use 2 mirrors to send light around a corner.

docs.title: Being Light Investigation (10 min)
docs.text:
Discussion: "Jesus says WE can be light too!"

Matthew 5:14 is a reference only; verify/read from the school's approved Bible rather than an unverified quotation.

Brainstorm: How can we be light to others?

  • Smile at someone lonely

  • Help someone who needs it

  • Share what we have

  • Tell the truth

  • Be kind with our words

"Light Cards": Students draw/write one way they will be light this week.

docs.title: Closing Celebration (6 min)
docs.text:
Light ceremony: If appropriate, briefly darken room.

Teacher switches on an enclosed LED light: "One small light helps us see." No real flame.

Discuss: "How can your small act of kindness light up someone's day?"

Faith Connection: "Just like mirrors reflect light, we can reflect Jesus's light to everyone around us. This Advent, let's be mirrors that show His love!"

Closing Prayer: "Jesus, Light of the World, help us reflect Your light. Make us bright with kindness, love, and joy. Come, Lord Jesus! Amen."

docs.title: Session 1
docs.text:
• Identified different light sources

  • Explained how shadows form

  • Experimented with shadow size

docs.title: Session 2
docs.text:
• Explored reflection with mirrors

  • Named ways to "be light" to others

  • Created a "Light Card" commitment

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: Use plastic safety mirrors, low-power flashlights and enclosed LED lights only. No flames, lasers, glass mirrors, sun viewing or pointing beams at eyes. Keep enough room light to see aisles; students remain seated for dim-light demonstrations. If reflection is difficult, teacher models one mirror before two. Reserve final 3 minutes each meeting for tool return and cleanup.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We explored light and shadows! Talk with your child about how Jesus is the Light of the World and how we can be 'light' to others. During Advent, look for candles and lights that remind us Jesus is coming!"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus S (Science), R (Religion), A (Art)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Understand that stars are distant suns 2. Identify that stars appear to move across the sky 3. Explain why stars were important for ancient navigation 4. Create a star-related craft or project

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect the Christmas star to the Magi's journey 2. Understand how God uses creation to guide us 3. Recognize that seeking Jesus is life's most important journey

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: God Guides Through Creation — God used a star to guide the Magi to Jesus. Throughout history, God has used the natural world to speak to people. Creation points us to the Creator.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Matthew 2:2; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Biblical connection
docs.text: Matthew 2 describes Magi following a star; it does not establish their number, modern scientific profession, precise travel duration or the star's physical identity. Omit those claims; approved retelling VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Pictures of stars and constellations

  • Star charts (simple)

  • Black paper

  • Gold/silver star stickers or yellow paper

  • Hole punches

  • Flashlights for "constellation viewers"

  • The Magi story (book or printout)

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Advent Prayer: "Star of Wonder, Star of Light! Lord, just as You guided the Magi with a star, guide us to Jesus this Christmas season. Amen."

Read/Tell: Brief telling of the Magi following the star (Matthew 2:1-12).

Wonder questions:

  • "How did the Magi know to follow the star?"

  • "How long do you think they traveled?"

  • "What did they find at the end?"

docs.title: Star Science (8 min)
docs.text:
Star facts for 1st-2nd graders:

  • Stars are very far away suns

  • They look small because they're so far

  • At night, we can see stars because the sun isn't lighting up the sky

  • People have used stars to find their way for thousands of years

Discussion:

  • "Have you ever seen stars at night?"

  • "Why can't we see stars during the day?"

Star patterns: Show simple constellations (Big Dipper, Orion).

Faith Connection: The Magi story expresses seeking Jesus. It is not evidence identifying a modern astronomical event.

docs.title: Star Project (12 min)
docs.text:
Choose one activity:

Option A: Constellation Viewer

  • Black paper rolled into tube

  • Teacher uses a hole punch before class to make the pattern; no student pin/needle puncturing.

  • Look only toward a diffuse classroom lamp, never the Sun, laser or bright focused beam.

Option B: Star of Bethlehem Craft

  • Large star shape

  • Decorate with gold/silver

  • Write "Follow the Star to Jesus"

Option C: Magi Journey Map

  • Draw simple map

  • Add star in sky

  • Show path from East to Bethlehem

docs.title: Closing Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Share creations.

Discuss:

  • "The Magi traveled a long way to find Jesus. What 'journey' can we take to get closer to Jesus?" (Prayer, Mass, being kind, reading the Bible)

Faith Connection: The Magi story can remind us to seek Jesus; distinguish the faith account from our observations of star patterns.

Closing Prayer: "Lord, like the Magi, help us follow the star to You. Guide our journey this Advent. We want to find You and worship You like the Wise Men did. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Shared one fact about stars

  • Connected the Christmas star to the Magi story

  • Completed star project

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence
docs.text: No sun viewing, sharp punctures or dark-room walking. Constellation pictures are flat models: stars may lie at different distances. Grade 1 points to/counts a pattern and tells a star fact; Grade 2 explains a model limitation. Use final 3 project minutes for cleanup. Outdoor night viewing is optional only; pictures indoors provide an equitable alternative.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We learned about the Star of Bethlehem! Go outside on a clear night and look at stars together. Talk about how the Magi followed a star to find Jesus. How can your family 'follow the star' to Jesus this Christmas?"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus M (Math), R (Religion), A (Art)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Set specific, achievable goals 2. Break goals into smaller steps 3. Create a visual goal tracker 4. Understand measurement of progress

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect personal growth to growing in faith 2. Identify ways to grow closer to God 3. Understand that God helps us achieve our goals

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Growing in Virtue — God wants us to grow and become the best version of ourselves. Setting goals helps us grow in virtue — becoming more kind, more patient, more loving, more like Jesus.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 16:3; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced. Goal success is not guaranteed by prayer.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Thérèse of Lisieux — She set small goals to do ordinary things with great love. She called this "the Little Way" — small steps toward becoming a saint.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Goal planning worksheets

  • Trackers/charts (blank)

  • Markers/crayons

  • Stickers for goal tracking

  • "My Goals" booklet template

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
New Year Prayer: "Lord, thank You for a new year! Help us set good goals and grow to be more like Jesus. Guide our plans and give us strength to do our best. Amen."

Discuss:

  • "A new year is a fresh start!"

  • "What is a goal?" (Something you want to learn or do)

  • "Why do people set goals?"

docs.title: Goal Setting (8 min)
docs.text:
Three types of goals:

  1. Learning Goal — Something you want to learn
  2. Learn to read bigger books
  3. Learn to add bigger numbers

  4. Learn something new in STREAM

  5. Kindness Goal — A way to help others

  6. Help at home more
  7. Be a better friend

  8. Share with others

  9. Faith Goal — Growing closer to God

  10. Pray every day
  11. Be more thankful
  12. Learn about a saint

Students choose one goal from each category.

docs.title: Goal Planning (12 min)
docs.text:
Make goals SMART:

  • **S**pecific — What exactly will you do?

  • **M**easurable — How will you know you did it?

  • **A**chievable — Can you really do this?

  • **R**elevant — Is this important to you?

  • **T**ime-bound — When will you do it?

Student work: 1. Write/draw 3 goals (one of each type) 2. For each goal, write ONE SMALL STEP to start 3. Create a tracker to mark progress

Example:

  • Goal: Pray every day

  • First step: Say morning prayer when I wake up

  • Tracker: Mark a star for each day I pray

docs.title: Closing Commitment (5 min)
docs.text:
Share goals with a partner.

Prayer commitment: "Let's ask God to help us with our goals."

Students hold their goal sheets.

Faith Connection: "St. Thérèse taught that small steps lead to big changes. Every time you take a small step toward your goal, you're growing! And guess what? God is cheering you on!"

Closing Prayer: "Lord, we offer You our goals for this year. Help us take small steps every day. When it's hard, give us strength. When we forget, remind us. Help us grow to be more like Jesus. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Set three goals (learning, kindness, faith)

  • Identified first step for each goal

  • Created a goal tracker

docs.title: Nonreader / privacy / follow-up
docs.text: Grade 1 chooses one classroom learning or kindness action and draws/tells a first step; Grade 2 may set three goals. Keep trackers at school and revisit during the next opening, not as required home work. Do not score or publicly rank prayer/sacrament participation or infer faith from tracker completion. Technology: None primary path. Use final 2 planning minutes to tidy supplies.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We chose classroom growth goals and first steps. Ask your child to tell or show one step they can practice. Trackers stay at school; optional home discussion needs no materials."

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Evidence workshops / STREAM Exploration Stations Time / domains Four meetings, each exactly 30 minutes / C, E, A, M; not "all domains" Big idea Focused making, measuring and revision produce evidence of learning. Student objective "I can show my plan, test or compare it, and explain one change." Why Thirty minutes permits one meaningful workshop, not four six-minute stations plus transitions. Catholic connection Reuse materials and honor every child's contribution; teacher application of CCC 2407/2415. Standards Local CST-C3: material care; CST-E2: build/test/redesign (meeting 1); CST-A2: symmetry/pattern (2-3); CST-M1: same-unit measurement (¼); CST-M2: pattern/data representation (¾). Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path. Prior robot lessons remain the place for assessed code; an optional robot demo cannot replace these workshop outcomes. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low/moderate; 10-15 minutes for each reusable kit; 4 minutes cleanup each meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Choose one workshop kit per meeting; do not put water/paint/robots out simultaneously.
  2. Prepare a picture instruction card showing plan -> try -> compare -> change.
  3. Assign table teams of 2-3 but give each child a separate evidence page. Grade 1 tells/draws; Grade 2 adds units/reasons.
  4. Keep prior science sink/float and robot ideas as optional future extensions needing separate safety and assessment planning, not hidden required stations.

docs.title: Supplies / scaling
docs.text:
• Per student per meeting: half-sheet and crayon.
  • Per team meeting 1: 20 wooden planks or cardboard blocks, ruler/equal cubes, soft eraser as optional load.
  • Per team meeting 2: folded paper and crayons (no wet paint required).
  • Per team meeting 3: 12 pattern blocks or teacher-cut colored paper shapes.
  • Per team meeting 4: ruler or equal cubes and three accessible classroom objects.
  • Class: timer, board results chart, reusable trays; tape only if using cardboard.
  • Teacher-only: roster, kit screening and storage labels.
Students Teams / kits per workshop Planks (meeting 1) Shapes (meeting 3) Half-sheets/meeting 10 4 80 48 10 15 5 100 60 15 20 7 140 84 20 25 9 180 108 25

At 25 everyone stays at tables. Teacher visits three tables per practice phase; independent evidence is a brief drawing/demo, not 25 long presentations.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Redesign = change after a test; stable = stays standing; symmetry = matching across a line; repeating unit = the part repeated; unit = same-size measuring amount; data = recorded results. Different hand spans are not interchangeable units. Drawings can show design decisions without writing. Misconception: finishing a passport proves learning. Only the demonstrated workshop criterion does. If asked "Why no robots today?" Tools match the question; we already have separate lessons for actual programming.

docs.title: Four exact 30-minute meetings
docs.text:
Meeting 1: Stable structure 1. 0-4: Show challenge: tabletop structure at least five equal blocks tall, stands 10 seconds, height below 30 cm; discuss reusing planks. 2. 4-8: Model a narrow/wide base and height measurement; each child sketches a possible base. 3. 8-20: Teams build, test for 10 seconds, change one feature and retest; each child helps one test/measurement. 4. 20-24: Record two results and show changed base. 5. 24-26: Individual: explain a change using test evidence. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 2: Symmetry studio 1. 0-4: Show matching versus nonmatching designs. 2. 4-8: Fold paper; teacher marks matching points across fold. 3. 8-20: Each child makes a purposeful symmetric design; partner checks two matching features. 4. 20-24: Revise one mismatch or explain intentional asymmetry; never equate beauty with perfection. 5. 24-26: Individual points to line and two matching features. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 3: Pattern communication 1. 0-4: Recall a two-color AB example. 2. 4-8: Model repeating unit and intentional broken pattern. 3. 8-20: Children make two AB units (Grade 1) or three ABB/AAB units (Grade 2), trade predictions and repair one broken pattern. 4. 20-24: Draw pattern and explain what comes next. 5. 24-26: Individual identifies unit and predicts next two shapes. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

Meeting 4: Measurement gallery 1. 0-4: Choose one object to compare; recall equal units. 2. 4-8: Teacher models no gaps/overlaps from endpoint. 3. 8-20: Children measure three objects with same units; Grade 2 nearest whole cm if ready; record/draw lengths. 4. 20-24: Compare longest/shortest and represent results as aligned strips. 5. 24-26: Individual demonstrates measuring start and justifies one comparison. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What did your test show? Which part repeats? Did units have gaps? Why did you save usable materials? Grade 1 uses oral explanations and sketches, two matching features, AB prediction, correct endpoint and longer/shorter comparisons. Grade 2 gives measured two-trial structure results, ABB/AAB rule and three labeled comparable lengths with reasoning. Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for each meeting's stated criterion and care action; do not assign science/robot mastery from unrelated products.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: No planks: fold cardboard blocks or make a low paper structure; same standing criterion. Limited rulers: use equal paper strips. No pattern blocks: colored paper shapes. All four workshops work indoors with no devices; no hidden loan requirement. Early finishers revise/explain rather than visit unprepared stations.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Structures below 30 cm; hands out before collapse test; no heavy top loads or furniture climbing. Screen recycled materials; no glass, exposed staples or wet materials. Keep aisles clear and tools age appropriate. Support: prebuilt base, thick blocks, picture steps, partner stabilization and adult scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 defend a design tradeoff or compare repeated measurements; maintain individual evidence.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Count and sort kit parts; return tools, recycle scraps, store each child's labeled evidence. Four-minute cleanup is already counted. Family snippet: Over four workshops we tested structures, revised symmetry and patterns, and measured with equal units. Catholic connection: responsible reuse and respect. Ask: "What did you change after checking your work?" Optional: find a pattern or compare two familiar objects orally; no purchase/device or routine homework. CCC 2407/2415. Optional 1 Corinthians 12:4,11 is a reference, not a verified quotation. Saint biographies are not required; verify any added names/details before use.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus R (Religion) + All STREAM Areas

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect STREAM learning to Catholic school identity 2. Create a project showcasing Catholic values 3. Explain how faith and learning work together 4. Celebrate Catholic education

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Articulate what makes Catholic school special 2. Identify Catholic scientists and their contributions 3. Express gratitude for Catholic education

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Faith and Reason — In Catholic schools, we learn that faith and science work together. God gave us minds to explore His creation, and faith helps us understand the deeper meaning of what we discover.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 9:10; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text:
Catholic Scientists:

  • St. Albert the Great — Studied science and nature

  • Fr. Georges Lemaître — Proposed the Big Bang theory

  • Gregor Mendel — Father of genetics

  • Sr. Mary Kenneth Keller — Computer scientist and educator; degree chronology/institution VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching a "first" claim.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Catholic Scientists poster/pictures

  • "What Makes Us Special" worksheet

  • Craft materials for "Catholic STREAM" project

  • School values list

  • Celebration decorations

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Catholic Schools Week Prayer: "Thank You, God, for our Catholic school! Thank You for teachers who help us learn and grow in faith. Bless all Catholic schools everywhere. Help us share Your love through all we do. Amen."

Discuss:

  • "What makes our school special?"

  • "How is a Catholic school different?"

  • Answers may include: We pray, we learn about God, we go to Mass, we serve others, we treat everyone with dignity

docs.title: Catholic Scientists (8 min)
docs.text:
Introduce Catholic scientists:

"Did you know many scientists were Catholic? They believed studying science helped them know God better!"

Share brief stories: 1. Gregor Mendel — A monk who studied pea plants and discovered how traits pass from parents to children 2. Sr. Mary Kenneth Keller — A Catholic sister who worked in computing and education; exact contribution VERIFICATION REQUIRED. 3. Fr. Georges Lemaître — Priest/cosmologist associated with expanding-universe models; exact contribution VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Do not say he fully explained the origin of everything.

Discussion:

  • "These scientists loved God AND loved science!"

  • "In Catholic schools, we learn that faith and science go together"

  • "God gave us brains to discover and hearts to believe"

docs.title: "What Makes Us Special" Project (12 min)
docs.text:
Create a "Catholic STREAM" banner or poster:

Students contribute to a class project showing:

  • S — "Science shows us God's creation"

  • T — "Technology helps us serve others"

  • R — "Religion guides everything we do"

  • E — "Engineering solves problems with love"

  • A — "Art celebrates God's beauty"

  • M — "Math shows God's order and patterns"

Individual contribution: Each student adds a drawing or words to the class banner.

Alternative: Individual "I Love My Catholic School" cards with STREAM elements.

docs.title: Closing Celebration (5 min)
docs.text:
Share the completed project.

Gratitude circle: Each student shares one thing they're thankful for about their Catholic school.

Faith Connection: "In Catholic schools, we don't just learn facts — we learn how to love God and love others. Our STREAM learning helps us become people who can make the world better!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for Catholic schools where faith and learning come together. Thank You for our teachers, friends, and families who support us. Help us use everything we learn to serve You and others. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Contributed to class Catholic STREAM project

  • Identified at least one Catholic scientist

  • Expressed what makes Catholic school special

docs.title: Substitute source gate
docs.text: If vetted biographies are not supplied, omit the scientist-story block and spend those 8 minutes observing a classroom plant, drawing two details and honestly distinguishing observation from belief. This preserves the faith/reason purpose without teaching uncertain history. Grade 1 tells/draws; Grade 2 explains one distinction. No devices required; Technology: None primary path. Reserve 3 banner minutes for cleanup.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We celebrated Catholic Schools Week! Ask your child: 'What makes our Catholic school special?' 'What Catholic scientist did you learn about?' Thank you for choosing Catholic education. Together, we help your child grow in faith, knowledge, and love!"

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) STREAM Focus T (Technology), E (Engineering), M (Math)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Program Dash robot using block coding 2. Create sequences with multiple commands 3. Use loops to repeat actions 4. Navigate Dash through challenges

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect programming to following God's plan 2. Understand perseverance when code doesn't work 3. Practice patience and problem-solving as virtues

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Respectful sharing and responsible technology use are applications of CCC 2407. People have moral agency, not robot-like programmed obedience. Do not equate a computer command with God's relationship to people.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 3:5-6; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Saint Carlo Acutis — Canonized September 7, 2025; Vatican source. Additional computing biography details require verification; focus on responsible use.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Dash robots (1 per group of 2-3)

  • iPads with Blockly app

  • Floor tape for paths/mazes

  • Challenge cards

  • Construction paper for destinations

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, help us learn to guide Dash today. Just like we program the robot, help us follow Your guidance in our lives. Give us patience when things don't work the first time. Amen."

Introduce Dash:

  • "Dash is a robot we can program!"

  • Show Dash's features: eyes, lights, sounds, wheels

  • "We'll use the Blockly app to tell Dash what to do"

docs.title: Blockly Introduction (6 min)
docs.text:
Basic commands demonstration:

  • Move forward — Dash drives forward

  • Turn — Dash turns left or right

  • Light — Change Dash's eye color

  • Sound — Make Dash talk or make sounds

Show how to:

  • Drag blocks onto the workspace

  • Connect blocks together

  • Press "Start" to run the program

docs.title: Guided Practice (8 min)
docs.text:
Challenge 1: Make Dash move forward and change color.

Together:

  • Drag "move forward" block

  • Add "set eye color" block

  • Run the program

Challenge 2: Make Dash move forward, turn, move forward.

Students try with partners.

docs.title: Free Exploration (8 min)
docs.text:
Open exploration time:

  • Try different commands

  • Make Dash dance

  • Create a short program

Teacher circulates: "What did you make Dash do?"

docs.title: Closing (4 min)
docs.text:
Share: Groups show one thing they programmed.

Faith Connection: "Programming takes patience! When something doesn't work, we try again. That's how it is with following God too — sometimes we make mistakes, but we keep trying!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank you, God, for the gift of learning. Help us be patient when things are hard. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Review (3 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Jesus, guide our minds and hands today. Help us work together and never give up. Amen."

Quick review: "What commands did we learn for Dash?"

docs.title: Loop Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
New concept: Loops

  • "A loop repeats commands over and over"

  • "Instead of putting the same block 5 times, we can use a loop!"

Demonstrate:

  • Show "repeat" block

  • Put actions inside loop

  • "Repeat 4 times: move forward, turn right" = a square!

docs.title: Challenge Course Setup (2 min)
docs.text:
Set up floor challenges:

  • Simple path with tape

  • Start and end points marked

  • Optional obstacles

docs.title: Challenge Time (15 min)
docs.text:
Teams work on challenges:

Challenge 1: Follow the Path

  • Program Dash to follow the taped path

  • Start to finish without going off track

Challenge 2: Navigate Around

  • Program Dash around an obstacle

  • Return to starting area

Challenge 3: Shape Drawing (if time)

  • Make Dash trace a square or triangle

Teacher support:

  • "What do you need Dash to do first?"

  • "How will you fix that?"

  • "Try it and see what happens!"

docs.title: Celebration & Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Teams share successes.

Reflection:

  • "What was challenging?"

  • "How did you solve problems?"

  • "What would you do differently?"

Faith Connection: "When your program didn't work, you didn't give up — you tried again! That's called perseverance. God wants us to keep trying, even when following Him seems hard. He's always there to help us get back on track!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank you, God, for robots and coding and learning. Thank You for friends who help us figure things out. Help us follow Your path with trust and perseverance. Amen."

docs.title: Session 1
docs.text:
• Created a simple Dash program

  • Used at least 2 different commands

  • Participated in exploration

docs.title: Session 2
docs.text:
• Attempted challenge course

  • Used loops in programming

  • Demonstrated perseverance in debugging

docs.title: Technology / SAFETY / evidence
docs.text: Required primary path: tested Dash/Blockly/tablet kits for stored code. Preflight loan, app labels and current compatibility; charge by model guide. Low-speed marked dry floor bays, no chasing/overhead loads; teacher handles cords. Test an explicit short forward-distance/90-degree turn sequence; a repeat-four square is a model needing calibration, not guaranteed accuracy. Grade 1 predicts and runs two actions; Grade 2 changes one movement and explains a measured nearer/farther result. Collect each child's actual run/debug evidence; role turns after every run. No devices: arrow/token sequence and debug only, not robot operation or physical code mastery. Reserve 4 practice minutes each meeting for cleanup.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We programmed Dash robots! Ask your child: 'What did you make Dash do?' 'What was tricky?' 'How did you solve problems?' Talk about how we can persevere in life — keep trying even when things are hard, trusting God to guide us!"

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) STREAM Focus E (Engineering), R (Religion), A (Art)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Apply human-centered design thinking 2. Create solutions that address real needs 3. Test and iterate on designs 4. Present design solutions

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect Catholic Social Teaching to design 2. Understand preferential option for the poor 3. Practice empathy and compassion in design thinking

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Catholic Social Teaching: Preferential Option for the Poor — God calls us to care especially for those who are struggling. Engineers and designers can create things that help people in need.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Matthew 25:40; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Vincent de Paul — He organized practical help for poor people. He found creative solutions to help those in need with food, medicine, and shelter.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Design scenario cards

  • Planning worksheets

  • Building materials: cardboard, paper, tape, craft supplies

  • Testing materials

  • Presentation space

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Jesus, You said when we help others, we help You. Open our hearts to see the needs of others. Guide our hands as we design to help. Amen."

Read Matthew 25:40 only from the approved Bible; do not reproduce an unverified abbreviated quotation.

Discuss: "Who are 'the least of these'? Who needs help?"

docs.title: Design Challenge Introduction (6 min)
docs.text:
Present scenarios (choose one for class):

Scenario A: "An elderly person has trouble carrying groceries."

  • What's hard for them?

  • What would help?

Scenario B: "A child in a wheelchair can't reach drinking fountains."

  • What's the problem?

  • What could we design?

Scenario C: "Someone who can't see needs help knowing what's around them."

  • What challenges do they face?

  • How could we help?

Empathy discussion:

  • "How would YOU feel if you had this challenge?"

  • "What would you want someone to design for you?"

docs.title: Design Thinking: Brainstorm & Plan (15 min)
docs.text:
Individual brainstorm (4 min): Draw 2-3 ideas.

Partner share (4 min): Share ideas with partner. Combine ideas!

Choose and plan (7 min):

  • Select one design to build

  • Draw detailed plan

  • List materials needed

  • Identify how you'll test if it works

docs.title: Closing Preview (5 min)
docs.text:
Share plans with another group.

Faith Connection: "When we design to help others, we're doing what Jesus asked! We're being His hands in the world."

Closing Prayer: "Bless our designs, Lord. Help us think carefully about how to help others. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Review (3 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Jesus, help us build with love today. May our creations serve others and honor You. Amen."

Review plans: "What are you building? How will it help?"

docs.title: Building Time (17 min)
docs.text:
Students build their designs.

Teacher circulates:

  • "Tell me how this helps."

  • "How will you test it?"

  • "What changes are you making?"

Encourage iteration:

  • Test as you build

  • It's okay to change your plan

  • Ask for help when needed

docs.title: Quick Testing (4 min)
docs.text:
Test designs with a toy figure and a tabletop paper load only. Default: paper carry tray holds three crumpled paper balls for five seconds; redesign one fold and retest. Ask about user preferences rather than assuming every older/disabled person needs the same help.

  • Does it work?

  • What would make it better?

docs.title: Presentations (4 min)
docs.text:
Quick presentations: Each group shares:

  • "We designed this for..." (who it helps)

  • "It works by..." (how it helps)

  • "We learned..." (what they discovered)

docs.title: Closing Celebration (2 min)
docs.text:
Faith Connection: "You were Jesus's hands today! You thought about others' needs and created to help them. That's what Catholic engineers do — they use their skills to serve!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank you, God, for minds that create and hearts that care. Help us always use our gifts to serve 'the least of these.' We want to be Your hands in the world. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Demonstrated empathy for the user's needs

  • Created a design plan

  • Built a prototype

  • Explained how design helps others

docs.title: SAFETY / access
docs.text: All products are models, not real medical or assistive devices. No human lifting, body-worn restraint, blindfolding, climbing to a fountain/shelf or overhead loads. Teacher precuts cardboard, screens recyclables and limits tests to paper loads. Grade 1 orally demonstrates one feature/test; Grade 2 explains one evidence-based revision. Reserve final 4 building/planning minutes each meeting for cleanup/storage.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We were designers for others! Ask your child: 'Who did you design for?' 'How does your invention help them?' 'What would you improve?' Talk about how your family can be 'helping hands' for people in need in your community."

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Mathematics and design / Pi Day Circles Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, M, A Big idea We can compare distances around circles using the same unit. Student objective "I can compare two circle edges and use circles to make a repeating design." Why Accurate measurement and purposeful patterns matter more than memorizing digits. Catholic connection Honest evidence: report approximate measures without pretending they are exact; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159 (source below). Standards Local CST-C1: name measurement uncertainty; CST-M1: compare two boundaries; CST-M2: extend a repeating pattern; CST-A2: intentional form/pattern. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: paper/string directly show the mathematics. Robot art is not required and attaching a marker to a rolling Sphero is not part of this lesson. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Choose two smooth round lids about 8 cm and 12 cm across (neither wider than 15 cm), so their boundaries fit the 60 cm yarn. Remove sharp metal edges. Trace a square to compare.
  2. Cut 60 cm lengths of yarn; prepare one equal-size block chain per team. Demonstrate wrapping yarn once with no overlap or stretching.
  3. Draw AB and AAB circle patterns on the board. Do not use food rewards.
  4. Per student: one sheet and crayon.
  5. Per team of 2-3: two round lids, two yarn lengths, 20 equal blocks about 2 cm wide (or 20 equal 2 cm paper squares) and scrap paper for comparing laid-out yarn. Check that the unit chain spans the longer boundary before class.
  6. Class: tape and board, circle/square examples; reusable lids/yarn.
  7. Teacher-only: scissors for precutting yarn; optional ruler to show approximation.
Students Teams / lid pairs Yarn lengths Paper sheets 10 4 8 10 15 5 10 15 20 7 14 20 25 9 18 25

docs.title: Vocabulary / teacher background
docs.text: Circle = flat round shape; circumference = distance around its boundary; diameter = distance across through the center; approximate = close, not exact; repeating unit = part that repeats. Pi is a finite number about 3.14, the ratio of circumference to diameter. Its decimal representation does not terminate or repeat. Endless digits do not mean infinite magnitude. No ratio calculation is required of Grades 1-2. Misconception: every round-looking object is a flat circle. A ball is a sphere; its flat outline may look circular. If asked "Is pi as big as God?" No. Mathematics describes a finite quantity; a devotional analogy is not a mathematical or theological measurement.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Find a circle versus square. Explain Pi Day's 3/14 date briefly without digit recitation or theology claims.
  2. 4-8: Model wrapping yarn around one lid, marking the join, laying it flat and comparing to the same equal blocks.
  3. 8-18: Team members each help measure both lids. Align yarn starts; predict then compare. Grade 2 counts equal blocks, including "a little more than" if needed; Grade 1 points to longer/shorter. Repeat once to notice small measurement differences.
  4. 18-23: Each child traces circles in an intentional AB (Grade 1) or AAB/ABB (Grade 2) pattern. Partner extends it and explains the repeating unit.
  5. 23-26: Individual exit: identify the longer boundary, explain one measurement step and point to the repeating unit; say why a measure may be approximate.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: Which yarn is longer when starts line up? What made our two attempts differ? What part of your pattern repeats? - Grade 1: correctly compare two boundaries; demonstrate lining up endpoints; create two complete AB units and predict the next circle. - Grade 2: record two approximate counts in the same units and justify comparison; create/extend three units of AAB or ABB; identify one uncertainty. - Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for comparison, measurement method, pattern and honest uncertainty. No coding credit from circle artwork.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Slipping yarn: tape the starting end or teacher models a paper strip. No lids: use two teacher-drawn circles and paper strips; describe these as drawings. No equal blocks: use identical paper squares. Entire lesson works indoors without devices. Early finishers compare a third circle, not speed.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No food/treats, loose coins, sharp can lids, neck loops or strings tied to students. Precut yarn; teacher manages scissors. Accessible tabletop work only.

docs.title: Support / challenge / cleanup
docs.text: Support: pretraced circles, oral prompts and partner stabilization without taking the child's decision. Grade 1 responds by pointing/drawing. Challenge: Grade 2 compare around/across lengths informally; no required division. Cleanup: count reusable lids/blocks, coil yarn into bags, recycle scraps and retain each child's pattern.

docs.title: Family snippet / sources
docs.text: We compared circle boundaries with yarn and designed a repeating circle pattern. Catholic connection: honest measurement, including uncertainty. Ask: "How did you decide which circle was bigger around?" Optional: point out two circles in a room or picture; no materials/device required. No routine homework. Pi explanation gives definition and approximate value. CCC 159 concerns faith and science; the classroom honesty connection is an application, not an official benchmark. Ecclesiastes 3:11 may be read from a school-approved Bible; no unverified quotation is reproduced.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Growth / Growing Things Time / domains Three 30-minute meetings at roughly weekly intervals / C, S, M Big idea Repeated observations show changes; unequal growth alone does not explain causes. Student objective "I can observe a seedling, measure the same way, and describe what changed." Why Growers use records and responsible care, not guesses or tallest-plant contests. Catholic connection Care for plants/resources, honestly report no growth too; CCC 2415. The Sower is a faith parable, not an experimental explanation. Standards Local CST-C3: care/resource choice; CST-S1: dated observation/question; CST-S3: seed/seedling model; CST-M1: height comparison; CST-M2: dated record/class display. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path. A teacher photo of changes is optional, not required. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes first setup plus 2-3 minutes school-day care check; 5 minutes cleanup each meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Check school seed/potting-mix allergy guidance. Select one untreated bean or radish variety; read packet depth/water guidance. No fertilizer, pesticides or edible harvest in class.
  2. Prestart two teacher backup pots 7-10 days earlier. Draw three dated backup observations if live growing conditions are unavailable; clearly identify teacher/picture data.
  3. Teacher makes drainage holes before class. Put pots in leakproof trays by a safe bright indoor window, not on a freezing sill/heater. No electrical grow light required.
  4. Mark a height baseline at the soil surface. Assign a named adult to check moisture on school days and before weekends; water when needed, not automatically daily. Keep care at school, including school breaks or arrange approved adult care.
  5. Make a three-column record: date / drawing / height. Leave "no shoot yet" distinct from a missing measurement.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Per student: one folded record sheet, pencil/crayon, individual roster check.
  • Per team of 2-3: one pot with drainage, two seeds, about 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, ruler or equal cubes; measuring tool reused.
  • Class: one small water jug, scoop, spill cloth, handwashing access, board display.
  • Teacher-only: seed packet, hole tool, backup pots, plant care log; optional plant pictures.
Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 teacher backups Potting mix including 2 backup pots Student sheets 10 4 12 1.2 L 10 15 5 14 1.4 L 15 20 7 18 1.8 L 20 25 9 22 2.2 L 25

At 25 keep materials on nine table trays. Teacher controls the water jug; no queue carrying wet pots. Rotate observer, measurer, recorder roles and still collect each child's record.

docs.title: Vocabulary / teacher background
docs.text: Seed = contains a young plant and stored food; germinate = begin growing; seedling = young plant; nutrient = substance needed for growth; data = recorded observations. Many seeds need water, oxygen and suitable temperature to germinate. Seedlings need light for making food, plus water/air/nutrients and support. Soil is a useful growing medium, not plant food or a universal requirement; plants can grow without soil under appropriate conditions. This is a longitudinal observation, not a controlled experiment proving needs. Misconception: an unsprouted seed means its caretaker was bad or lacked faith. If asked "Why did mine not grow?" Seed viability, temperature, water and other factors may matter; our records do not isolate the cause.

docs.title: Meeting 1: plant and predict (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Show seed/seedling; state objective and care boundary. Optional original prayer asks for careful stewardship.
  2. 4-8: Explain seed food versus seedling needs; demonstrate packet-based planting depth and soil-surface ruler baseline.
  3. 8-18: Teams scoop mix, plant two seeds, lightly water according to packet and label pot/date. Each child draws what is visible and predicts a future change orally.
  4. 18-22: Make a care log and place pots in trays; choose an adult checker. Explain that not every seed will sprout.
  5. 22-25: Individual evidence: point to seed/seedling, name one care action and one observation.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Meeting 2: observe and measure (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve pots; compare to first dated drawing, not another team's tallest plant.
  2. 4-8: Teacher models height from soil surface to top of shoot, same tool each time. Grade 1 may use equal cubes; Grade 2 nearest whole cm. Do not include pot height.
  3. 8-19: Each child measures or points to the baseline and records one observation; record "no visible shoot" truthfully. Compare own two dates. Teacher checks individuals while partners work.
  4. 19-23: Inspect moisture with teacher and update care log; discuss what we know versus what we cannot yet explain.
  5. 23-25: Optional Sower paraphrase (Matthew 13:3-9) and care reflection: plant growth is not a score for anyone's faith.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Meeting 3: communicate changes (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall measurement baseline and previous record.
  2. 4-13: Final measurement/drawing using same units; each student compares two dated observations.
  3. 13-19: Display one current height per team on class chart; separate "no shoot" from "not recorded." Grade 2 explains why different heights do not identify one cause.
  4. 19-23: Pairs present change/no change and a question. Keep plants at school unless a family chooses a free take-home plant; provide teacher care instead where needed.
  5. 23-25: Individual exit: show two dated observations and one responsible care decision.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What changed since that date? Where does the ruler start? What if a seed does not sprout? Does our evidence prove why plants differ? - Grade 1: two dated drawings, correct baseline demonstration, longer/shorter/same comparison and one care action, all oral/drawn. - Grade 2: at least two dated measures in the same units and explanation of change; distinguish observation from an untested cause. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for observation, measurement, comparison and care; never grade germination success or home participation.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: No sprouts: retain genuine record and measure backup plant; do not relabel teacher data as student's. Mold: teacher removes affected pot sealed, cleans tray per school policy, supplies pictures. No bright window/no live growing allowed: use the three dated teacher drawings and equal-length paper plant models; assess reading/comparing observations, not live plant care mastery. Indoor work remains available all Minnesota winter; no outdoor planting required.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: No tasting seeds/plants/mix, unknown soil, spraying faces, standing water near electronics, student puncturing or glass pots. Wash hands. Teacher handles spill/mold and packet safety. Support: prefilled pots, picture steps, accessible table, adult scribing, thick equal blocks; nonreaders point/draw/tell. Challenge: Grade 2 use differences between two heights or propose a future fair test without claiming this one proves it.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Return tools, wipe trays/tables, put labeled pots safely back, wash hands and store records; adult checks care outside meetings. Family snippet: We kept dated plant records and compared change honestly, including no growth. Our Catholic connection was stewardship. Ask: "What did your evidence show, and what are you still wondering?" Optional: notice a plant or picture at home; no seed purchase, watering homework or device required. CCC 2415; optional Matthew 13 and 1 Corinthians 3:6 references use school-approved Bible (wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Seed-specific timing/depth must be verified against the selected packet; no universal sprouting deadline is promised.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes STREAM Focus E (Engineering), S (Science), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Design and build a project related to new life/spring 2. Observe signs of new life in nature 3. Apply engineering design process 4. Connect science of life cycles to project

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect new life in nature to Jesus's Resurrection 2. Understand that Easter brings new life 3. Recognize God's power over death and darkness

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Resurrection and New Life — At Easter, we celebrate Jesus rising from the dead. Spring shows us new life all around — flowers blooming, butterflies emerging, baby animals being born. Creation reflects the Resurrection!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: John 11:25; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching historical details
docs.text: St. Mary Magdalene — She was the first to see Jesus risen from the dead on Easter morning. She went from sadness to JOY when she saw that new life had conquered death.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Pictures of spring/new life (butterflies, flowers, baby animals)

  • Building materials: paper, cardboard, pipe cleaners, pom poms

  • Scissors and tape

  • Spring nature items (optional: seeds, flowers)

  • Resurrection story visual

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Easter Prayer: "Risen Jesus, You conquered death and brought us new life! As we see new life in spring, help us remember Your Resurrection. Alleluia! Amen."

Signs of new life:

  • "What signs of spring do you see?"

  • List: flowers, butterflies, baby birds, green leaves, longer days

  • "After the cold and darkness of winter, new life comes!"

Faith Connection: "Easter is like the biggest spring ever! Jesus was in the dark tomb, but He rose to new life. He's stronger than death!"

docs.title: Engineering Challenge Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Today's Challenge: Build something that shows NEW LIFE

Options: 1. Butterfly — Design a butterfly with moving wings 2. Flower — Create a flower that can "bloom" (open and close) 3. Bird Nest — Build a nest that can hold eggs 4. Anything else that shows new life in spring!

Design criteria:

  • Shows the idea of "new life"

  • Has at least one moving or interactive part

  • Uses available materials creatively

docs.title: Design & Build (16 min)
docs.text:
Quick plan (3 min):

  • Choose your project

  • Sketch your idea

  • List materials

Building time (13 min): Students create their new life projects.

Teacher prompts:

  • "How does this show new life?"

  • "What's your moving part?"

  • "What would make it better?"

Encourage creativity:

  • There's no one right way!

  • Try different approaches

  • It's okay if it's not perfect

docs.title: Sharing & Closing (5 min)
docs.text:
Quick share: Students show creations and explain:

  • "This shows new life because..."

  • "It moves like this..."

Faith Connection: Spring growth can be a reminder of Easter hope, not a scientific demonstration of resurrection. A dormant plant and developing chrysalis are living, not dead and resurrected.

Closing Prayer: "Risen Jesus, thank You for the gift of new life! Thank You for spring, for Easter, and for the promise that we will live forever with You. Help us share the joy of Your Resurrection with everyone we meet. Alleluia! Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Created a project representing new life

  • Included an interactive or moving element

  • Explained how project connects to new life theme

  • Connected spring/new life to Resurrection

docs.title: SAFETY / indoor default / evidence
docs.text: Use paper flowers with a folded opening petal as the default; no real eggs, animal collection, sharp wire ends or body-worn moving parts. Indoor spring pictures work in any weather. Grade 1 shows opening/closing twice and draws a change; Grade 2 explains one revision after a failed opening. Use final 3 building minutes for cleanup. Artistic symbolism does not establish biological causation.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text:
"We celebrated new life today! Your child made a project showing spring and new life. Ask them: 'How does your project show new life?' 'How is Easter like spring?' Look for signs of new life together in your neighborhood. Talk about how Jesus's Resurrection is the ultimate new life!"

This is Year B of a two-year rotation, not a curriculum requiring Year A completion. docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus S (Science), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Use observation skills to explore nature 2. Record observations through drawing and words 3. Ask scientific questions about what they observe 4. Follow classroom routines and expectations

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Express wonder at God's creation 2. Identify themselves as explorers of God's world 3. Practice thankfulness for nature

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Wonder at Creation — God made the world and called it "good." Scientists explore this good creation, discovering its beauty and order. When we observe nature carefully, we see God's handiwork.

docs.text: St. Kateri Tekakwitha — A Native American saint who loved nature and saw God in the forests, rivers, and animals. She teaches us to find God in creation.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text:
Gather in Circle

docs.title: Introduction: We Are Scientists! (5 min)
docs.text:
What do scientists do?

  • Look carefully (OBSERVE)

  • Ask questions (WONDER)

  • Try things (EXPERIMENT)

  • Share what they learn (COMMUNICATE)

Year B welcome:

  • "This year we'll explore God's creation in NEW ways!"

docs.title: Nature Observation Activity (15 min)
docs.text:
Observation stations (rotate every 5 min):

Station 1: Touch & Feel

  • Various natural objects in bags

  • Feel without looking

  • Describe textures

Station 2: Look Closely

  • Magnifying glasses

  • Examine leaves, rocks, feathers

  • What details do you notice?

Station 3: Sorting

  • Natural objects to sort

  • By color? Size? Texture?

  • Make groups and explain why

Wonder questions throughout:

  • "What do you notice?"

  • "What do you wonder?"

  • "Why do you think it looks like that?"

docs.title: Recording Observations (5 min)
docs.text:
In science journals:

  • Draw ONE thing you observed

  • Write or dictate one thing you noticed

  • Write or dictate one question you have

docs.title: Closing (3 min)

Share one wonder:

  • Each student shares one thing they noticed OR wondered

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for eyes to see, hands to touch, and minds to wonder. Thank You for St. Kateri who shows us how to love nature. Help us be curious scientists who see Your love in everything. Amen."

docs.title: SAFETY / access
docs.text: Teacher screens clean large specimens; no wild feathers, droppings, mold, unknown plants, tasting or forced mystery-bag touch. Children may look at pictures instead. Grade 1 tells/draws two details and a question; Grade 2 sorts by two evidence-based properties. Technology: None primary path. Use final 3 observation minutes for return/handwashing; retain observations, not participation alone.
