docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Dash Robot Adventures Time / domains Two 30-minute meetings / C, T, M Big idea A program is stored instructions; driving by joystick is a different kind of input. Student objective "I can run a short stored program and use a test to improve it." Why Responsible designers predict, test and share tools fairly. Catholic connection Respect every partner's contribution and agency; teacher application of human dignity and solidarity, CCC 2407. People are not robots obeying a programmer. Standards Local CST-C2: inclusive turn-taking; CST-T1: show input/output and stop; CST-T2: order/debug code; CST-M1: compare travel to target. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Required primary path: Dash and compatible tablet with Blockly, because children execute physical robot programs. Unplugged alternative assesses sequences, not robot operation. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first setup plus manufacturer charging time; 4 minutes cleanup/meeting.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Confirm actual loan, model, school-approved app/permissions and charging guidance. Use Blockly's official description and the installed block guide; do not assume generic Forward/Stop labels.
  2. Test a short program on the actual floor: drive forward 20 cm at low speed; turn right 90 degrees; drive forward 20 cm. Write installed block labels/settings on board and show Run/Stop.
  3. Mark 1 m dry floor bays and a paper target 20 cm ahead, clear of exits. Keep observers outside each bay.
  4. Make three picture cards and a tabletop token. Assign teams of 2-3 with programmer, observer and safety-checker roles; swap after each run.

docs.title: Supplies / scaling
docs.text:
• Per student: half-sheet, crayon, teacher roster evidence box.
  • Per team: one charged robot/tablet kit, three cards, token, 20 cm target strip.
  • Whole class: tape, timer, soft paper target, whiteboard; no obstacle course needed.
  • Teacher-only: chargers and installed app guide; cords stay stored during class.
Students Teams / kits for simultaneous practice Papers 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

At 25 use one supervised station with three 4-minute waves of three teams if only three kits exist; other teams rehearse with cards. If only one kit exists, teacher demonstration plus limited turns is partial device assessment: record children awaiting a turn, not universal mastery. Reduce moving robots to what the adult can safely supervise.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Input = our instructions; output = movement/light; sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; debug = find/change a mismatch; distance = how far. Blockly executes connected blocks. Manual Go control is not evidence of writing stored code. A robot may veer due to floor/charge; distinguish this from a wrong block. Misconception: coding success is driving fastest. Accuracy and explanation matter. If asked "Does God program us?" No. People make meaningful choices; this lesson's Catholic connection is responsibility and inclusion, not mechanical obedience.

docs.title: Meeting 1 (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3: State safe stop signal and sharing objective. Optional original prayer: "God, help us include every partner and learn honestly from our tests."
  2. 3-7: Predict a tabletop three-card sequence; each child moves token once.
  3. 7-11: Teacher shows stored Blockly program and contrasts with manual driving; demonstrate Run and Stop before student use.
  4. 11-23: Teams execute tested short programs. Each child predicts, runs/stops and compares ending to target; swap roles. Grade 1 may begin with forward plus light; Grade 2 adds the turn/second movement.
  5. 23-26: Individual oral/drawn exit: show input and output; order cards matching own run. Teacher records actual device participation.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Meeting 2 (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Recall the previous run; new entrants rehearse two cards rather than needing Year A.
  2. 4-8: Teacher deliberately makes the first movement too short; model prediction, observation and one distance change.
  3. 8-20: Each child changes one block/parameter, reruns and compares to target. Grade 2 describes nearer/farther before and after; no automatic maze completion or expertise claim.
  4. 20-24: Pairs show original versus changed sequence and explain output. Optional finite repeat of a light/wait sequence for ready Grade 2 children.
  5. 24-26: Individual evidence check and remaining-turn roster.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / measurable success
docs.text: What is stored before you press Run? How is this different from driving? Which instruction caused a change? How did your group include everyone? - Grade 1: point to/orally order two actions, personally start/stop one stored run with supervision, show a change and one equitable turn choice. - Grade 2: build/order three actions, predict the ending, change one instruction and explain observed improvement using nearer/farther or measured distance. - Record 0 not observed / 1 prompted / 2 independent for each child's sequence, device operation, debug and inclusion. No credit for a teammate's run.

docs.title: If things go wrong / no-device and indoor fallback
docs.text: Connection: check correct robot and charge once; switch after two minutes, explicitly noting unassessed device skills. Token fallback uses the same prediction/change sequence; assess CST-T2 only, not Dash programming/operation mastery. Veering: stop and lower speed/shorten path on a flat surface. All work is indoors; no weather dependency.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Low-speed dry floor bays only; stop if robot crosses boundary. Never chase, race, ride or hold a running robot. Teacher handles charging/cables. Safe accessible tabletop token alternative is available without stigmatizing a child. Support: picture cards, narration, adult scribing, two actions and large buttons; nonreaders never copy typed directions. Challenge: Grade 2 explains two trials or a finite light loop, not sensors/autonomous navigation.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Stop, save only to school-controlled device as permitted, power down, count kits/cards, clear lesson tape and return to labeled trays; teacher charges. Family snippet: We predicted and debugged stored robot instructions and shared turns respectfully. Ask: "What input changed the robot's output?" Optional: move a paper token with three spoken instructions; no device or purchase. No routine homework. Blockly official app; CCC 2407. Solanus Casey biography is optional and VERIFICATION REQUIRED before use; it is not needed to assess patience.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Observation / Senses and Discovery Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A Big idea Different safe tools/senses reveal different details; everyone can contribute evidence. Student objective "I can describe two details and compare two objects using a safe way to observe." Why Observations support comparisons without requiring every child to use every sense. Catholic connection Respect dignity and access; do not compare a child's body to another as better/worse. Teacher application of CCC 2407. Standards Local CST-C2: choose an inclusive observation method; CST-S1: describe two details; CST-A1: sketch observed detail; CST-M2: sort by a stated property. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: direct observation suffices. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Screen clean large textured objects: cloth, smooth plastic lid and corrugated cardboard. Remove scents, food, feathers, spices and unknown plant materials.
  2. Teacher seals two identical rice shakers permanently, checks leakage and never opens them in class. Alternative: teacher claps two gentle sound patterns; children can observe motion instead of listening.
  3. Put texture examples and two lids of visibly different sizes at each table. Draw a two-box observation sheet on the board; folding plain paper suffices.
  4. Offer look, safe optional touch, or picture/tactile replica; never surprise-touch or blindfold a child. Show quiet space and opt-out choices.

docs.title: Supplies
docs.text:
• Per student: one folded sheet, crayon.
  • Per team of 2-3: three large clean texture examples, two smooth lids; optional plastic magnifier.
  • Whole class: two permanently sealed shakers, timer, sorting mat, handwashing.
  • Teacher-only: shaker sealing/checking, roster, object screening; no taste/smell supplies.
Students Teams / texture sets Papers 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

At 25 use table work plus one teacher sound demo; no five-station traffic or shared mouth instruments.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Observe = notice safely; texture = surface feel or appearance; compare = describe what is alike/different; evidence = noticed detail; sort = group by a property. Sight/hearing/touch are options, not requirements. Scientists use instruments when direct senses are unavailable or unsafe. Tasting an unknown substance is never a scientific observation method for this class. Misconception: a guessing game answer matters more than evidence. "Bumpy ridges" is better evidence than "I think it is a shell." If asked "Why aren't we tasting?" Taste can expose allergens/unsafe substances; today's objectives need no food.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: State objective, access choices and safe touch rule; optional original prayer thanks God for each person's contributions.
  2. 4-8: Teacher models two details on cardboard using looking and optional touch; contrast observation with guess.
  3. 8-17: Teams examine texture examples; each child draws/points/describes two details. Partner compares two objects using rough/smooth, size or visible ridges. Teacher checks individuals.
  4. 17-21: Teacher demonstrates quiet sealed shaker sounds or gentle claps with visible movement. Children compare patterns by hearing or seeing; no requirement to hear.
  5. 21-26: Each child sorts two objects by one stated property and explains/draws evidence. Grade 2 sorts same objects a second way. Partners name a method that includes someone who chooses not to touch/hear.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup and handwashing.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What did you notice rather than guess? Which observation method is safe for you? Can the same objects be grouped another way? - Grade 1: oral/pointed/drawn two details, one alike/different comparison and one grouping reason; choose an accessible method. - Grade 2: two precise details, two defensible grouping rules and an explanation that a different method can still supply evidence. - Teacher marks not yet / prompted / independent for details, sorting and inclusion; never scores use of all senses.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Leaking shaker: remove immediately and use claps/visible motion. Sensory overload: quiet visual/tactile table by choice. Missing objects: use large teacher drawings with visible texture marks; distinguish pictured observations from touch evidence. Entire lesson is indoors and no-device ready.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: No tasting, smell jars, blindfolds, reaching into unknown bags, loud shaking near ears, loose beans/rice or forced touch. Teacher seals and counts shakers. Respect sensory and physical access without implying anyone is less blessed. Support: two picture choices, sentence starter "I notice...", oral response, larger objects and adult scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 justify two classifications or ask what a magnifier might reveal.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Return/count objects, wipe washable surfaces per school practice, recycle scraps and wash hands. Family snippet: We compared details using safe accessible observation methods. Our Catholic connection was including every observer. Ask: "What detail helped you sort an object?" Optional: describe a familiar object or picture together; no tasting or purchase. No routine homework. CCC 2407; Psalm 139:14 is an optional reference in a school-approved Bible, not an unverified quotation. Isidore's specific sensory practices are not historical evidence and are omitted.

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus E (Engineering), M (Math), S (Science)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Apply engineering design process to build tall structures 2. Explore concepts of balance, stability, and height 3. Measure height using non-standard and standard units 4. Test, iterate, and improve designs

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect towers to the Tower of Babel story 2. Understand the difference between prideful building and serving others 3. Work cooperatively as a team

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED
docs.text: Genesis 11 is a theological story to read from an approved source, not a guarantee that a faithful engineer's structure succeeds. Good engineers learn from failed models and can serve others without a winning tower.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Psalm 127:1; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Joseph the Worker — Patron of workers and craftsmen. He built things with his hands to provide for his family and serve others, not for pride.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• KEVA planks (large supply)

  • Measuring tools (rulers, non-standard units)

  • Recording sheets

  • Images of famous towers

  • Building area with crash zones

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, help us be good builders today. Not builders who are proud, but builders who work together and help others. Bless our hands and minds as we create. Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: Famous Towers (5 min)
docs.text:
Show images:

  • Leaning Tower of Pisa

  • Eiffel Tower

  • Church steeples

  • Lighthouse towers

Discussion:

  • "Why do people build towers?"

  • "What makes a tower stay up?"

  • "What makes a tower fall down?"

Tower of Babel connection:

  • Tell brief story: People built a tower to make themselves famous

  • "God wants us to build to SERVE others, not to brag"

  • "Today we'll build towers to learn engineering!"

docs.title: Engineering Investigation (8 min)
docs.text:
Key concepts:

Base:

  • Wider base = more stable

  • Demonstrate: One block base vs. four blocks base

Balance:

  • Weight must be even

  • Show: Unbalanced tower falls

Height:

  • Higher = harder to balance

  • Each level adds challenge

Let students explore:

  • What happens with different base sizes?

  • What happens when you add weight on top?

docs.title: Build Challenge Round 1 (12 min)
docs.text:
Challenge: Build the TALLEST tower you can!

Rules:

  • KEVA planks only

  • Must stand for 10 seconds

  • Work in partners

  • Stay in your area

Teacher circulates:

  • "How tall is your tower?"

  • "What happens when you add more?"

  • "Why do you think it fell?"

Measure towers:

  • Use hand spans or rulers

  • Record heights

docs.title: Closing (3 min)
docs.text:
Quick share:

  • What worked?

  • What made towers fall?

Preview: "Next time: even TALLER towers!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for teaching us about building. Help us use what we learn to help others. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "St. Joseph, you worked with your hands to serve your family. Help us work well today to build and learn. Amen."

docs.title: Review & Strategy (5 min)
docs.text:
What we learned:

  • Wide bases help

  • Balance matters

  • Adding slowly works better

New strategies:

  • Cross-patterns for stability

  • Layer building

  • Checking balance before adding

Challenge announcement:

  • "Today: tallest tower that can hold a small weight on top!"

  • Added difficulty: Must support a small object

docs.title: Tower Engineering Challenge (18 min)
docs.text:
Phase 1: Build (12 min)

  • Partners work together

  • Build tallest stable tower

  • Prepare to add weight

Phase 2: Test (6 min)

  • Add small weight to top (eraser, small ball)

  • Must stand for 10 seconds with weight

  • Measure final height

Recording:

  • Tower height (in hand spans or inches)

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Motion / Ramp Races: compare rather than race Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, M Big idea Changing one test condition and keeping others alike helps us compare results. Student objective "I can release the same car without a push and compare its stopping distances." Why Evidence, repeated tests and honest records are useful beyond competition. Catholic connection Honest evidence and respect for others' results; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159. Physical laws are not the moral meaning of Catholic natural law. Standards Local CST-C1: distinguish data/guess; CST-S2: keep fair-test conditions; CST-S3: gravity/motion model; CST-M1: measure distance; CST-M2: two-condition results. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: direct measurement; no speed sensor or video needed. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Test a 40-50 cm rigid cardboard ramp with one and two thin books, maximum support height 10 cm. Tape securely in a shallow tray/table lane with end catch box; runout cannot enter an aisle.
  2. Mark fixed starting point and ramp-end line. Use same toy car, ramp, lane and release method for both heights. Do not change cars or landing surfaces during this test.
  3. Prepare two-column low/high recording paper; teacher makes a shared example.
  4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, personal prediction.
  5. Per team of 2-3: one car, ramp, two books, tape, measuring strip of equal 2 cm marks or equal cubes, catch box.
  6. Class: timer, class chart; reusable kits.
  7. Teacher-only: ramp preflight, height check, roster. No small loose balls or launched loads.
Students Teams / complete ramp kits Individual sheets 10 4 10 15 5 15 20 7 20 25 9 25

At 25 use nine parallel table lanes only if table area contains each run. Otherwise three supervised lanes with three 4-minute waves; off-lane teams predict and compare teacher example data. Record any student not observed releasing/measuring.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Gravity = Earth's pull on objects; distance = how far; trial = one test; condition = test setting; fair test = keep important things the same except the planned change. At these small classroom heights gravity is effectively unchanged. A higher starting position can provide more gravitational potential energy. Runout depends on ramp/surface/car; farther stopping distance does not measure speed directly, and results may differ. Misconception: gravity pulls harder from a higher ramp. It does not in this setup. If asked "Which car was faster?" We measured stopping distance, not time/speed; that needs a different test.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3: Explain comparison objective and lane rule; each child predicts low/high/same by pointing.
  2. 3-7: Model no-push release and measuring from ramp end to car's final front position; count equal units, always same reference.
  3. 7-10: Identify what stays the same and changed book height; pairs rehearse roles: releaser, measurer, recorder.
  4. 10-22: Run three low and three high trials per team, swapping roles. Record each result, including surprises; Grade 1 uses marks/cubes, Grade 2 whole cm if ready. Do not force a predicted pattern.
  5. 22-26: Each child points to one result for each condition, compares, and names one controlled feature; ask whether the trials agree.
  6. 26-30: Cleanup.

docs.title: Questions / measurable evidence
docs.text: Did you push? Where does measurement start? What changed? Does one result prove a rule for every car? - Grade 1: release without push, compare one low/high result orally or with drawn lengths, name same car/start. - Grade 2: record at least two trials per condition, compare spread/typical result informally, name one changed and two unchanged features; no required averages. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for release, measurement and evidence-based comparison. Winning a race is not assessed.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Car leaves lane: stop, lower ramp and add catch sides. Car does not roll: inspect wheels/ramp join and retest at same low setting; document change. Inconsistent results are valid; revisit release and surface. No kits: teacher demonstrates while children compare honest shared results, noting direct manipulation not individually assessed. Indoors year-round, no devices needed.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: Ramp below 10 cm; gentle releases only; cars not projectiles. No heavy loads, standing on furniture, chasing or lanes across routes. Teacher approves stable supports. Support: prebuilt lane, two trials per condition with scaffolded comparison, tactile equal-unit strip, scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 proposes a later different-surface test while explaining why not to combine changes today.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Park/count cars, detach only lesson tape, stack books/ramps, store data. We tested ramp heights and compared measured stopping distances with honest records. Ask: "What did you keep the same?" Optional: describe a ramp seen in a picture or school; no home experiment required. No routine homework. CCC 159. Physics explanation uses standard elementary mechanics; official benchmark alignment remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Albert the Great biography is optional and must be verified before adding.

docs.text: Thanksgiving is a form of prayer; CCC 2637-2638. Do not present a four-item classroom mnemonic as the Catechism's exhaustive classification.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Thérèse of Lisieux — Found joy in small things and was constantly grateful. Her "Little Way" teaches us to thank God for everyday blessings.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• iPads with ScratchJr

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, thank You! Thank You for families, food, friends, and fun. Thank You for this school and for each other. Help us create projects today that show our gratitude. Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: Gratitude Coding (5 min)
docs.text:
What are you thankful for?

  • Quick brainstorm: family, pets, food, home, friends, toys, nature

  • "St. Thérèse was thankful for even SMALL things"

  • The specific attributed "flowers" saying is unverified; omit it. Children can express their own gratitude without an attributed quote.

Today's project:

docs.title: Planning (3 min)
docs.text:
Think about YOUR project: 1. What are 2-3 things you're thankful for? 2. What characters will say these things? 3. What background fits?

Quick sketch:

docs.title: ScratchJr Creation (17 min)
docs.text:
Step-by-step guidance:

Step 1: Choose background

  • Find a thankful scene

  • Home, nature, table scene

Step 2: Add character

  • Choose a person, animal, or object

  • Place on screen

Step 3: Add speech

  • Find speech bubble block

  • Type "I'm thankful for ___________!"

  • Add wait time

Step 4: Add more!

  • Another character?

  • Another thankful thing?

Stretch challenges:

  • Two characters have a conversation

  • Add sound effects

  • Multiple scenes

Teacher circulates:

docs.title: Sharing (3 min)
docs.text:
Quick gallery walk or partner share:

  • Tell them what you're thankful for

Celebration:

  • "You can share this with your family"

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
St. Thérèse connection:

  • "She found joy in tiny blessings"

  • "What 'small thing' are you thankful for?"

  • "Gratitude is a kind of PRAYER!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for EVERYTHING — big and small. Thank You for the creativity to make projects that share our gratitude. Help us be thankful people every day, not just at Thanksgiving. Amen."

docs.title: Technology / nonreader / privacy
docs.text: Required primary path: school-approved ScratchJr tablets for executed code. Grade 1 dictates or records a short message instead of typing; demonstrate green-flag plus two ordered actions. Grade 2 changes one action and explains output. No devices: paper panels and oral sequence/debug; no app-operation/executed-program mastery claim. Do not upload names/photos/voices outside approved storage. Use final 3 creation minutes for save/return/cleanup. Optional home discussion needs no tablet.

docs.text: St. Nicholas — Famous for giving gifts in secret. He gave to those in need without expecting anything in return. He inspires our gift-giving at Christmas.

St. Nicholas story:

docs.text: John 8:12; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Biblical connection
docs.text: Matthew 2 describes Magi and a star; their number and modern scientific profession are not established there. Read an approved retelling (VERIFICATION REQUIRED); do not use the story as scientific evidence for a particular astronomical event.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Flashlights

  • Star projector or pin-prick star jars

  • Black paper

  • Sequins, foil

  • Light exploration materials

  • Magi story resources

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, You created the stars in the sky — billions of them! You placed a special star to guide the Wise Men to Jesus. Help us learn about Your amazing lights in the sky today. Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: What Are Stars? (8 min)
docs.text:
Stars are suns!

  • "Our sun is a STAR"

  • "Other stars are so far away they look tiny"

  • "There are BILLIONS of stars — God made them all!"

Wonder questions:

  • "Have you ever looked at stars at night?"

  • "What did you notice?"

  • "Why do they twinkle?"

The Christmas Star:

  • Tell the story of the Magi

  • "The story describes Magi following a star; it does not give a modern scientific profession."

  • "They saw a special star and followed it"

  • "Their journey is a faith account, distinct from today's measured light investigation."

Key learning:

  • Stars give light

  • A special star guided the Wise Men

  • Light helps us find our way

docs.title: Star Exploration (10 min)
docs.text:
Activity options:

Option A: Pin-prick star jars

  • Teacher-prepared paper constellation cards with holes made by an adult hole punch; no glass jars, metal lids or student pins.

  • Flashlight inside creates "stars"

  • Observe patterns

Option B: Constellation cards

  • Look at constellation patterns

  • Connect dots to see shapes

  • Count stars in each

Discussion:

  • "How many stars can you see?"

  • "Do you see any patterns?"

  • "What shapes do the stars make?"

docs.title: Star Art (8 min)
docs.text:
Create a star scene:

  • Black paper for night sky

  • Gold/silver stars (various sizes)

  • Include one BRIGHT star (Christmas star)

  • Optional: Add Magi following the star

While creating:

  • "The Wise Men followed the star for a LONG journey"

  • "They trusted the light would lead them"

  • "Jesus is the light we follow!"

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Faith connection:

  • "The Magi story and our star observations are different kinds of accounts."

  • "Science and faith go together!"

  • "Jesus is the brightest light of all"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for stars that light up the night. Thank You for the special star that led the Wise Men to Jesus. Help us follow Jesus, the Light of the World. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Jesus, You are the Light of the World. Help us learn about light today and remember that You guide our way. Amen."

docs.title: Review & Light Properties (5 min)
docs.text:
Review:

  • What did we learn about stars?

  • Who followed the Christmas star?

Light properties to explore:

  • Light travels in straight lines

  • Light can be blocked (shadows!)

  • Light bounces (reflection)

  • Light can make patterns

docs.title: Light Investigations (18 min)
docs.text:
Rotation through stations:

Station 1: Shadow Play

  • Flashlight + objects

  • What shapes do shadows make?

  • How does moving the light change shadows?

Station 2: Light Lines

  • Shine flashlight through tubes

  • Does light go around corners?

  • Light travels STRAIGHT!

Station 3: Sparkle and Reflect

  • Shine light on shiny things

  • Where does the light go?

  • What makes things sparkle?

Station 4: Color Exploration

  • Colored cellophane over flashlight

  • What colors appear?

  • What happens when colors overlap?

Teacher questions throughout:

  • "What do you observe?"

  • "What happens when you...?"

  • "Why do you think that happened?"

docs.title: Light of the World Art (3 min)
docs.text:
Quick creation or addition to star art:

  • Add light rays to their star scene

  • Draw how light spreads out

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Connection:

  • "Light helps us SEE"

  • "Light guides our way in darkness"

  • "Jesus does the same for us — He helps us see truth and guides our lives!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, Jesus, for being our Light. When we're confused, help us see clearly. When we're lost, guide us like the star guided the Wise Men. Shine through us so others can see Your love. Amen."

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence / cleanup
docs.text: Low-power flashlights only; no lasers, flames, glass, sun viewing or beams at eyes. Keep enough light for safe aisles; dim only while seated. Replace loose sequins/glitter with foil or crayon patterns. Light travels approximately straight in a uniform medium; reflection/refraction can change direction. Grade 1 shows a blocking/reflecting observation orally; Grade 2 compares one changed light position. Reserve 3 activity minutes each meeting for cleanup. Technology: None primary path; projector optional.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We explored stars and light! Ask your child: 'What are stars?' 'Who followed the Christmas star?' 'What did you learn about light?' We connected Jesus as the 'Light of the World' to physical light. On a clear night, look at stars together. Talk about how the Wise Men followed a star to find Jesus."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Explained that stars are distant suns

  • Explored light properties through investigation

  • Connected Christmas star to Magi story

  • Created star-themed art

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Teacher information Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Winter / Winter Wonders Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A, M Big idea Ice can melt; a symmetric model represents selected features, not every real snow crystal. Student objective "I can describe a change in ice and show a matching pattern in a paper model." Why Careful models and evidence replace absolute claims about nature. Catholic connection Each person's dignity does not depend on a perfect pattern or comparison to a snowflake; truthful wonder is a teacher application of CCC 159 and 2407. Standards Local CST-C1: distinguish model/observation; CST-S1: before/after observation; CST-S3: ice/water change; CST-A2: purposeful symmetry; CST-M2: matching/repeated pattern. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None primary path: teacher sketch or printed crystal photo; no online video needed. Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10 minutes plus freezing ahead; 5 minutes cleanup included.

docs.title: Before class / supplies
docs.text:
1. Put one small ice cube in each wide plastic tray shortly before class; obtain school freezer permission. Prepare a second melted-water tray for comparison if melting is slow.
  2. Show a vetted photograph/sketch of a six-branched snow crystal and an irregular clump. State sketches are models, not photos. No outdoor exposure required.
  3. Pre-fold paper once for Grade 1; teacher can pre-fold a six-sector paper for challenge, but sixfold folding is not required to learn reflection symmetry.
  4. Per student: paper, crayon, blunt scissors by ability or pre-cut shape.
  5. Per team of 2-3: tray, cube, towel, observation card.
  6. Class: two crystal examples, timer, sink, dry collection tray.
  7. Teacher-only: ice handling, backup water tray, scissors for difficult folds.
Students Teams / ice trays Cubes plus 2 backups Papers 10 4 6 10 15 5 7 15 20 7 9 20 25 9 11 25

At 25 trays stay at tables; one teacher collects water, never a crowd at the sink.

docs.title: Vocabulary / background
docs.text: Solid = keeps its shape here; liquid = flows/takes container shape; melt = solid ice becomes liquid water; symmetry = matching parts across a line; model = representation. Ice crystals often show sixfold structure; real flakes can be broken, irregular, columns, plates or clumps. We cannot prove "no two ever alike" by comparing a few. A fourfold cut-paper design is a symmetry model, not a claim that all snow crystals have four branches. Misconception: melting destroys water. It changes state. If asked "Why six branches?" Ice's crystal arrangement often produces sixfold forms; official detailed crystallography source is VERIFICATION REQUIRED before extending beyond this simple account.

docs.title: Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Observe the cube and draw its starting shape; state no tasting/touch requirement. Children predict change in warm room.
  2. 4-8: Compare crystal examples: notice patterns without universal claims. Model folding a sheet so two sides match.
  3. 8-18: Each child makes a mirrored paper design with cutouts or matched drawn marks. Grade 1 uses one fold/precut shapes; Grade 2 traces/checks a line of symmetry and explains model limitations. Teacher checks individual's pattern.
  4. 18-22: Observe ice tray again, compare before/after and the prepared water tray if needed. Record "still ice" honestly; distinguish observed versus teacher-provided sample.
  5. 22-25: Individual exit: identify ice/water change and show two matching model features; state paper is a model, not real snow.
  6. 25-30: Cleanup/drying.

docs.title: Questions / success
docs.text: What changed? What stayed water? How can you check whether these marks match? Does our model show every kind of snow? - Grade 1: oral/drawn before/after comparison and two matching features across a fold. - Grade 2: identify solid/liquid, mark/check a symmetry line and explain one model limitation; report no melting if that was the observation. - Teacher scores not yet / prompted / independent for change, matching features and model distinction. Fine cutting quality is not scored.

docs.title: If things go wrong / indoor fallback
docs.text: Ice not melted: compare to labeled teacher-prepared liquid sample, keep real observation and discuss more time; never claim child observed complete melting. No ice access: use teacher-drawn dated change sequence; assess explanation/model, not firsthand change observation. No scissors: fold and draw matching marks. All work indoors at -10 F.

docs.title: SAFETY / support / challenge
docs.text: No snow collection, ice tasting, frozen-metal contact, hot water, food, glass or outdoor cold exposure. Water stays in trays away from electrical equipment. Teacher dries spills immediately. Blunt scissors with demonstrated carrying rule or precuts. Support: picture choices, scribing, larger fold lines, no forced touching. Challenge: Grade 2 compare reflection and repeated radial patterns without claiming every flake is perfect.

docs.title: Cleanup / family / sources
docs.text: Teacher empties trays, pupils wipe tables, return scissors, collect paper scraps; floor must be dry before leaving. Family snippet: We observed ice changing and used paper to model matching patterns. Catholic connection: honest wonder and equal dignity. Ask: "How was your paper model different from real snow?" Optional: find a matching pattern indoors or in a picture; no cold-weather activity required. No routine homework. CCC 159 and CCC 2407. NOAA snow-crystal page retrieval was blocked during review; detailed crystal claims remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Psalm 147:16 may be read from a school-approved Bible; no attributed quotation is reproduced.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus M (Math), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Understand measurement as tracking change 2. Set simple, achievable goals 3. Create a visual goal tracker 4. Understand growth over time

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Recognize that God wants us to grow 2. Set goals for kindness and faith, not just skills 3. Trust God to help us grow

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Growth in Virtue — God calls us to grow — not just taller, but in love, kindness, and faith. Setting goals helps us cooperate with God's plan for our growth.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Luke 2:52; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Saint Pier Giorgio Frassati — Canonized September 7, 2025; Vatican source. Specific student/goal anecdotes are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Height measuring chart

  • Goal-setting worksheets

  • Growth tracker templates

  • Crayons/markers

  • Plant seeds or seedlings (optional)

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, You helped Jesus grow in wisdom and love. Help us grow this year too — not just taller, but kinder, smarter, and closer to You. Show us how to set good goals. Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: Growing in Every Way (5 min)
docs.text:
Growth conversation:

  • "How do you know you're growing?" (taller, bigger shoes, learning more)

  • "You grow in ways you can SEE and ways you CAN'T see"

Luke 2:52 — Jesus grew in:

  • Wisdom — Learning and understanding

  • Stature — Body growing

  • Favor with God — Faith and prayer

  • Favor with man — Kindness and friendship

All four matter!

Saint Pier Giorgio (anecdotes VERIFICATION REQUIRED):

  • "He was a student who worked hard at school"

  • "He was also very kind and helped poor people"

  • "He loved to climb mountains AND pray"

  • "He grew in EVERY way!"

docs.title: Measuring Physical Growth (5 min)
docs.text:
Quick measurement activity:

  • Measure heights (or hands, or shoe length)

  • Record numbers

  • "We'll measure again later to see growth!"

Math connection:

  • "Numbers help us track change"

  • "We can SEE growth when we measure"

docs.title: Setting Growth Goals (12 min)
docs.text:
Four goal areas (matching Jesus):

1. Learning Goal (Wisdom):

  • "What do you want to LEARN this year?"

  • Examples: Learn to read better, learn math facts, learn about animals

  • Write or draw goal

2. Body Goal (Stature):

  • "How will you take care of your body?"

  • Examples: Run faster, eat healthy foods, get enough sleep

  • Write or draw goal

3. Faith Goal (Favor with God):

  • "How will you grow closer to God?"

  • Examples: Pray every day, learn a new prayer, listen at Mass

  • Write or draw goal

4. Kindness Goal (Favor with People):

  • "How will you be kind to others?"

  • Examples: Share more, include someone lonely, help at home

  • Write or draw goal

Create goal page:

  • Four sections

  • Draw or write each goal

  • Decorate!

docs.title: Growth Tracker (4 min)
docs.text:
Simple tracker:

  • Chart or sticker system

  • Check off when working on goals

  • "Growth takes TIME and PRACTICE"

Plant connection (if available):

  • Plant a seed together

  • "Just like this seed will grow, YOU will grow!"

  • "We'll watch it and watch ourselves grow too"

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Encouragement:

  • "Growing takes time — be patient with yourself"

  • "God is always helping you grow"

  • "Even when it's hard, keep trying!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for helping us grow. Help us keep our goals and become more like Jesus — wise, healthy, faithful, and kind. When we struggle, help us try again. We trust You to help us grow. Amen."

docs.title: Privacy / Grade 1 / follow-up
docs.text: Compare lengths of classroom objects rather than public body-height rankings. Grade 1 selects one classroom action, draws/dictates first step; Grade 2 may choose four goals. Track at school; revisit next opening. Never publicly rank bodies, prayer or home resources, or assess strength of faith from a tracker. Technology: None primary path. Last 2 planning minutes tidy supplies; no required home care/planting.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We chose classroom growth goals and first steps. Ask your child to tell or show a step they can practice. Trackers stay at school; optional conversation needs no purchase or home tracking."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Participated in measurement activity

  • Set goals in multiple areas

  • Created goal page/tracker

  • Connected growth to faith

Lesson Version: 1.0 — Year B | **

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 4 sessions (30 min each) Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus Student-Directed (All Areas)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Identify problems and brainstorm solutions 2. Design and build original creations 3. Test ideas and iterate 4. Present inventions and explain thinking

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. See themselves as creative like God 2. Design inventions that help others 3. Practice perseverance when things don't work

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Human Creativity — Made in God's image, we share in His creativity. Inventors use their God-given imagination to solve problems and help others. When we create, we reflect our Creator!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Isaiah 43:19; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Vocation connection
docs.text: Health-care workers, designers and neighbors can solve problems in service of others. Thomas Dooley's cause status and specific invention claims were not verified and are omitted; no saint title is assigned.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Recycled materials collection

  • Cardboard, tape, glue

  • Craft supplies

  • Simple tools (kid-safe scissors)

  • Invention planning sheets

  • Testing space

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, You are the great Creator. You made us creative too! Help us think like inventors today — seeing problems and imagining solutions. May our ideas help others. Amen."

docs.title: What is an Inventor? (8 min)
docs.text:
Discussion:

  • "What is an inventor?"

  • "What inventions do you use every day?"

  • Pencils, zippers, velcro, books...everything was invented!

Inventor mindset:

  • "I see a problem"

  • "I wonder how to fix it"

  • "I try something"

  • "If it doesn't work, I try again!"

Service example: A classroom helper asks for a tray to carry three paper balls between tables. Ask the user's preference and test a safe model; medical invention stories require verified sources before use.

docs.title: Finding Problems to Solve (10 min)
docs.text:
Brainstorm problems:

  • "What's hard to do?"

  • "What could be better?"

  • "What does someone need?"

Categories:

  • School problems (carrying things, organizing)

  • Home problems (reaching, cleaning)

  • Play problems (storing toys, playing games)

  • Helping problems (pets, siblings, parents)

Choose YOUR invention focus:

  • Pick ONE problem you want to solve

  • Draw the problem

  • Think: Who would this help?

docs.title: Initial Sketches (8 min)
docs.text:
Draw your invention idea:

  • What will it look like?

  • What will it do?

  • What materials might you need?

Not perfect — just IDEAS!

Share with partner:

  • Explain your problem

  • Explain your invention idea

  • Get feedback

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Preview: "Next time: Start building!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for creative minds. Help us think of ways to help others. Bless our invention ideas! Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Creative God, guide our hands today as we build. When things don't work, help us keep trying. Amen."

docs.title: Planning Review (5 min)
docs.text:
Review your invention plan:

  • What problem are you solving?

  • What will you build?

  • What materials do you need?

Get materials:

  • Choose from available supplies

  • Think creatively — what could work?

docs.title: Building Time! (20 min)
docs.text:
Create your invention!

Inventor rules:

  • It doesn't have to be perfect

  • It's okay if it doesn't work the first time

  • Ask for help when stuck

  • Be safe with materials

Teacher circulates:

  • "Tell me about your invention"

  • "What problem does it solve?"

  • "What's working? What's tricky?"

When stuck:

  • Try a different material

  • Try a different shape

  • Ask a friend for ideas

  • Look at other inventions for inspiration

docs.title: Progress Check (3 min)
docs.text:
Quick share:

  • Show your progress

  • What's working?

  • What do you still need to figure out?

Closing Prayer: "Thank You for time to build today. Help us keep working on our inventions. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, help us test our inventions and make them better. When things don't work, give us perseverance to try again. Amen."

docs.title: Testing Phase (12 min)
docs.text:
Test your invention:

  • Does it work?

  • Does it solve the problem?

  • What happens when you use it?

Inventor observation:

  • What works well?

  • What doesn't work?

  • What could be better?

Record results:

  • Draw what happened

  • Note what to change

docs.title: Improvement Phase (13 min)
docs.text:
Make it better!

Iteration — the inventor's secret:

  • "Real inventors never get it right the first time"

  • "They try, learn, and improve"

  • "That's called ITERATION"

Make changes:

  • Fix what didn't work

  • Add features

  • Strengthen weak parts

  • Make it look better

Test again:

  • Does the improvement help?

  • Keep adjusting!

docs.title: Closing (3 min)
docs.text:
Perseverance reflection:

  • "Was it hard when things didn't work?"

  • "What helped you keep trying?"

  • "Inventors never give up!"

Preview: "Next time: Share your inventions!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for perseverance. Help us keep trying even when it's hard. Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Thank You, God, for these weeks of inventing. Help us share our creations with joy. May our inventions inspire others! Amen."

docs.title: Final Preparations (5 min)
docs.text:
Get ready to share:

  • Final touches on invention

  • Practice your explanation

  • Set up display

docs.title: Invention Fair (18 min)
docs.text:
Each inventor presents: 1. "The problem I wanted to solve was..." 2. "My invention is called..." 3. "Here's how it works..." 4. "I want it to help..."

Demonstration:

  • Show the invention

  • Show how it works

  • Let others try it (if appropriate)

Audience response:

  • "I like how you..."

  • "I wonder if..."

docs.title: Celebration (5 min)
docs.text:
Inventor celebration:

  • Everyone clap for everyone!

  • "You are ALL inventors!"

  • "You used your God-given creativity"

Inventor certificates or stickers.

Faith connection:

  • "God is the ultimate Creator"

  • "You are made in His image"

  • "When you create, you're like God!"

  • "Keep inventing ways to help others!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for making us creative. Thank You for the problems that make us think and the inventions that help people. Help us keep seeing problems as opportunities to create solutions. Bless these young inventors! Amen."

docs.title: SAFETY / assessed default / indoor fallback
docs.text: All inventions are tabletop models: no medical use, human loads, electrical mains, hot/sharp tools, body restraints, projectiles or animal testing. Screen recyclables. Default tray criterion: hold three crumpled paper balls for five seconds without spill; change one fold and retest. Grade 1 tells/draws a test/change; Grade 2 records two outcomes and defends the revision. At 25 use partner/table demonstrations rather than 25 long talks. Reserve final 4 making minutes each meeting for cleanup. Technology: None primary path; recycled cardboard supports all weather.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We had an Invention Lab! Your child designed and built an original invention to solve a problem. Ask them: 'What problem did you solve?' 'How does your invention work?' 'What was hard?' 'What did you learn?' Encourage inventing at home — cardboard boxes are great invention materials!"

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Identified problem to solve

  • Designed and built invention

  • Tested and improved design

  • Presented invention and explained thinking

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 30 minutes Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus All Areas (Celebration)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Demonstrate STREAM learning to visitors 2. Explain what they've learned this year 3. Work as a team on group activities 4. Share enthusiasm for STREAM with others

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Articulate what makes Catholic schools special 2. Demonstrate faith integration in STREAM 3. Welcome and serve visitors

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Catholic Education — Catholic schools teach faith AND reason together. STREAM shows that science and faith are partners, not enemies. We celebrate learning about God's world!

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 22:6; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED
docs.text: Elizabeth Ann Seton is associated with Catholic education; use a vetted biography. Do not claim she founded the first Catholic school in America; Catholic schools predate her work.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Station materials (varied)

  • Display materials

  • Visitor name tags

  • Celebration supplies

  • Student work samples

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, thank You for our Catholic school! Thank You that we learn about Your world AND about You. Help us share what we've learned today and welcome our visitors with joy. Amen."

docs.title: What Makes Us Special? (5 min)
docs.text:
Catholic Schools Week discussion:

  • "Why is our school special?"

  • "What do we do in STREAM?"

  • "How is it different from regular STEM?"

Key message:

  • "We learn science and faith TOGETHER"

  • "We see God in everything we learn"

  • "We learn to serve others with our skills"

St. Elizabeth Ann Seton:

  • "Her educational contribution needs a verified biography; the 'first Catholic school in America' claim is omitted."

  • "She wanted children to learn AND grow in faith"

  • "Our school continues her mission!"

docs.title: Station Preparation (8 min)
docs.text:
Set up celebration stations:

Station 1: Robot Show

  • Dash Robot demonstration

  • Simple coding explanation

  • Visitors try basic commands

Station 2: Building Challenge

  • KEVA structure display

  • Invite visitors to build

  • Tower challenge!

Station 3: Science Wonder

  • Show nature collections

  • Share "I wonder" questions

  • Magnifying glass exploration

Station 4: Invention Gallery

  • Display inventions from lab

  • Explain problems solved

  • Show creativity!

Assign students to stations:

  • Practice explanations

  • Know what to say

  • Be welcoming!

docs.title: Celebration Time (12 min)
docs.text:
Visitors rotate through stations OR stations are open exploration

Student roles:

  • Explain the activity

  • Help visitors participate

  • Share what you learned

  • Show how faith connects

Teacher circulates:

  • Support students

  • Engage visitors

  • Celebrate!

docs.title: Closing (3 min)
docs.text:
Thank visitors:

  • "Thank you for celebrating with us!"

  • "We love learning at our Catholic school!"

Class reflection:

  • "What was it like to share with visitors?"

  • "What questions did people ask?"

  • "What are you proud of?"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for Catholic Schools Week. Thank You for visitors who celebrated with us. Thank You for a school where we learn about You in everything. Bless our school, our teachers, our families. Amen."

docs.title: Technology / SAFETY / staffing
docs.text: Recommended primary path: supervised Dash/tablet demonstration; no-device alternative uses saved design/test evidence and cards, not robot mastery. If no visitors/extra adults, partners share at tables and perform one measured demonstration each. No unsupervised moving robot station; low-speed marked bays and towers below 30 cm. Visitors follow school safeguarding/photo policies. Reserve final 3 activity minutes for cleanup; assess an individual's explanation, not visitor attendance.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We celebrated Catholic Schools Week in STREAM! Your child helped lead activities and share learning with visitors. Ask: 'What station did you help with?' 'What did you tell visitors?' 'What makes our Catholic school special?' Thank you for choosing Catholic education!"

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Participated in station activities

  • Explained STREAM learning to visitors

  • Welcomed and helped others

  • Articulated Catholic school identity

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus E (Engineering), S (Science), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Understand cause and effect relationships 2. Create simple chain reaction machines 3. Work collaboratively on team projects 4. Test and refine designs

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect chain reactions to ripple effects of kindness 2. Understand how small acts lead to big effects 3. Design machines with kind purposes

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Ripple Effect of Love — One act of kindness leads to another. Just like a chain reaction machine where one action triggers the next, our kindness creates ripples that spread far beyond what we see.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: Proverbs 11:25; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Thérèse of Lisieux — Her "Little Way" teaches that small acts of love add up to great things. Each tiny kindness is like a domino that starts a chain reaction of good!

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Dominoes

  • Cardboard tubes (paper towel, toilet paper)

  • Ramps and tracks

  • Small balls

  • Books for supports

  • Tape

  • Simple machine examples

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, help us learn about chain reactions today. Help us see how our small actions can start big things — especially our acts of kindness! Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: Cause & Effect (6 min)
docs.text:
What is a chain reaction?

  • "One thing causes the next thing"

  • "Like dominoes falling!"

Demonstration:

  • Set up small domino chain

  • One push → many dominoes fall

  • "ONE action → MANY effects!"

Rube Goldberg machines:

  • Show video or images of elaborate machines

  • "These silly machines do simple tasks in complicated ways"

  • "They're fun to make and watch!"

Kindness connection:

  • "Kindness works like chain reactions"

  • "YOU smile at someone → THEY feel happy → THEY'RE kind to someone else → and on and on!"

  • This is a teacher kindness metaphor, not a verified saying of Therese. Kindness does not mechanically guarantee another person's response.

docs.title: Simple Chain Experiments (12 min)
docs.text:
Experiment 1: Domino Lines

  • Line up dominoes

  • Test spacing — too far? Too close?

  • Push the first one — watch the chain!

Experiment 2: Ramp Chain

  • Ball rolls down ramp

  • Hits something at bottom

  • That thing moves or does something

Experiment 3: Tube Tunnel

  • Ball goes through tube

  • Exits and triggers next step

Discovery questions:

  • "What happens if they're too far apart?"

  • "What happens if something is in the way?"

  • "How can you make it work better?"

docs.title: Design Challenge Introduction (8 min)
docs.text:
Challenge:

  • Design a "Friendship Machine"

  • A chain reaction that ends with something kind

  • Examples: Delivers a note, rings a bell, waves a flag that says "You're Great!"

Planning:

  • What will your machine DO at the end?

  • What steps will lead to that?

  • Draw a simple plan

Teams:

  • Work in small teams

  • Share ideas

  • Start gathering materials

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Preview: "Next time: Build your Friendship Machines!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for chain reactions. Help us start good chain reactions with our kindness today! Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "St. Thérèse, teach us your Little Way. Help us do small things with great love today. Amen."

docs.title: Building Phase (18 min)
docs.text:
Teams build their Friendship Machines!

Requirements:

  • At least 3 steps in the chain

  • Must end with something "kind" (delivers message, rings chime, etc.)

  • Must work when tested

Building tips:

  • Test each step as you build

  • If one part doesn't work, fix it before moving on

  • Be patient — it takes many tries!

Teacher circulates:

  • Help troubleshoot

  • Encourage perseverance

  • Ask about the kind purpose

When machines fail (they will!):

  • "That's how inventors learn!"

  • "What went wrong?"

  • "What could you change?"

  • "Try again!"

docs.title: Testing & Demonstration (8 min)
docs.text:
Teams demonstrate their machines:

  • Set up

  • Explain what will happen

  • START the chain!

  • (Celebrate successes and attempts!)

Share the kind purpose:

  • "Our machine delivers a 'You're Awesome' note!"

  • "Our machine rings a 'Kindness Bell!'"

docs.title: Reflection & Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Discussion:

  • "What was hard about chain reactions?"

  • "What happened when one part didn't work?"

  • "How is this like kindness?"

Kindness chain:

  • "Your kindness starts a chain reaction"

  • "You might not see all the effects"

  • "But it keeps going!"

Challenge: "This week, start a kindness chain reaction. Do something kind and watch what happens!"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for the fun of building and learning. Help us start kindness chain reactions everywhere we go. May our small acts of love create big ripples of good! Amen."

docs.title: SAFETY / evidence / cleanup
docs.text: Use large balls that cannot fit in a child's mouth, low tabletop ramps, catch boxes and dominoes; no projectiles, marbles, human loads or loud bells near ears. Teacher screens tubes/edges. Default ending: gently tip a paper kindness flag. Grade 1 orally explains two causal steps; Grade 2 shows three steps and a failed-link revision. Last 4 making minutes each meeting are cleanup. Technology: Optional primary path for a teacher-selected offline image/video; physical model works without screens.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We built Friendship Machines — chain reaction contraptions with kind purposes! Ask your child: 'How does a chain reaction work?' 'What did your machine do?' We learned that kindness creates chain reactions too. Challenge: Do an intentional act of kindness together and watch for the ripple effect!"

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Understood cause and effect

  • Created functional chain reaction

  • Worked cooperatively in team

  • Connected machines to kindness ripple effects

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 1-2 Duration 2 sessions (30 min each) Curriculum Year B STREAM Focus S (Science), E (Engineering), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Identify what plants need to grow 2. Understand plant life cycles 3. Design a garden with purpose 4. Plant seeds and observe growth

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect plant growth to spiritual growth 2. Practice patience and care for living things 3. See gardening as stewardship of creation

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching doctrinal details
docs.text: Spiritual Growth — Just like plants need sun, water, and soil, our faith needs nourishment too — prayer, Mass, kindness. Jesus often used plant parables to teach about faith.

docs.title: Scripture reference
docs.text: 1 Corinthians 3:6; VERIFICATION REQUIRED: use the school's approved Bible; no quotation reproduced.

docs.title: Saint Connection - VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching biographies
docs.text: St. Fiacre — Patron saint of gardeners who saw gardening as prayer. He cared for God's creation and fed the poor from his garden.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Seeds (fast-growing: beans, sunflowers)

  • Soil

  • Cups or pots

  • Water

  • Garden design paper

  • Plant life cycle images

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Dear God, You created plants that give us food, beauty, and oxygen. Help us learn to care for Your green creation today. May our gardens grow and teach us about growth! Amen."

docs.title: Introduction: Plant Needs (8 min)
docs.text:
What do plants need to grow?

  • ☀️ Sunlight — Energy from the sun

  • 💧 Water — Drink for the plant

  • 🪴 Growing medium — Support and nutrients; soil is not plant food. Plants make food using light; appropriate soilless growth is possible.

  • 💨 Air — Plants breathe too!

Like us!

  • We need food, water, air, and care

  • Plants are living things too!

  • We're stewards — caretakers — of plants

St. Fiacre connection:

  • "He was a monk who loved gardening"

  • "He grew food for poor and hungry people"

  • "Gardening was his prayer to God"

  • "We can make gardening a prayer too!"

docs.title: Plant Life Cycle (6 min)
docs.text:
The circle of life: 1. Seed — This is the start of our selected flowering-plant example, not every kind of plant. 2. Sprout — First little plant emerges 3. Seedling — Baby plant grows 4. Adult plant — Full-grown, makes flowers 5. Flowers & fruit — Makes new seeds! 6. Seeds — And it starts again!

Show images or diagram.

Wonder:

  • "Isn't it amazing that a tiny seed becomes a big plant?"

  • "A seed has a young plant and stored food; it still needs suitable water, oxygen and temperature to germinate, then light and nutrients to grow."

docs.title: Planting Activity (10 min)
docs.text:
Plant your seeds!

Steps: 1. Fill cup with soil (not too packed) 2. Make small hole with finger 3. Place 2-3 seeds 4. Cover gently with soil 5. Water carefully (not too much!) 6. Label with name

Teacher demonstrates each step.

Care instructions:

  • Keep soil moist (not soggy)

  • Put in sunny spot

  • Check the selected untreated seed packet for possible timing; growth is not guaranteed in 5-7 days.

docs.title: Faith Connection (2 min)
docs.text:
Spiritual growth:

  • "Plants need water, sun, and care to grow"

  • "OUR faith needs nourishment too!"

  • "Prayer is like water for our souls"

  • "Mass is like sunshine for our faith"

  • "Kindness is like good soil"

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Take home or leave at school:

  • Care for your plant this week

  • Observe what happens

  • Be patient!

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for seeds and growth. Help us care for our plants and learn from them. As our plants grow, help OUR faith grow too! Amen."

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: "Creator God, You planted the Garden of Eden. Help us design beautiful gardens today that honor You and help others. Amen."

docs.title: Plant Check & Share (3 min)
docs.text:
How are plants doing?

  • Any sprouts yet?

  • What do you observe?

  • Are you caring for them?

docs.title: Garden Design Challenge (10 min)
docs.text:
Design a dream garden!

Garden purposes:

  • Food garden — Vegetables and fruits to eat

  • Flower garden — Beauty and butterflies

  • Helping garden — Vegetables for food shelf

  • Prayer garden — Quiet space to pray

  • Pollinator garden — Flowers for bees and butterflies

Choose your garden type:

  • What's the PURPOSE of your garden?

  • Who will your garden help?

Design elements:

  • What will you plant?

  • Where will paths go?

  • Any special features? (Bench, statue, birdbath)

docs.title: Draw Your Garden Design (12 min)
docs.text:
Create a garden plan:

  • Bird's eye view (from above)

  • Show what's planted where

  • Label plants

  • Include special features

  • Color it!

Design thinking:

  • "What do your plants need?"

  • "Where will the sun be?"

  • "How will you water them?"

  • "Who will enjoy this garden?"

docs.title: Sharing Gardens (3 min)
docs.text:
Quick gallery walk or partner share:

  • Show your garden design

  • Explain the purpose

  • Tell who it helps

Celebration:

  • "You are garden engineers!"

  • "Real gardens start with plans like these"

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
St. Fiacre challenge:

  • "Can you care for a plant this spring?"

  • "Can you help with gardening at home?"

  • "Can you notice plants and thank God for them?"

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for the gift of gardens. Thank You for St. Fiacre who showed us gardening is prayer. Help us care for plants and see Your love growing all around us. Amen."

docs.title: SAFETY / school care / constraints
docs.text: Teacher makes drainage holes; plastic pots in leakproof trays, no tasting mix/seeds/plants or pesticides, handwashing required. Name an adult to check moisture on school days/weekends/breaks; water when needed, not automatically. School care is the default; home care is voluntary. Indoor bright space/pictures replace outdoor planting in winter. Grade 1 shows two plant needs and an access path orally; Grade 2 revises a plan to fit a 30 x 40 cm model with clear 10 cm care strip. Reserve 5 making minutes each meeting for cleanup. Technology: None primary path.

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection (optional; no routine homework)
docs.text: "We planted seeds and designed gardens! Your child has a growing plant to care for. Help them water it and watch for growth. Ask: 'What do plants need?' 'What kind of garden did you design?' 'Who would your garden help?' Consider planting something together this spring!"

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
• Identified plant needs

  • Planted seeds correctly

  • Designed purposeful garden

  • Connected plant growth to faith growth
