docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 2 sessions (45 min each) STREAM Focus S (Science), T (Technology), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Explain reflection and refraction with scientific accuracy 2. Diagram light ray paths through different media 3. Build and explain optical devices 4. Apply understanding to real-world technologies

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect Jesus as "Light of the World" to scientific light properties 2. Understand how light metaphors in Scripture relate to physical light 3. Appreciate optical science in understanding creation

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Light as Theological Symbol — Light appears throughout Scripture and Catholic tradition as a symbol of God, truth, and salvation. Understanding the physics of light deepens our appreciation of these theological truths.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." — John 8:12

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Robert Grosseteste - historical bishop associated with optics, not a canonized saint. Detailed biography and philosophical claims: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Do not present medieval theories as current physics.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Low-brightness flashlights only; no laser pointers

  • Mirrors (plane, concave, convex)

  • Lenses (convex, concave)

  • Prisms

  • Water containers for refraction

  • Ray tracing worksheets

  • Materials for optical device construction

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "God of Light, You created light on the first day of creation. You sent Jesus as the Light of the World. Help us understand the physics of light and see Your truth illuminated through it. Amen."

Wonder moment: "Light is the fastest thing in the universe — 186,000 miles per SECOND. Yet we can study it, predict it, and use it. Let's explore how light behaves."

docs.title: Reflection Deep Dive (12 min)
docs.text:
Law of Reflection:

Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection

Key terms:

  • Incident ray — Light approaching the mirror

  • Reflected ray — Light bouncing off

  • Normal line — Perpendicular to surface

  • Angle of incidence — Angle between incident ray and normal

  • Angle of reflection — Angle between reflected ray and normal

Demonstration: 1. Shine light at mirror 2. Measure angles 3. Verify: always equal!

Types of mirrors:

  • Plane mirror: Flat, virtual image, same size

  • Concave mirror: Curves inward, can magnify, real or virtual image

  • Convex mirror: Curves outward, always smaller virtual image, wider view

Real applications:

  • Car mirrors (convex for wide view)

  • Makeup mirrors (concave for magnification)

  • Telescope mirrors (concave to gather light)

Activity: Ray tracing with plane mirrors — predict and verify reflection angles.

docs.title: Refraction Exploration (13 min)
docs.text:
What is refraction?

  • Light bends when changing medium

  • Different media = different speeds

  • Speed change causes direction change

Snell's Law (conceptual):

  • Light bends TOWARD normal when slowing down (air → water)

  • Light bends AWAY from normal when speeding up (water → air)

Demonstration: 1. Pencil in water appears bent 2. Light through prism separates colors 3. Light through different lenses

Lenses:

  • Convex (converging): Thicker in middle, brings light together

  • Concave (diverging): Thinner in middle, spreads light apart

Real applications:

  • Eyeglasses

  • Cameras

  • Microscopes

  • Telescopes

Activity: Refraction observations — document light behavior through water and lenses.

docs.title: Faith-Science Connection (5 min)
docs.text:
Light symbolism in Scripture:

  • "Let there be light" — First act of creation

  • "Light of the World" — Jesus's identity

  • "Arise, shine, for your light has come" — Isaiah's prophecy

Connection: "Light REVEALS. Physical light lets us see. Jesus, as Light of the World, reveals truth, exposes sin, guides our path. The physics of light helps us understand these metaphors more deeply!"

History note: Grosseteste's historical ideas about light are not current physical theory. Use a verified historical source before presenting his views; VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: Preview (2 min)
docs.text: "Next session: We'll build optical devices and apply what we've learned!"

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Review (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, help us apply our understanding of light to create useful things. May our engineering be an act of worship and service. Amen."

Quick review:

  • What's the law of reflection?

  • What causes refraction?

  • Convex vs. concave lenses?

docs.title: Optical Device Engineering (8 min)
docs.text:
Challenge introduction:

Option A: Periscope

  • Uses mirrors to see over/around obstacles

  • Two plane mirrors at 45° angles

  • Application: Submarines, parades, trenches

Option B: Simple Telescope

  • Uses two convex lenses

  • Objective lens gathers light

  • Eyepiece lens magnifies

  • Application: Astronomy, nature observation

Option C: Camera Obscura

  • Pinhole projects inverted image

  • Basis of all photography

  • Application: Understanding how cameras work

Option D: Kaleidoscope

  • Multiple mirrors create patterns

  • Reflection creates symmetry

  • Application: Art, understanding reflection angles

Design requirements: 1. Understand the optics involved 2. Diagram the light path 3. Build functional device 4. Explain how it works scientifically

docs.title: Design & Diagram (8 min)
docs.text:
Planning:

  • Choose your device

  • Research/review how it works

  • Draw ray diagram showing light path

  • Plan construction

Ray diagram requirements:

  • Show incident and reflected/refracted rays

  • Label mirrors and/or lenses

  • Indicate angles where relevant

  • Show image formation

docs.title: Construction (18 min)
docs.text:
Build time!

Station materials available:

  • Mirrors and mirror holders

  • Lenses

  • Cardboard tubes

  • Tape and glue

  • Cardboard for construction

Teacher circulates:

  • "Explain the ray path in your device"

  • "What happens if you change this angle?"

  • "Where is the image formed?"

Troubleshooting guidance:

  • Not working? Check alignment

  • Image blurry? Adjust lens position

  • Dim? Check for light leaks

docs.title: Testing & Demonstration (5 min)
docs.text:
Test your device:

  • Does it work as expected?

  • Can you explain the optics?

  • What would improve it?

Peer demonstrations:

  • Show your device

  • Explain the science

  • Let others try it

docs.title: Closing Reflection (2 min)
docs.text:
Optical engineering applications:

  • Medical imaging

  • Communications (fiber optics)

  • Photography and film

  • Astronomy

  • Microscopy

Faith Connection: Light is a meaningful theological symbol; reflection/refraction are physical descriptions, not proof of theological claims.

Closing Prayer: "God of Light, thank You for the beauty and order in how light works. Thank You for scientists who helped us understand it and engineers who apply it. Help us be light to others, reflecting Your love and truth. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-S3 - individual reflection/refraction explanation; CST-T1 - safe optical-tool use; CST-A1 - labeled individual ray diagram. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: SAFETY AND PACING
docs.text: No lasers or looking at the Sun through any lens, mirror, telescope, periscope, or pinhole device. Use indoor targets and low-brightness flashlights away from eyes; plastic mirrors/lenses preferred, adult handles damage. Keep water in trays away from power. Meeting 1 originally allocated only 37 minutes: use remaining 8 as 4-minute individual diagram/exit and 4-minute cleanup, for 45 total. In meeting 2 reserve the last 4 construction minutes for cleanup preparation and return equipment during closing; devices stay dry and indoors.

docs.title: Session 1
docs.text:
• Explained reflection with law of reflection

  • Described refraction and lens behavior

  • Completed ray tracing activities

  • Connected light physics to faith symbolism

docs.title: Session 2
docs.text:
• Designed optical device with ray diagram

  • Built functional device

  • Explained optics scientifically

  • Connected learning to applications

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We explored advanced light science and built optical devices! Ask your child: 'What's the law of reflection?' 'Why does light bend in water?' 'How does your optical device work?' We connected physical light to Jesus as Light of the World. Look for optics in daily life — glasses, mirrors, cameras. How does understanding light help us appreciate Scripture's light imagery?"

Unit Version: 1.0 | Last Updated: 2025-12-05

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes STREAM Focus S (Science), M (Math), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Describe scale of the solar system and universe 2. Explain basic astronomical concepts 3. Use mathematical reasoning for cosmic calculations 4. Understand current space exploration

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect cosmic scale to God's infinite nature 2. Appreciate Catholic astronomers' contributions 3. Understand the Vatican Observatory's mission

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: The Vatican Observatory — The Church operates one of the oldest astronomical research institutions in the world. This demonstrates that faith and scientific exploration of the cosmos go hand in hand. Understanding the universe helps us appreciate its Creator.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands." — Psalm 19:1

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Fr. Georges Lemaitre - priest and physicist associated with expanding-universe cosmology. Detailed biography: VERIFICATION REQUIRED; the previously unsourced quotation is removed.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Scale model materials

  • Calculators

  • Planet data cards

  • Images of cosmic objects

  • Computer for visualizations (optional)

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord of the universe, Your creation extends beyond our imagination. As we explore the cosmos today, fill us with wonder and humility. Help us see Your glory in the heavens. Amen."

Wonder statistics:

  • Speed of light: 186,000 miles per second

  • Distance to nearest star: 4.24 light years

  • Stars in Milky Way: 200-400 billion

  • Observable universe: 93 billion light years diameter

  • Estimated galaxies: 200 billion+

Question: "How do we even BEGIN to understand such enormous scales?"

docs.title: Scale of the Solar System (12 min)
docs.text:
Scale model activity:

Distance-only indoor scale: 1 AU = 10 cm. Earth is 10 cm from the Sun marker; 1 AU is about 150 million km (NASA Earth facts). Thus 1 model cm represents about 15 million km. Planet marker sizes are not to this scale. Have each student place Earth and calculate a hypothetical 2 AU location (20 cm); do not mix planet-size objects with incompatible distances.

Optional eight-planet extension: obtain current mean distances from NASA's planetary fact sheet, record units, convert consistently, and teacher-check before use. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for that extension's values.

Key insight: "Space is mostly EMPTY. The planets are tiny compared to the distances."

Speed of light demonstration:

  • Light from Sun reaches Earth in 8 minutes

  • Light from Neptune: 4 hours

  • Light from nearest star: 4.24 YEARS

Calculate:

  • If you could drive to the Sun at 60 mph, how long? (177 years!)

  • To nearest star? (48 million years!)

docs.title: Beyond the Solar System (10 min)
docs.text:
Scale keeps expanding:

Milky Way Galaxy:

  • The Milky Way contains an estimated hundreds of billions of stars; stars and star systems are not interchangeable counts.

  • Takes 230 million years for Sun to orbit galaxy center

  • 100,000 light years across

Local Group:

  • Milky Way is one of 80+ galaxies in our "neighborhood"

  • Andromeda Galaxy: 2.5 million light years away (and approaching!)

Observable Universe:

  • Estimated 200 billion galaxies

  • Each with billions of stars

  • 93 billion light years diameter

The humbling math:

Stars in observable universe: ~10²⁴ (1 septillion) That's more stars than grains of sand on all Earth's beaches

docs.title: Catholic Astronomy (8 min)
docs.text:
Vatican Observatory:

  • Founded 1891 (but roots back to 1582)

  • Telescopes in Italy and Arizona

  • Jesuit astronomers conduct serious research

  • Why? "The Church has a long-standing commitment to understanding God's creation"

Fr. Georges Lemaître:

  • Catholic priest AND physicist

  • Proposed expanding universe theory (1927)

  • Called it the "hypothesis of the primeval atom"

  • Later called "Big Bang" by others

  • Scientific models describe expansion and early cosmic conditions; they do not by themselves establish a theological creation event. The unsupported Einstein quotation is removed.

No conflict!

  • "Big Bang describes HOW, faith addresses WHY"

  • "Science tells us the mechanism, faith tells us the meaning"

  • "The more we understand the universe, the more we can appreciate its Creator"

Faith reflection: "Psalm 19 says 'the heavens declare the glory of God.' When we look at the scale, the complexity, the beauty of the cosmos — how can we NOT be in awe of the Creator?"

docs.title: Personal Response Activity (8 min)
docs.text:
Creative response (choose one):

Option A: Scale poem Write a poem that expresses the scale of the universe and your response to it.

Option B: Calculation challenge Calculate: If you sent a message to Proxima Centauri (nearest star) and got a reply, how long would the round trip take? (8.48 years)

Option C: Cosmic reflection Write a response to this prompt: "What does the scale of the universe tell you about God? About yourself?"

Share responses briefly.

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Summary:

  • The universe is unimaginably vast

  • Catholic scientists have been at the forefront of understanding it

  • Scale humbles us but also shows the majesty of the Creator

  • Faith and astronomy work together

Closing Prayer: "God of the universe, we are tiny before Your creation, yet You know us and love us. Thank You for giving us minds that can explore Your cosmos. Thank You for scientists who help us understand. May we always see Your glory in the heavens. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-S3 - distinguish distance and size scales; CST-M3 - individual 1 AU/2 AU conversion; CST-C1 - distinguish a scientific model from a theological claim. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text:
All scale work is indoors; do not require a 900 m outdoor course or nighttime exposure. Never observe the Sun through optical equipment. Home stargazing is optional and adult-supervised; no routine homework.

  • Demonstrated understanding of solar system scale

  • Performed cosmic calculations

  • Engaged with Catholic astronomy contributions

  • Reflected on faith-science connection

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We explored astronomy and the scale of the universe! Ask your child about the scale model of the solar system. Ask: 'Who was Fr. Georges Lemaître?' 'What is the Vatican Observatory?' 'How do you feel when you think about how big the universe is?' Look at the stars together tonight. Psalm 19 says they 'declare the glory of God.'"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes STREAM Focus M (Math), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Apply SMART goal framework systematically 2. Break complex goals into measurable milestones 3. Create project timeline with dependencies 4. Use data tracking for progress monitoring

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect goal-setting to discernment and vocation 2. Include faith goals alongside personal/academic goals 3. Understand perseverance as a virtue

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Discernment and Direction — The Church encourages prayerful discernment about our path in life. While God has a plan, we cooperate through intentional choices. Goal-setting is a way to steward our time and talents responsibly.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future." — Jeremiah 29:11

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Ignatius of Loyola — Developed the Spiritual Exercises, a systematic approach to discernment and spiritual growth. He modeled intentional, goal-oriented spiritual development.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• SMART goal worksheets

  • Planning templates

  • Calendars (monthly, semester)

  • Tracking templates

  • Progress journal pages

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, You have a plan for each of us. Help us set goals that align with Your will. Give us wisdom to plan well and perseverance to follow through. May this new year bring growth in every area of our lives. Amen."

New Year reflection:

  • "What are you proud of from last year?"

  • "What do you want to be different this year?"

  • "Where do you sense God calling you to grow?"

docs.title: SMART Goals Deep Dive (10 min)
docs.text:
SMART Framework:

Letter Meaning Question S Specific What exactly do I want to accomplish? M Measurable How will I track progress? What numbers? A Achievable Is this realistic given my resources? R Relevant Does this matter to me? Does it align with my values? T Time-bound When will I complete this? What are deadlines?

Example transformation:

❌ Vague: "I want to be better at math." ✅ SMART: "I will improve my math grade from B- to B+ by May by completing all homework, attending tutoring twice weekly, and practicing 20 minutes daily."

❌ Vague: "I want to pray more." ✅ SMART: "I will pray for 10 minutes every morning before school for the next semester, using the Examen prayer method."

Practice together: Transform: "I want to be healthier" → SMART version

docs.title: Goal Categories & Setting (15 min)
docs.text:
Four goal categories:

1. Academic/Learning Goal

  • School achievement

  • New skill development

  • Reading/study habits

2. Physical/Health Goal

  • Exercise, sleep, nutrition

  • Sports improvement

  • Screen time management

3. Relationship/Service Goal

  • Family relationships

  • Friendship goals

  • Service to others

4. Faith/Spiritual Goal

  • Prayer habits

  • Mass participation

  • Scripture reading

  • Virtue development

Individual goal development:

  • Write ONE goal in each category

  • Apply SMART framework to each

  • Include measurement method

Peer review:

  • Share with partner

  • Check: Is it truly SMART?

  • Suggestions for improvement

docs.title: Project Planning (10 min)
docs.text:
Breaking down goals:

For your most important goal:

1. Identify milestones:

  • What are the major checkpoints?

  • Example: "Improve math grade" → (1) Complete all homework this month (2) Attend tutoring for 4 weeks (3) First quiz improvement (4) Mid-term grade check (5) Final grade

2. Create timeline:

  • Map milestones on calendar

  • Identify key dates

  • Build in buffer time

3. Identify dependencies:

  • What needs to happen first?

  • What resources do you need?

  • Who can help?

4. Tracking system:

  • How will you monitor progress?

  • Weekly check-ins?

  • Data to collect?

Create simple Gantt-style chart for one goal.

docs.title: Accountability & Closing (5 min)
docs.text:
Accountability structures:

  • Who will hold you accountable?

  • When will you check progress?

  • What happens if you fall behind?

Faith Connection: "St. Ignatius developed a systematic approach to spiritual growth — the Spiritual Exercises aren't random; they're carefully planned. God gives us the ability to plan, to set goals, to pursue growth intentionally. That's not unspiritual — it's good stewardship of our time and talents!"

Commitment:

  • Choose your #1 goal

  • Identify your accountability partner

  • Set your first milestone date

Closing Prayer: "Lord, bless these goals we've set. Help us pursue them with perseverance, adjust them with wisdom, and remember that all our plans are under Your greater plan. May this year be one of growth — academically, physically, relationally, and spiritually. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
Individual local check (not official): CST-E1 - name one criterion and dependency in a school-project goal; CST-M2 - represent three milestones on a timeline; CST-C3 - explain a time/resource constraint. Use project goals rather than compelled health/spiritual disclosures. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

  • Created SMART goals in all four categories

  • Developed milestone plan for one goal

  • Created timeline with checkpoints

  • Identified accountability structure

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We learned advanced goal-setting today! Ask your child to share their SMART goals in four areas: academic, physical, relational, and spiritual. Help them identify accountability strategies. Consider setting family goals together. How can you support each other's growth this year?"

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 4 sessions (45 min each) STREAM Focus Student-directed

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Design and manage an independent project 2. Conduct research and apply findings 3. Create meaningful output (product, program, presentation) 4. Present and defend their work

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect personal interests to serving others 2. Identify faith connections within their topic 3. Practice stewardship of God-given talents and interests

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Stewardship of Talents — God gives each person unique gifts, interests, and abilities. We're called to develop these fully and use them for good. Passion projects allow students to pursue God-given interests deeply.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters." — Colossians 3:23

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Saint Pier Giorgio Frassati - canonized September 7, 2025; his joyful service is described in the canonization homily. Additional biography: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Project proposal templates

  • Research resources

  • Building/making materials (varied based on projects)

  • Presentation materials

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, You have given each of us unique interests and gifts. Help us discover what YOU want us to explore. Guide our choices and bless our learning. Amen."

Passion project introduction:

  • "For the next four weeks, YOU choose what to learn"

  • "Deep dive into something that fascinates you"

  • "Must include STREAM elements"

  • "Must connect to faith"

  • "Must produce something shareable"

docs.title: Project Categories & Examples (10 min)
docs.text:
Categories:

Engineering/Building:

  • Design and build a robot

  • Create a kinetic sculpture

  • Engineer a solution to a problem

Programming/Technology:

  • Code a game or app

  • Build an interactive website

  • Create animations or digital art

Science Research:

  • Investigate a scientific question

  • Conduct experiments

  • Research and present findings

Making/Art:

  • Design and fabricate an invention

  • Create artistic work with technical elements

  • Build musical instruments

Service Design:

  • Design something that helps others

  • Create resources for a cause

  • Build accessibility tools

Faith connection requirement:

  • Historical Catholic connection?

  • Service/ethical dimension?

docs.title: Proposal Development (25 min)
docs.text:
Proposal requirements:

1. Project Description (What?)

  • What will you create or investigate?

  • Why does this interest you?

  • What will your final product be?

2. STREAM Connection (How?)

  • Which STREAM areas does this involve?

  • What skills will you develop?

  • What will you learn?

3. Faith Connection (Why does it matter?)

  • How does this connect to Catholic faith?

  • How might this serve others?

  • What values does this project express?

4. Plan & Timeline

  • Week 2 goal:

  • Week 3 goal:

  • Week 4 goal (presentation):

5. Resources Needed

  • Materials needed

  • Help needed

  • Research sources

Teacher conferences during work time:

  • Review proposals

  • Provide guidance

  • Approve projects

docs.title: Closing (5 min)
docs.text:
Proposal share:

  • Brief share of project ideas

  • Generate excitement

  • Identify potential collaborators

No routine homework: Finalize a bounded proposal in class. School supplies materials; family purchases/donations are never prerequisites.

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Status Check (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, bless our work today. Help us focus, persevere, and create something meaningful. Amen."

Quick status:

  • Where are you in your plan?

  • What do you need today?

  • Any obstacles?

docs.title: Research Phase (15 min)
docs.text:
Quality research:

  • Multiple sources

  • Credible sources (how to evaluate)

  • Take organized notes

  • Record citations

Teacher available for:

  • Research guidance

  • Source evaluation

  • Direction when stuck

docs.title: Development/Creation Phase (20 min)
docs.text:
Active work time:

  • Building

  • Programming

  • Creating

  • Experimenting

Teacher circulates:

  • Check progress

  • Troubleshoot

  • Encourage

  • Document work

docs.title: Progress Documentation (5 min)
docs.text:
Update project log:

  • What did you accomplish today?

  • What challenges did you face?

  • What's your plan for next session?

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Status (3 min)
docs.text: Prayer: "Lord, help us refine our work today. Give us attention to detail and commitment to excellence. Amen."

docs.title: Extended Work Time (35 min)
docs.text:
Focused creation time:

  • Continue building/creating

  • Refine and improve

  • Test and iterate

  • Prepare presentation elements

Mid-session check (brief):

  • How are you progressing?

  • What will you present?

  • What help do you need?

docs.title: Presentation Preparation (7 min)
docs.text:
Presentation requirements:

  • 4-5 minutes presentation

  • Show your work/product

  • Explain your process

  • Discuss faith connection

  • What you learned

  • What you'd do differently

Plan your presentation structure.

docs.title: Opening Prayer (2 min)
docs.text: Prayer: "Lord, thank You for these weeks of learning. Help us present well and learn from each other. May we celebrate the gifts You've given each person. Amen."

docs.title: Presentations (35 min)
docs.text:
Format: At 10/15/20/25 students, use paired portfolio exchanges: each student has 3 minutes to present plus 1 minute for a question, then switch. Teacher samples technical demonstrations using the individual logs; do not promise 25 plenary talks in 35 minutes.

Presentation elements: 1. What did you create/investigate? 2. Show/demonstrate your work 3. What did you learn? 4. How does this connect to faith? 5. What would you do next?

Audience:

  • Active listening

  • One positive comment

  • One thoughtful question

docs.title: Celebration & Reflection (8 min)
docs.text:
Celebrate:

  • Recognize achievements

  • Appreciate diversity of interests

  • Acknowledge growth and effort

Reflection questions:

  • What surprised you about this process?

  • What did you learn about yourself?

  • How might you continue this interest?

Faith Connection: Saint Pier Giorgio Frassati's service invites students to consider how their interests can serve others; use the verified canonization homily rather than unsourced details about studies or hobbies.

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for the unique gifts and interests You've given each of us. Thank You for these weeks to explore them. Help us continue developing our talents and using them for Your glory and others' good. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text: Individual local check (not official): CST-E1 - proposal criterion/constraint; CST-E2 - original test, revision, and retest; CST-E3 - supported conclusion and limit; CST-C3 - resource-use decision. Each student's dated log must contain all four; a finished group product is insufficient. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Teacher approves only safe classroom materials; no unsupervised bodily, medical, electrical, or chemical projects.

docs.title: Project Assessment
docs.text:
• Clear proposal with STREAM and faith connections

  • Consistent work across sessions

  • Quality final product/presentation

  • Reflection on learning

docs.title: Presentation Assessment
docs.text:
• Clear explanation of project

  • Demonstrated learning

  • Articulated faith connection

  • Responded to questions

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We completed passion projects! Each student chose a topic and created something meaningful over four weeks. Ask your child: 'What was your project?' 'Show me what you created!' 'What did you learn?' 'How did it connect to faith?' Encourage them to continue pursuing their interests — they're gifts from God!"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes STREAM Focus All Areas (Leadership Focus)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Design and lead STREAM activities for younger students 2. Explain concepts at appropriate levels 3. Manage group activities effectively 4. Demonstrate STREAM leadership

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Model servant leadership 2. Share what makes Catholic STREAM education distinctive 3. Demonstrate the integration of faith and reason

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Servant Leadership — Jesus modeled servant leadership: "Whoever wants to be great must be servant of all." Leading younger students in STREAM activities is an act of service that develops leadership while helping others.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity." — 1 Timothy 4:12

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. John Bosco — Patron of youth who pioneered engaging educational methods. He met young people where they were and used play, activity, and hands-on learning to teach both academics and faith.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Materials for teaching stations (varies)

  • Simple activity supplies

  • Teaching instruction cards

  • Assessment rubrics

  • Reflection journals

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Mission (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord Jesus, You showed us servant leadership. Help us lead younger students today with patience, kindness, and joy. May we share the gift of STREAM learning and our Catholic faith. Amen."

Catholic Schools Week context:

  • "This week we celebrate what makes Catholic schools special"

  • "Today YOU are the teachers"

  • "This is servant leadership in action"

Mission:

  • Design and lead a 10-15 minute STREAM activity for younger students

  • Activity must include faith connection

  • Must be hands-on and engaging

  • You'll present to K-2 or 3-4 classes (or parents/guests)

docs.title: Activity Design (15 min)
docs.text:
Choose or assign station topics:

Station A: Building Challenge

  • Simple structure challenge

  • Clear instructions

  • Faith connection: building together

Station B: Robot Demo

  • Demonstrate Sphero or Dash

  • Let visitors try simple commands

  • Faith connection: humans as creative like God

Station C: Code Introduction

  • Simple coding concept

  • Unplugged or device-based

  • Faith connection: order and logic in creation

Station D: Science Investigation

  • Simple experiment

  • Clear scientific question

  • Faith connection: discovering God's creation

Station E: Engineering Design

  • Simple design challenge

  • Engineering process

  • Faith connection: problem-solving to help others

Design requirements: 1. Opening (1 min): Welcome, faith connection, instructions 2. Activity (8-12 min): Hands-on engagement 3. Closing (2 min): What they learned, closing thought

Develop:

  • Script/outline for your station

  • Materials list

  • Practice explanation

  • Backup plan if something doesn't work

docs.title: Practice & Feedback (15 min)
docs.text:
Peer practice:

  • Run through your station with classmates

  • Time it

  • Get feedback

Feedback focus:

  • Is the explanation clear?

  • Is the activity engaging?

  • Is the faith connection natural?

  • What could be improved?

Refine based on feedback.

docs.title: Teaching Preparation (8 min)
docs.text:
Teaching tips:

  • Get down to their level (physically)

  • Speak slowly and clearly

  • Check for understanding: "Show me..."

  • Encourage, encourage, encourage

  • If something goes wrong, stay calm

  • Remember: relationship first

Servant leadership reminder:

  • "This isn't about showing off — it's about SERVING"

  • "Success = THEY learn and have fun"

  • "Your patience and kindness matter more than perfection"

Logistics:

  • Rotation schedule

  • Station locations

  • Materials placement

  • Transition signals

docs.title: Closing & Sending (2 min)
docs.text:
Commissioning:

  • "You represent STREAM and Catholic education"

  • "Be patient, kind, and joyful"

  • "You can do this!"

Closing Prayer: "Lord, bless our teaching today. Help us be patient and kind. May the younger students learn and have fun. May they see Your love through us. Give us confidence and joy. Amen."

docs.title: After Teaching: Reflection (follow-up)
docs.text:
Reflection questions: 1. What went well? 2. What was challenging? 3. How did you see growth in the students you taught? 4. What did YOU learn about teaching? 5. How did you integrate faith?

Leadership reflection:

  • What does it mean to be a servant leader?

  • How did teaching younger students change your understanding of the material?

  • How might God be calling you to use leadership skills?

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
Individual local check (not official): CST-C2 - explain a respectful access/servant-leadership decision; CST-E3 - teach one concept and check a peer's explanation during rehearsal. This 45-minute lesson plans/rehearses only. Actual buddy-class teaching requires separately booked time and adult supervision; no completed-teaching claim without that evidence. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

  • Designed appropriate activity

  • Led station effectively

  • Demonstrated patience and encouragement

  • Integrated faith naturally

  • Reflected on experience

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"During Catholic Schools Week, your 5th/6th grader led STREAM activities for younger students! Ask them: 'What did you teach?' 'How did it go?' 'What was challenging?' 'What did you learn about teaching?' We discussed servant leadership — leading by serving others. How does your child show leadership at home?"

docs.title: Unit Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 2 sessions (45 min each) STREAM Focus T (Technology), M (Math)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Create and use custom blocks (functions) 2. Implement cloning and object management 3. Use advanced list operations 4. Design multi-sprite interactive programs

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Connect programming organization to order in creation 2. Understand abstraction as reflecting God's hierarchical creation 3. Create programs that serve or teach others

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Order in Creation — God created an ordered universe with hierarchies and systems. Good programming mirrors this: organized code, clear structures, and elegant solutions. Excellence in coding reflects the Creator's excellence.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "For God is not a God of disorder but of peace." — 1 Corinthians 14:33

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Thomas Aquinas — Master of organized thinking who created the Summa Theologica with beautiful logical structure. His clear organization of complex ideas mirrors good code structure.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Computers with Scratch

  • Advanced concepts reference sheet

  • Project planning templates

  • Code organization guides

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, You created an ordered universe with beautiful systems. Help us write code that is organized, clear, and excellent. May our programming skills honor You. Amen."

Today's focus: "Level up your coding with custom blocks and cloning!"

docs.title: Custom Blocks (Functions) (12 min)
docs.text:
What are custom blocks?

  • Reusable code chunks

  • Like making your own Scratch block

  • Called "functions" in most languages

Why use them?

  • Avoid repeating code

  • Make code more readable

  • Easier to debug

  • Change once, works everywhere

Creating a custom block: 1. Go to "My Blocks" 2. Click "Make a Block" 3. Name it (descriptive!) 4. Add input parameters if needed 5. Define what it does

Example: 

Define [draw square (size)]
    Repeat 4
        Move (size) steps
        Turn right 90 degrees

Now you can use draw square (50) or draw square (100) anywhere!

Practice: Create a custom block for something you do repeatedly in your programs.

Parameters:

  • Make blocks flexible with inputs

  • draw polygon (sides) (size) — now it can draw ANY shape!

docs.title: Cloning (12 min)
docs.text:
What is cloning?

  • Creating copies of a sprite during runtime

  • Each clone acts independently

  • Great for: enemies, particles, projectiles, repetitive elements

How to clone:

  • create clone of [myself] — makes a copy

  • when I start as a clone — what the clone does

  • delete this clone — removes the clone

Example: Falling snow 

When green flag clicked
Forever
    Create clone of myself
    Wait 0.1 seconds

When I start as a clone
    Go to x: (pick random -240 to 240) y: 180
    Repeat until y position < -180
        Change y by -5
    Delete this clone

Clone properties:

  • Each clone has its own position, variables, appearance

  • Clones can interact with each other

  • Be careful: too many clones can slow things down!

Practice: Create a simple project using clones.

docs.title: Faith Connection (5 min)
docs.text:
Organized code as worship:

  • St. Thomas Aquinas organized complex theological ideas beautifully

  • His Summa has clear structure: questions, articles, objections, replies

  • Good code has similar organization

  • "Excellence in our work honors God"

Discussion: "When we write messy, disorganized code that 'just works,' we're settling for less than our best. When we write clean, organized code, we're exercising our God-given ability to create order."

docs.title: Work Time & Preview (12 min)
docs.text:
Begin project:

  • Start a project that uses custom blocks OR cloning

  • Must include faith connection in final product

Preview: "Next session: advanced lists and multi-sprite coordination!"

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Review (4 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Lord, continue to guide our learning. Help us create programs that are both technically excellent and meaningful. Amen."

Review: "What are custom blocks? What is cloning?"

docs.title: Advanced List Operations (10 min)
docs.text:
Beyond basic lists:

List operations:

  • length of [list] — how many items

  • item (1) of [list] — get specific item

  • item (last) of [list] — get last item

  • item (random) of [list] — random selection

  • [list] contains [thing] — check if item exists

List manipulation:

  • replace item (1) of [list] with [value] — update item

  • insert [value] at (1) of [list] — add at position

  • delete (1) of [list] — remove item

Practical uses:

  • High score tracking

  • Inventory systems

  • Quiz question banks

  • Conversation trees

  • Save/load game states

Example: Quiz from list 

Set [score] to 0
Set [question_num] to 1
Repeat (length of [questions])
    Ask (item (question_num) of [questions])
    If answer = item (question_num) of [answers] then
        Change score by 1
        Say "Correct!"
    Else
        Say (join "The answer was " (item (question_num) of [answers]))
    Change question_num by 1

docs.title: Multi-Sprite Coordination (8 min)
docs.text:
Sprites working together:

Broadcast messaging:

  • broadcast [message] — send to all sprites

  • when I receive [message] — respond to broadcast

  • Coordinates action across sprites

Example: Game states 

// In main controller sprite:
When green flag clicked
Broadcast "game start"

When [space] key pressed
Broadcast "game over"

// In player sprite:
When I receive "game start"
Show
Go to starting position

When I receive "game over"
Hide

Variable sharing:

  • Global variables: all sprites can see

  • Sprite-only variables: private to one sprite

  • Choose appropriately!

docs.title: Project Development (20 min)
docs.text:
Project options:

Option A: Educational Game

  • Quiz or learning game

  • Uses lists for content

  • Clones for game elements

  • Custom blocks for organization

Option B: Interactive Story

  • Multiple characters (sprites)

  • Broadcast messaging for coordination

  • User choices affect outcome

  • Lists for dialogue/options

Option C: Simulation

  • Model a system (ecosystem, physics, social)

  • Clones for multiple agents

  • Variables track state

  • Custom blocks for behaviors

Requirements:

  • Use at least TWO advanced concepts (custom blocks, cloning, advanced lists, broadcasting)

  • Clear organization

  • Faith connection (content or purpose)

  • Comments in code explaining sections

Work time with teacher support.

docs.title: Closing (3 min)
docs.text:
Share progress:

  • What are you creating?

  • Which advanced concepts are you using?

  • What's your faith connection?

Faith Connection: "Programming is a form of creation. When we write organized, elegant code, we reflect God's ordered creation. When we use our programming skills to teach, help, or serve others, we use technology for good."

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for the gift of logic and creativity. Help us continue growing as programmers who create excellent, purposeful programs. May our skills serve You and others. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
Individual local check (not official): CST-T2 - trace a custom-block call or clone's behavior and fix one bug; CST-T3 - identify school-only storage/no private inputs; CST-A2 - explain one purposeful feedback/control design. One trace/test record per student, not a shared screenshot. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Custom square drawing requires the Pen extension/pen-down to leave a visible line; movement alone does not draw. Clones share global variables; only sprite-local variables have per-clone values. No public accounts or uploads.

  • Demonstrated custom block usage

  • Implemented cloning appropriately

  • Used advanced list operations

  • Created organized, commented code

  • Included faith connection

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We learned advanced Scratch programming! Ask your child to explain: 'What are custom blocks (functions)?' 'What is cloning in programming?' 'Show me your project!' We discussed how organized code reflects God's ordered creation. Encourage your child to continue developing their programming skills — they're building abilities that can serve others!"

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit Grades 5-6 / Physical Computing A Time Two 45-minute meetings, 90 total, including 4-minute cleanup each Domains Catholic inclusive design, science systems, technology tools, engineering Big idea A complete powered path lets a switch control a light; a usable signal also needs clear communication. Student objective I can explain a closed path, test an ON/OFF indicator twice and justify an accessibility improvement. Why Safe testing and user feedback matter more than a flashy display. Catholic connection Respect each user's dignity and access, not just successful builders; sources. Local standards / evidence CST-S3: full path; CST-T1: state predictions/repair; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-C2: access decision. Local program codes only. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for operation; paper shows reasoning only. Prerequisites Open/closed is taught here; no earlier electronics or Ohm's-law arithmetic required. Prep / cleanup First inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 4 minutes per meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
Release the hardware route only after completing the OLP Snap Circuits guide. Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project from the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Do not assume a push button, protected holder, LED/resistor specification or battery count. The filename is retained for existing links, not LittleBits wiring.

User brief: "A classroom model needs an ON/OFF light and a label readable from 1 m by someone who cannot rely on color alone." It is not a medical, emergency or real safety device, and it will not be distributed to patients.

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text:
• Per pupil: pencil/journal, one circuit/state/design sheet for both meetings.
  • Per team: diagram sheet, cardstock label, ruler and shared marker; dry work area. Keep the circuit on its supplied grid; label stands beside it.
  • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with selected project parts, diagram/grid and tray. Cells/reserves follow the guide's setup card.
  • Teacher/class: manufacturer instructions, setup card, board, timer, evidence roster, adult-controlled cells and dry storage. Demo uses a station kit.
Pupils Teams / diagrams / labels / rulers Hardware kits / trays Waves Individual sheets / pencils 10 4 4 1 10 15 5 5 1 15 20 7 7 1 20 25 9 5 2 25

No separate LED/resistor harness, mounting tape, extra base, app or new workbook purchase for the Snap route. The protected-AA alternative remains separate.

docs.title: VOCABULARY, BACKGROUND AND SAFETY
docs.text:
Circuit: full conducting return path. Input/output: switch action/light. Load: component transferring electrical energy. Open: interrupted path. Criterion/constraint: success requirement/limit. Tradeoff: a choice with benefits and costs. Battery chemical energy becomes electrical energy and then light/thermal energy; current is not "used up" at the lamp.

Evidence change: Snap's slide switch has two states tested twice, not the old independently controlled supply/button four-state test. Teach ON/OFF, not push/release. LED polarity/current-limiting evidence is not claimed from a lamp project. The separate protected-AA option retains its four-state key.

Misconception: a lit lamp proves any wiring is safe. If asked: "Can I join the battery terminals?" No; that is a dangerous short. Trace a safe open path on paper instead.

SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/age/holder gates; adult isolates the source before snap changes and inspects before restoring power. No pupil cell access, loose/button cells, mains/USB substitutions, shorts, bypassed protection, extra branches, fan blades, soldering or take-home circuits. Warm/damaged/smelly/leaking -> stop/report, adult isolates, OUT OF SERVICE. Keep labels beside the grid, not over parts or contacts.

docs.title: Meeting 1: exactly 45 minutes - path and troubleshooting
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Purpose. Read the user brief; discuss why a clear signal can support dignity and access.
  2. 4-9: Model. Trace the approved return path, demonstrate OFF/ON, source isolation and adult inspection. Explain the two-state evidence change.
  3. 9-12: Predict. Each child labels source/switch/light/conductors/return, predicts OFF/ON and identifies a drawn gap.
  4. 12-26: Wave A. Guide routine: isolated team build, adult check, each child's two OFF/ON cycles, one teacher-managed open-path repair and checked retest. Waiting teams label diagrams and draft an accessible ON/OFF label.
  5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
  6. 27-41: Wave B / individual evidence. Remaining teams get the same hardware routine. Finished teams record predicted/actual results and explain one repair and safe resource choice; smaller classes use the window for repeat tests and individual checks.
  7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store parts and cells, save data and note unfinished physical evidence.

docs.title: Meeting 2: exactly 45 minutes - accessible indicator
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Retrieve. Revisit each child's state/path record without assuming prior mastery.
  2. 4-9: Define criteria. Two correct OFF/ON cycles; a peer reads/interprets the label from 1 m, without color-only cues. Constraints: supplied grid, unchanged approved circuit, paper label beside it.
  3. 9-12: Plan. Each child predicts an access obstacle and sketches a justified label/layout change.
  4. 12-26: Wave A. Build/check/test; peer reads label at 1 m without coaching. Record pass/not yet, revise one paper feature and repeat the same test. No electrical redesign outside the documented project.
  5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers station kits.
  6. 27-41: Wave B / explain. Remaining teams run the same routine. Finished teams document before/after results; each child explains path, observed change, user benefit and limitation/tradeoff. Do not claim a real alert device is safe.
  7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store; collect individual diagrams/state/revision records. Paper only goes home.

docs.title: SUCCESS, SUPPORT AND TROUBLE
docs.text:
Each child contributes to the isolated build, operates the switch, labels the full path, predicts two states, records two cycles and explains test-backed repair/redesign evidence. Log observed / prompted / not yet for physical contribution/testing separately from diagram reasoning; a functioning team kit does not certify every child's operation.

Score 1 participation only; 2 prompted path/test; 3 independent path, state and before/after explanation; 4 additionally defends an access tradeoff and the model's limitations.

  • Grade 5/support: traced diagram, large word/symbol labels, oral records, motor assistance; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
  • Grade 6/challenge: justify label size/layout/readability tradeoffs using feedback. Compare two drawn faults; no undocumented loads or V=IR requirement.
  • 25 pupils: nine teams, five stations, two 14-minute hardware waves. Inspection/access overruns defer evidence, never compress safety checks.
  • No light: isolate/report; adult compares approved diagram/contacts/cells, then supplies a checked reserve. Never bypass protection or improvise parts.

docs.title: ALTERNATIVES / INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The guide retains the original separate protected-AA push-switch/LED-resistor route and its four-state evidence key; no Snap/LittleBits components are attached to that supply. Use the same waves, replacing slide-switch tests with the specified supply/button states. Record which hardware and state table were used. Without safe hardware, retain the timed paper diagram/state/design work; record reasoning/design only; electrical operation not observed and schedule supervised completion. All work is dry and indoors.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: switched circuits and accessible signals. Did: tested ON/OFF twice and revised a label using peer feedback. Learned: a complete path and clear communication matter. Catholic connection: dignity in design. Name the actual Snap, protected-AA or paper route; for the AA route describe its four-state test instead. Ask: "What did your test show, and how did the label change?" No homework, family purchases or take-home powered circuits.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes STREAM Focus M (Math), T (Technology), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Understand π as a ratio and its significance 2. Calculate pi through measurement and simulation 3. Code a Monte Carlo simulation to estimate π 4. Apply pi in engineering calculations

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Appreciate mathematical constants as part of God's ordered creation 2. Connect infinity of π's digits to God's infinite nature 3. Recognize mathematics as discovering (not inventing) truth

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Mathematical Truth - Careful measurement and reasoning are compatible with faith. Whether mathematical objects are discovered or invented is a philosophical discussion, not a defined Catholic doctrine.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "He has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and with the span of his hand marked off the heavens." — Isaiah 40:12

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: Fr. Marin Mersenne — 17th-century priest who made significant contributions to mathematics and music theory. He corresponded with Descartes, Pascal, and other great mathematicians, seeing no conflict between faith and mathematical inquiry.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Circular objects and string

  • Rulers

  • Computers with Scratch (or calculators)

  • Pi digit sheets

  • Graphing materials

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "God of infinite wisdom, Your creation contains beautiful mathematical truths. Help us explore the mystery of pi today and see Your order in mathematics. Amen."

Pi Day context (March 14 = 3/14):

  • "Pi appears EVERYWHERE in creation"

  • "Not just circles — physics, probability, nature"

  • "It's irrational — infinite non-repeating digits"

  • "Yet it's constant — always exactly the same"

Wonder: "How can something be infinite yet constant? How can we know it precisely yet never write it completely?"

docs.title: Measuring Pi (10 min)
docs.text:
Original discovery method:

  • Pi = Circumference ÷ Diameter

  • EVERY circle, EVERY size, SAME ratio!

Activity: 1. Measure circumference of circular object (string method) 2. Measure diameter 3. Calculate ratio 4. Compare to actual pi (3.14159...)

Class data collection:

Object Circumference Diameter C/D Ratio Can 25.1 cm 8.0 cm 3.14 Lid 18.9 cm 6.0 cm 3.15

Discussion:

  • Why don't we get exactly 3.14159?

  • How could we be more precise?

  • What does "irrational" mean?

docs.title: Monte Carlo Estimation (15 min)
docs.text:
Visual approach to pi:

Imagine a square with a circle inside it (circle touches all sides).

  • Drop random points in the square

  • Count how many land inside the circle

  • The ratio relates to pi!

The math:

  • Square area = (2r)² = 4r²

  • Circle area = πr²

  • Ratio: Circle/Square = πr²/4r² = π/4

  • So: π = 4 × (points in circle / total points)

Scratch implementation: 

Set [in_circle] to 0
Set [total] to 0
Repeat 1000
    Set [x] to (pick random -100 to 100)
    Set [y] to (pick random -100 to 100)
    Set [distance] to (sqrt of ((x * x) + (y * y)))
    If distance < 100 then
        Change [in_circle] by 1
    Change [total] by 1
Set [pi_estimate] to (4 * (in_circle / total))
Say (join "Pi ≈ " (pi_estimate))

Students code and run simulation:

  • Try with 100 points

  • Try with 1000 points

  • Try with 10000 points

  • What happens as you increase points?

Key insight: More independent random samples tend to reduce typical sampling error, but any particular larger run can be farther from pi. Retain both results; do not promise monotonic improvement.

docs.title: Pi in the Real World (8 min)
docs.text:
Where pi appears:

Circles and spheres (obvious):

  • Wheels, balls, planets

  • Area = πr², Circumference = 2πr

Waves and oscillation:

  • Sound waves, light waves

  • Pendulum motion

  • Electronics signals

Probability and statistics:

  • Normal distribution (bell curve)

  • Random walks

Physics:

  • Einstein's field equations

  • Heisenberg uncertainty principle

  • Period of pendulum

Nature:

  • River shape varies; do not teach a universal river-meandering ratio of pi.

  • Spiral patterns

  • Eye structure

Engineering application:

  • Calculate gear circumference for robot

  • Estimate circumference of an actual wheeled model. Sphero is a rolling sphere with an internal drive, not a standard exposed wheel.

docs.title: Faith Connection (5 min)
docs.text:
Mathematical constants and God:

Pi is discovered, not invented:

  • "Pi existed before humans calculated it"

  • "We DISCOVER mathematical truth, we don't CREATE it"

  • "This mathematical philosophy is a discussion position, not a required Catholic belief."

Infinity of pi's digits:

  • "Pi has infinite decimal places, never repeating"

  • "We can calculate more digits, but never ALL digits"

  • "God is infinite — we can always know Him more, but never comprehend Him fully"

  • "Pi reminds us of infinity!"

Fr. Mersenne reflection: "Catholic priests and scientists have contributed to mathematics for centuries. They saw discovering mathematical truth as discovering God's creation."

docs.title: Closing (2 min)
docs.text:
Pi celebration:

  • Share estimation results

  • How close did simulations get?

  • Appreciate the beauty of mathematics

Closing Prayer: "Thank You, God, for mathematical beauty. Thank You that pi is constant throughout the universe — from atoms to galaxies. Help us see Your fingerprints in mathematics and pursue truth in all areas. Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text:
Local standards (not official): CST-M3 - individual circumference/diameter ratio with matching units; CST-S2 - repeated measurement and uncertainty; CST-C1 - distinguish numerical evidence from philosophical reflection. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Primary no-device route measures three circular objects; simulation is enrichment, not required evidence for students without Scratch.

  • Calculated pi through measurement

  • Coded Monte Carlo simulation

  • Compared estimates to actual pi

  • Connected mathematical constants to faith

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We estimated pi from circumference and diameter. Ask: 'Why did measurements differ from 3.14?' We practiced honest reasoning; views about discovered versus invented mathematics are philosophical, not a Catholic doctrine. No routine homework or home coding required."

docs.title: LESSON AT A GLANCE
docs.text: Field Teacher reference Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Environment A / Environmental Science & Stewardship Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total Domains C, S, M, A; tools support observation Big idea Responsible environmental decisions need comparable measurements and honest limitations. Student objective I can graph a weather dataset and propose a small stewardship action without claiming more than the evidence shows. Why Residents, farmers, and caretakers interpret weather and use resources responsibly. Catholic connection Care for people and our common home; paraphrase Laudato Si' and stewardship sources, not proof of a scientific prediction. Local standards / evidence CST-S2: individual comparison/control explanation; CST-M2: individual labeled graph and range; CST-A3: revised visual message tested by a peer; CST-C3: individual action and resource tradeoff. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; these four codes are local. Technology None for the primary paper-data path. Non-glass thermometers optional for live indoor practice; spreadsheet optional after paper analysis. Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; read integer temperatures including negatives, plot points, add/subtract. Grade 6 mean is scaffolded. No prior Year B required. Prep / cleanup First cards 20 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; optional thermometer equilibration 10 minutes before class. Cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

docs.title: BEFORE CLASS
docs.text:
1. Use teams of at most three (⅘/7/9). Copy the complete dataset below once/team; identify it as fictional Minnesota winter practice data, never as observed school weather.
  2. Draw graph axes: five dates on horizontal axis, temperature -15 to 5 degrees C vertically. Make high-contrast large copies available.
  3. If using thermometers, adult checks non-glass instruments and places two side-by-side indoors for 10 minutes before class. They measure room conditions, not outdoor weather.
  4. Read aloud: "We will not go outside, touch unknown water or trash, open an electrical meter, or infer drinking-water safety from pH."
  5. Prepare action brief: "The school wants a classroom reminder to shut exterior doors promptly without obstructing access or exits. Test clarity, not actual energy savings."

docs.title: MATERIALS
docs.text: Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25 Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25 Graph sheet; individual exit sheet 1 each/student, reused across unit 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Dataset sheet 1/team 4 5 7 9 Ruler; marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9 Reused paper sign, A4 or letter size 1/team 4 5 7 9 Masking tape 0.5 m/team, classroom display only 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m Timer; large board graph 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1 Non-glass thermometers, optional 2/class, not per team 2 2 2 2

docs.title: SELF-CONTAINED DATA
docs.text:
All readings in this invented example are at 12:00 noon using comparable shielded instruments at the same height; site A is a fictional paved area, B a fictional grassy area. Snow/cloud cover and location could still confound interpretation.

Date A air temperature (degrees C) B air temperature (degrees C) Practice context Jan 6 -10 -11 Cloudy Jan 7 -8 -9 Cloudy Jan 8 -4 -6 Sunny Jan 9 -12 -12 Cloudy Jan 10 -6 -7 Sunny

Teacher key: A range = 8 degrees C; B range = 6 degrees C. A mean = -8; B mean = -9. A-B differences = 1, 1, 2, 0, 1 degrees C; mean difference = 1. These five points cannot establish climate change, an urban heat island, or a causal surface effect.

docs.title: VOCABULARY
docs.text: Weather: conditions over a short time. Climate: long-term patterns. Variable: a factor that may change. Range: highest minus lowest value. Uncertainty: limits on what is known. Stewardship: responsible care and use of gifts/resources.

docs.title: TEACHER BACKGROUND
docs.text:
Surface temperature and air temperature differ. Comparable air measurements need consistent height, shielding, time, and instrument. A small difference may be instrument uncertainty. Graphs communicate evidence; they do not create new evidence. Never erase an inconvenient value.

Common misconception: one cold week disproves climate change. Climate requires long-term records, not five invented days.

If asked, "Did grass make it colder?" Answer: We can describe this dataset's difference, but cannot isolate cause without more controls and repeated observations.

docs.title: Meeting 1 - measurement protocol
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce common-home stewardship and ask why accuracy is a responsibility to neighbors.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Distinguish weather/climate, air/surface; label practice data fictional.
  3. 12-20 (8 min): Each student reads two negative values, computes their difference, and identifies time/height/shield controls.
  4. 20-30 (10 min): Teams compare five A/B pairs. Optional indoor instruments: record both readings at 20 and 25 minutes without moving them; distinguish real room readings from invented outdoor data.
  5. 30-38 (8 min): Draft a repeatable outdoor protocol on paper, including adult weather permission, instrument checks, same time, and missing-data notation. Do not execute outdoors.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: state two controls and one reason the comparison cannot prove cause.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Store data and tools.

docs.title: Meeting 2 - graph and interpret
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Check controls; keep the raw data intact.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Model an axis and one plotted pair; use symbols plus labels, not color alone.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Everyone independently plots all ten points, titles graph, labels degrees C, and keys A/B.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Compare ranges and differences. Grade 5 uses a number line. Grade 6 computes means using the worked key only after trying.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Partners critique graph accuracy and clarity; each revises one label/scale or explains why no revision is needed.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual claim: cite two actual numbers and a limitation; no climate trend claims.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): File individual graphs and clean up.

docs.title: Meeting 3 - communicate a bounded action
docs.text:
1. 0-5 (5 min): Read action brief. This action is a stewardship choice, not an energy saving proven by the weather data.
  2. 5-12 (7 min): Set criteria: readable at 1 m; no blame; explicitly keep entrances accessible.
  3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams make one purposeful visual sign and include a small truthful data graph/caption.
  4. 22-32 (10 min): Exchange with a neighboring team. Each tester states the action without coaching; record number interpreting correctly out of testers.
  5. 32-38 (6 min): Revise and retest. For nine teams use paired exchanges, not nine full-class talks.
  6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain the stewardship tradeoff, one visual revision, and a proposed real measurement needed before claiming energy savings.
  7. 41-45 (4 min): Classroom display only with teacher permission; clean up.

docs.title: QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS
docs.text: Which values are real observations here? How would a sunlit thermometer bias a reading? What does a range tell us that a mean does not? Who might be excluded by a rushed door-closing rule? What data would test energy savings?

docs.title: WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE
docs.text: Each student names two controls and one uncertainty, plots at least 9 of 10 points correctly with units, gives a supported comparison, and explains an accessible action. Art evidence is a purposeful visual choice and a recorded revision, not neatness. Grade 6 additionally computes both means and identifies the limited sample.

docs.title: IF THINGS GO WRONG
docs.text: Thermometers disagree: report both and uncertainty; do not average away the discrepancy. No tools/printing: board-copy dataset and draw graph. Negative numbers overwhelm: provide number line and begin with differences. Sign misread: enlarge/action-label it, test again. Never invent "measured savings."

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No outdoor requirement; no -10 F exposure, road/parking-lot sampling, unknown water, trash handling, or electrical access. Adult manages instruments and spills; no glass/mercury thermometers. A pH strip cannot determine potability. Student plans are classroom proposals only, not permission to alter doors, thermostats, wiring, or habitat.

docs.title: SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6
docs.text: Grade 5: premarked axis and number line; dictate limitation. Challenge: compare ranges. Grade 6: scaffold signed sums; challenge redesign the measurement protocol to reduce one confound and explain why more data may still not establish cause. Provide seated work and large symbols.

docs.title: INDOOR FALLBACK
docs.text: The dataset, protocol, graphs, and sign tests are the primary complete indoor path. Live indoor readings practice tool use only; neither path proves real outdoor monitoring.

docs.title: CLEANUP
docs.text: Keep original datasets, collect rulers/instruments, cap markers, remove test signs from exits, recycle drafts, and retain individual graphs for the portfolio.

docs.title: FAMILY NEWSLETTER
docs.text: Explored: weather data and stewardship. Did: graphed fictional practice readings and tested a clear, inclusive reminder. Learned: honest comparisons include limitations. Catholic connection: care for people and resources. Ask: "What could your five-day graph not prove?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes STREAM Focus E (Engineering), S (Science), R (Religion)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Explore transformation in science (chemical, physical, biological) 2. Engineer devices that demonstrate transformation 3. Apply scientific principles to create meaningful projects 4. Connect scientific transformation to theological concepts

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Understand Resurrection as the ultimate transformation 2. Connect scientific transformation to spiritual transformation 3. Reflect on how Christ transforms our lives

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Resurrection and New Creation — The Resurrection is the central event of Christianity. Jesus transformed death into life, despair into hope, sin into redemption. We too are called to transformation — becoming new creations in Christ.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!" — 2 Corinthians 5:17

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. Paul — The ultimate transformation story. From Saul the persecutor to Paul the apostle. Encountered Christ on the road to Damascus and was completely transformed. His letters share this message of transformation.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Materials for transformation demonstrations

  • Engineering supplies for projects

  • No chemical-reaction station; use teacher-prepared sealed ice demonstration or dry mechanical/paper model only

  • Electronics for programming light sequences (optional)

  • Art supplies

docs.title: Opening Prayer & Introduction (5 min)
docs.text:
Prayer: "Risen Lord, You transformed death into life. Transform us today — our minds through learning, our hearts through faith. Help us see resurrection and new life in Your creation. Amen."

Easter context:

  • "Easter celebrates TRANSFORMATION — the greatest transformation ever"

  • "Death → Life, Despair → Hope, Sin → Redemption"

  • "Today we explore transformation in science and connect it to our faith"

docs.title: Transformation in Science (10 min)
docs.text:
Types of transformation:

Physical Transformation:

  • State changes: solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas

  • Same substance, different form

  • Example: Ice → Water → Steam

Chemical Transformation:

  • New substances created

  • Atoms rearrange

  • Example: Rust, burning, digestion

Biological Transformation:

  • Growth and development

  • Metamorphosis

  • Example: Caterpillar → Butterfly

Energy Transformation:

  • Energy changes form

  • Always conserved

  • Example: Chemical → kinetic → heat

Demonstration examples:

  • Describe chemical change using a labeled diagram only; no reaction mixing in this lesson

  • Ice melting (state change)

  • Butterfly lifecycle images (metamorphosis)

Resurrection connection: Metamorphosis is a living biological process, not death/resurrection and not proof of Easter. Use change as an explicitly limited symbol; Christ's Resurrection is a distinct claim of faith.

docs.title: Engineering Challenge (25 min)
docs.text:
Choose a transformation project:

Option A: Light Sequence Programming Create a Scratch or Sphero program that demonstrates transformation:

  • Darkness → Dawn → Full Light

  • Winter → Spring imagery

  • "Death" colors → "Life" colors

  • Requires: Variables, timing, gradual change

Option B: Transformation Mechanism Build a mechanical device that transforms:

  • Input → different output

  • Could be: darkness/light, closed/open, down/up

  • Requires: Engineering design, moving parts

Option C: Transformation Diagram Draw a labeled before/after state-change model. Explain what stays the same and what changes; no chemicals, heating, tasting, or pressure vessels.

Option D: Artistic/Musical Transformation Create art or music that shows transformation:

  • Digital art showing progression

  • Musical piece from minor to major

  • Visual narrative of transformation

  • Requires: Artistic skill, technical medium

All projects must: 1. Demonstrate clear transformation 2. Include written reflection on Easter connection 3. Be prepared to present and explain

Work time with teacher support.

docs.title: Presentation & Reflection (5 min)
docs.text:
Share projects:

  • What transformation did you create?

  • How does it connect to Easter?

  • What did you learn?

Final reflection questions:

  • "Where have YOU experienced transformation in your life?"

  • "Where do you want Christ to transform you?"

  • "How does transformation give you hope?"

Closing Prayer: "Lord Jesus, You are the God of transformation. You transform death to life, darkness to light, sin to redemption. Transform US. Make us new creations. Help us see Your resurrection power at work in our lives and in Your creation. He is risen! Amen."

docs.title: ✅ Assessment
docs.text: Local standards (not official): CST-S3 - individual physical/chemical/biological distinction; CST-A3 - purposeful before/after communication; CST-C1 - explicitly distinguish scientific process from faith symbol. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text:
No student-selected reactions, fire, hot water/steam, button cells, or unreviewed electronics. If ice is shown, adult uses a sealed tray and wipes spills; all other work is dry and indoors. Spiritual reflection may remain private.

  • Identified types of transformation in science

  • Created project demonstrating transformation

  • Connected scientific transformation to Easter themes

  • Reflected on personal transformation

docs.title: 📎 Home Connection
docs.text:
"We explored transformation in science connected to Easter! Ask your child: 'What types of transformation did you learn about?' 'What did you create?' 'How does your project connect to resurrection?' Discuss as a family: Where have you seen transformation in your lives? How does Christ transform us? He is risen indeed!"

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text: Grade Level Grades 5-6 Duration 45 minutes (plus Expo time) STREAM Focus All Areas (Celebration)

docs.title: STEM Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Present STREAM learning to authentic audience 2. Demonstrate technical and presentation skills 3. Reflect on year-long growth 4. Articulate future learning goals

docs.title: Faith Integration Objectives
docs.text: Students will be able to: 1. Express gratitude for STREAM journey 2. Recognize growth as gift from God 3. Commit to continued faith-reason integration 4. Celebrate as community

docs.title: Catholic Teaching Connection
docs.text: Graduation and Sending Forth — The Mass ends with "Go forth" — a sending into the world. Our STREAM graduation sends students forth equipped with skills, knowledge, and the integration of faith and reason to make a difference.

docs.title: Scripture Connection
docs.text: "I am confident of this, that the one who began a good work in you will continue to complete it until the day of Christ Jesus." — Philippians 1:6

docs.title: Saint Connection
docs.text: St. John Paul II — Called young people to be "not afraid" and to go into the world with faith and reason together. He championed both science and faith, showing they work in harmony.

docs.title: 📚 Materials Needed
docs.text:
• Expo display materials

  • Portfolio collections

  • Certificates

  • Photo documentation

  • Reflection journals

  • Celebration supplies

docs.text:
Dear STREAM Engineers, Scientists, and Innovators:

You did it! You spent this year wondering, building, coding, testing, failing, trying again, and succeeding. You've learned that:

  • Faith and reason go together — Science and faith aren't enemies; they're partners in understanding truth.

  • Failure is part of learning — Every engineer fails. The good ones learn from failure.

  • Your gifts are for serving others — The best STREAM work helps people.

  • You are creative like God — You're made in the image of the Creator, and you can CREATE!

As you go forward:

  • Keep asking "Why?" and "How?" and "What if?"

  • Keep making things with your hands and mind

  • Keep connecting your learning to your faith

  • Keep using your gifts to serve others

You're ready. Go make a difference!

"The one who began a good work in you will continue to complete it." — Philippians 1:6

Congratulations, STREAM Graduate!
