If asked, "Is the Sun a circle?" "It looks like a round disk from far away. The Sun is roughly sphere-shaped. We never look directly at it." No science mastery code is claimed from this explanation alone.

Faith/source boundary: This lesson's honest-evidence practice is a local pedagogical Catholic connection. A formal Church/official-standard alignment is VERIFICATION REQUIRED; no quotation or inference about God's preference for circles is used.

docs.title: SAFETY
docs.text: No food, small coins, long yarn, rolling races, or direct solar viewing. Teacher holds the ball; keep paper shapes on tables. Use blunt tools only; shapes are precut. No forced hand-over-hand assistance.

docs.title: Timed numbered steps: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Invite gratitude for our ability to notice and tell the truth. Show flat tracing and ball: "Do these have the same shape in every way?"
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Model tracing circle and square boundaries and feeling the teacher-held ball if desired. Count zero/four corners. Say "A picture of a ball is flat; the real ball is solid."
  3. 7-13 (6 min): Partners sort six large shapes, alternating turns; teacher brings ball to each table. Each child identifies circle, square, and solid ball with a word, point, or gesture.
  4. 13-19 (6 min): Arrange circle-square-circle-square. Each child predicts next two shapes and draws a repeating pattern on their strip. Choose colors/spacing to make the repeat readable to a partner; revise if partner cannot see it. Teacher starts shape/pattern checks while circulating.
  5. 19-22 (3 min): Finish remaining checks during partner sharing: child distinguishes flat circle from sphere and extends the AB repeat. Do not repeat documented checks or line up 25 children. Optional pi explanation is one sentence within this block, not extra time.
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Count six shapes into each kit, collect strips, return crayons and ball.

docs.title: Evidence and success
docs.text: Teacher records shape identification (three targets) and pattern extension (two next shapes): independent / prompted / not yet. Success is a correct circle/square/ball distinction and circle-square continuation, plus showing a design choice that makes the repeat clear. Children may arrange precut shapes or dictate a pattern instead of drawing; no handwriting or perfect circles required.

docs.title: Questions, support, and contingencies
docs.text:
• "What is flat? What has corners? What repeats? How did your spacing help your partner?"
  • Support: offer two shapes at a time; use raised outlines or verbal descriptions; let children place rather than draw.
  • Challenge: compare larger/smaller circles or make an AAB repeat; explain the next shape.
  • Oval mistaken for circle: show a teacher-made oval beside the traced circle; say it is stretched, without requiring radius vocabulary.
  • No ball: teacher rolls a large paper ball before class and identifies it as an approximate sphere, not perfect geometry.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: all work stays at seated tables; no nature hunt or outdoor date prerequisite.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text: We distinguished flat circles from solid spheres and designed patterns a partner could read. Ask: "What comes next in your pattern, and why?" Pi was optional adult context, not a memorization task. No homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / title K / Plant observation / Growing Things Time Three 25-minute meetings; adult checks plants between meetings Domains / big idea C, S, A, M / Living seeds may change over time; honest records include no visible change. Student objective "I can show what I see today, compare it with before, and choose a care action." Why Farmers, gardeners and scientists observe before deciding what a plant needs. Catholic connection Care for creation and resources, CCC 2402, paraphrase. Optional Lenten kindness/growth analogy is not evidence about plant biology. Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-S3, CST-A1, CST-M1; local, not official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty None / Beginner; observation not a controlled-variable experiment Prep / cleanup Moderate: 20 minutes initially; adult 2 minutes each school day / 3 minutes each class

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
1. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 children (pairs/final trio). Budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment; table totals include it. Each child has their own three-page record even when sharing a cup.
  2. Adult-only seed setup: use fresh untreated bean seeds whose packet supports the chosen indoor conditions; confirm allergies. Line each clear 240 mL lidded cup with two paper-towel squares. Add 15 mL water to dampen, not flood, towels; put two seeds against the side. Secure lids. Children handle only cup exteriors, not seeds or growing medium. Do not seal cups airtight for the whole unit: adult opens away from children daily for inspection and fresh air, then replaces lid.
  3. Set up two teacher demonstration cups in the same way, one today and one started 5-7 days earlier. The older one is a backup, not a guaranteed sprout. Use simple drawings labeled "example, not our result" if none germinates.
  4. Choose a room-temperature, bright indirect-light shelf away from freezing windows, heaters, exits and pupil reach. Label date/team; no outdoor planting is required.
  5. Prepare a 1 cm ticked strip per child, up to 10 cm. Sketch seed/root/shoot examples on the board. Seedling roots can be longer than ten ticks; record "more than 10" rather than demand advanced counting.
  6. Assign a named school adult for weekends/breaks in the class calendar. If nobody can check before a long break, postpone live setup or use dated demonstration drawings; never make family care a prerequisite.

docs.title: Exact materials across the unit
docs.text:
Allocation 10 15 20 25 Per child: observation half-sheets (three) 30 45 60 75 Per child: crayon; measuring strip 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Per team: clear 240 mL cup with secure lid 5 8 10 13 Per team: untreated seeds (two) 10 16 20 26 Per team: towel squares (two) 10 16 20 26 Team initial water, 15 mL per cup 75 mL 120 mL 150 mL 195 mL Teacher backup: two cups/lids; four seeds; four towel squares; 30 mL water 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

Teacher/class, any size: one 250 mL measuring jug, one 5 mL measuring spoon, one tray large enough for all cups, one marker, timer and roster, plus 100 mL reserve water and six reserve seeds. Thus total initial seeds including backups/reserves = 20/26/30/36; cups = 7/10/12/15; initial water = 105/150/180/225 mL. Reserve water is not an automatic daily dose.

No potting soil, special light, student scissors, loose seeds or take-home plant requirement. This is short-term germination, not a claim that mature plants thrive indefinitely on towels.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text:
Seed: young plant and stored reserves inside a protective coat. Germinate: begin growing. Root: takes in water/minerals. Shoot: young stem/leaves. Observation: what we actually notice. Teach by pointing at drawings and real visible structures.

Seeds need appropriate moisture, oxygen and temperature to germinate; species differ in light needs. Many seeds can start on damp paper without soil. Leaves later use light to make sugars; soil supplies support and minerals, not ready-made plant food. Seed reserves are limited. University of Minnesota Extension: starting seeds indoors supports stored reserves, drainage, moisture and light guidance.

Misconception: "Every seed will grow if I am good." Germination varies; a failed seed is not a child's fault or a measure of faith.

If asked, "Can it live without soil forever?" "It can begin using stored reserves and water. To keep growing it needs light and nutrients; people can provide these in different ways."

docs.title: SAFETY and between-class care
docs.text:
Seeds, lids and sprouts stay inside adult-managed cups; never eat them or use treated garden seeds. Adult checks allergies, inspects for mold, handles all opening/watering and removes moldy cups without students sniffing or touching them. No pesticides, fertilizer, heat mats or grow-light wiring. Children may observe drawings instead. If spills occur, stop handling and dry the surface immediately.

Each school day adult checks moisture and signs of mold: add 5 mL only if towel is drying, drain standing water, briefly open for fresh air. Do not have every helper water the same cup. Log date, action, and actual change. After meeting 3, adult may transplant healthy seedlings under a separate school care plan or dispose of seeds/towels; do not release classroom plants outdoors or require families to adopt them.

docs.title: Meeting 1: a starting record (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Prayer for stewardship; show enclosed seed. Ask "What can we see now?"
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Teacher models damp-paper setup with one demonstration cup and explains why children do not open cups. Distinguish food reserves from soil.
  3. 7-15 (8 min): Teams view seeds through cups, count two, alternate turns. Each child draws or dictates one actual detail on page 1; adult dates it and begins individual observation/prediction checks.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Each child points to actual observation and chooses a separate predicted change (root/shoot/no change). Record individual O evidence.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Decide a school care action; name the adult caregiver. Prediction is not recorded as growth.
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Return cups to tray, wipe exteriors/tables if wet, collect drawings and tools.

docs.title: Meeting 2: compare with before (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Retrieve page 1 and cups; say "We report what happened, not what we hoped."
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Model one real comparison, including no visible change if appropriate. Show older cup only as a dated comparison sample.
  3. 7-15 (8 min): Children observe root/shoot/no change. Hold measuring strip beside visible straight portion without opening cup. Count whole tick intervals with adult help; curved roots are only approximate comparisons. Teacher begins comparison/count checks while circulating.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Each child makes page 2 and points to one difference/same feature; teacher records comparison C and counting M evidence.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "What changed? What cannot we know just by looking?"
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Return cups, strips and crayons; wipe any moisture.

docs.title: Meeting 3: evidence and care (25 minutes)
docs.text:
1. 0-3 (3 min): Recall responsible care and honest evidence.
  2. 3-7 (4 min): Model comparing two dated pages, not comparing children as winners/losers.
  3. 7-15 (8 min): Observe, draw/dictate page 3, count visible leaves or tick intervals. Accept zero or no visible change. Teacher begins individual comparison/care checks.
  4. 15-20 (5 min): Finish remaining checks: child shows one actual comparison and selects a care action with a reason (water if drying; provide light for leaves; do not flood). Do not repeat already recorded checks or use a 25-child exit line.
  5. 20-22 (2 min): Partners tell an evidence-based growth/no-growth story. Optional Lent analogy: we practice care and kindness; plant growth does not prove spiritual growth.
  6. 22-25 (3 min): Store portfolio pages; adult collects all cups for the agreed end-of-unit plan.

docs.title: Evidence, success and contingencies
docs.text:
Record O (actual detail), C (comparison), M (count/comparison), and care action as independent / prompted / not yet. Success does not require germination: a truthful zero-leaf record and appropriate care choice count. Assess the child's account, not drawing beauty.

  • Questions: "Where is your evidence? Is that something you saw or predicted? Does dry paper need the same care as flooded paper?"
  • Support: enlarged stage drawings, dictated records, pointing to cup details, tactile paper root model and oral description; adult writes dates.
  • Challenge: compare two same-age cups, noting that uncontrolled differences prevent a causal claim.
  • No growth: use real no-change evidence; compare a clearly labeled example without pretending it was the child's seed.
  • Mold/allergy/no safe live supplies: use three dated teacher sketches with stated provenance; assess observing/representing changes in the model, not live germination.
  • Minnesota indoor fallback: the indoor shelf plan is primary; avoid cold-window contact. No spring weather guarantee.

docs.title: Optional family snippet
docs.text: We observed seeds three times, counted visible features, and recorded changes honestly, including no change. Ask: "What is something you saw, and what was only a prediction?" School adults provided all care; there is no homework or donation prerequisite.

docs.title: Week 33: New Life Engineering
docs.text: The existing filename is retained. This lesson teaches a science/art model, not engineering mastery; no criteria-based prototype is being tested.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Living systems / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, S, A; a butterfly has four life stages while the insect remains alive Objective / why "I can order four stages and explain that my picture is a model." Accurate models communicate living systems. Catholic connection Distinguish biology from Catholic Resurrection teaching; a chosen hope symbol is not scientific proof. Local standards CST-C1: truthful distinction; CST-S3: ordered system; CST-A1: representation. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / guided / 15 minutes first picture set, 5 reset / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and materials
docs.text:
Read K routines. Draw four >=5 cm pictures per child: small oval egg on leaf; long segmented caterpillar; hanging pupa/chrysalis; winged adult. Each child has a full set. Teacher has one large demonstration set; label the reverse for teacher use.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Student: four large stage cards 40 60 80 100 Student: model sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each Teacher: additional four-stage set 4 4 4 4

Teacher timer/roster; no glue, food, pasta, insect kit or field trip required.

docs.title: Vocabulary, background and source
docs.text: Life cycle: stages across generations. Larva: caterpillar. Pupa: living changing stage; a butterfly's chrysalis. Model: representation. Order/key: egg -> larva/caterpillar -> pupa/chrysalis -> adult butterfly -> next-generation eggs. Do not label a butterfly pupa a cocoon, death or tomb. Source: USDA monarch biology. Misconception: the pupa is dead. It is alive and changing. If asked about Easter, distinguish the taught belief in CCC 638-645 from this living-insect process; one does not establish the other.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Name living change; optional original prayer for care/truth. No assumed Easter date.
  2. 4-8: Model four stages in order; show that the pictures are not live animals.
  3. 8-17: Each child orders cards, draws arrows and shows one changed feature. Partner interprets the model; teacher begins individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child independently orders/points to four stages, explains living change and a model limit. Record prompts, not craft completion.
  5. 21-25: Save dated drawing, count four cards into each envelope and clear.

docs.title: Success, questions, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Assess order, biological change and representation/limit separately. Ask "Which stage is next? Is this a real butterfly? Is the pupa alive?" Support: two adjacent stages at a time and pointing/adult scribing. Challenge: add next-generation eggs without implying the same adult becomes an egg. Paper only: no live insect release, pasta, tiny decorations or specimens. Missing pictures: teacher draws the four described forms on the board; pupils point and make a directed drawing. Entire lesson works indoors in winter.

Family: We ordered a living butterfly's stages and explained a model's limits. Ask, "What comes after the caterpillar?" No home collection or routine homework.

docs.title: Lesson at a glance
docs.text: Field Plan Grade / unit / time K / Evidence portfolio / one 25-minute meeting Domains / big idea C, A; celebration values every child while reporting skills honestly Objective / why "I can show what I demonstrated and name a next practice step." Evidence supports a useful handoff. Catholic connection Truth, gratitude and dignity; no ranking of children by appearance or piety. Local standards CST-C1: claim/evidence/limit; CST-A3: communication. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup Optional approved documentation camera; none needed / guided / 10 minutes / 4 included

docs.title: Before class and supplies
docs.text:
Read K routines. Retrieve each child's dated evidence, ideally two observations of the same competency. A single new demonstration cannot establish year-long growth. Fresh-evidence fallback: 3-by-3 grid, START lower-left, target right then up, large token and RIGHT/UP/DOWN/STOP cards. Budget ⅝/10/13 kits; active teams 5/7/10/12.

Allocation 10 15 20 25 Kit: grid; token; four cards 5 / 5 / 20 8 / 8 / 32 10 / 10 / 40 13 / 13 / 52 Student: reflection/record sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

Teacher timer/roster and class evidence envelope. No snacks, slideshow, prizes, public photos or summer packet required.

docs.title: Vocabulary and background
docs.text: Evidence: an actual dated demonstration. Growth: change supported by comparable observations. Next step: a skill to practice. If asked whether everyone is ready for Grade 1, report documented skills/supports; attendance, certificates and group products do not establish every readiness target. Misconception: today's success proves a year of independent mastery.

docs.title: Exact sequence: 25 minutes
docs.text:
1. 0-4: Celebrate effort and gratitude; introduce honest demonstration.
  2. 4-8: Model explaining one record plus a limitation. For missing work, model RIGHT, UP, STOP and correction of an intentionally wrong DOWN.
  3. 8-17: Each child selects/explains evidence or performs the fresh route. Partners ask what the record shows; teacher begins individual checks.
  4. 17-21: Child shows a real result, states prompted/independent help as appropriate and names a next action. Record absent evidence, never invent it.
  5. 21-25: Share concurrently in pairs, date/save records for school handoff, return kits/crayons and clear. No serial 25-child speeches.

docs.title: Success, access, SAFETY and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Check truthful result, understandable explanation and next practice action. Support: picture choices, pointing, scribing and large parts. Challenge: compare two dated records and explain a limit. Desk-only paper kits; no food, public names/images or compulsory summer work. Missing portfolio: fresh dated evidence and a note that growth comparison was unavailable. Child cannot yet demonstrate: record the needed support, celebrate belonging and schedule instruction, not a success-shaped certificate. Works indoors with no devices; camera documentation needs school approval.

Family: We celebrated one demonstrated skill and an honest next step. Ask, "What can you show, and what will you practice?" Optional questions only.

docs.title: 👨‍🔬 Catholic Scientists Heritage Guide
docs.text:
This resource provides profiles of Catholic scientists to integrate into C-STEM lessons, demonstrating the rich history of the Church's contribution to scientific discovery.

October 2026 source status: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. These legacy profiles, personal-faith claims, priority claims and quotations are research leads, not verified primary-source biographies. Check each claim/quotation and context before lesson or newsletter use; do not copy disputed attributions as fact. The shared review's source record and Local Standards govern verified teaching claims. A biography is optional, not required in every lesson; Church history and scientific evidence must remain distinguishable.

"The Jesuits contributed to the development of pendulum clocks, pantographs, barometers, reflecting telescopes, and microscopes." — Historical record of Catholic scientific contributions

docs.title: 📋 Overview
docs.text:
The Catholic Church has a long, rich history of supporting scientific inquiry. By highlighting Catholic scientists in our lessons, we help students see that faith and science are complementary—not competing—ways of understanding God's creation.

How to Use This Guide: 1. Find a scientist relevant to your lesson topic 2. Include their story in your lesson introduction or "Catholic Heritage" section 3. Help students see how faith informed the scientist's work 4. Use reflection questions to deepen understanding

docs.title: Gregor Mendel (1822-1884)
docs.text:
"The Father of Genetics"

Field Life Sciences, Genetics Religious Life Augustinian Friar Major Contribution Laws of Heredity STEM Topics Biology, Genetics, Scientific Method

Story: Fr. Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar who conducted experiments with pea plants in his monastery garden. His careful observations and data collection led to the discovery of the fundamental laws of inheritance, which became the foundation of modern genetics. His work went largely unrecognized during his lifetime but became one of the most important scientific discoveries in history.

Faith Connection: Mendel saw his scientific work as studying God's creation. The order and patterns he discovered in genetics reflected his belief in a Creator who designed life with beautiful, discoverable laws.

Quote:

"My scientific work brought me great satisfaction, and I am convinced that it will be appreciated before long by the whole world."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Life cycles and inheritance

  • Scientific method and observation

  • Data collection and analysis

  • Patterns in nature

Reflection Questions: 1. How did Mendel's patience and careful observation lead to his discovery? 2. What does the order Mendel found in genetics tell us about God's creation? 3. How can we practice Mendel's patience in our own learning?

docs.title: Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543)
docs.text:
Pioneer of Heliocentric Astronomy

Field Astronomy, Mathematics Religious Life Catholic Canon Major Contribution Heliocentric Theory STEM Topics Astronomy, Earth Science, Space

Story: Copernicus was a Catholic canon (a church official) who proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun, rather than the other way around. His book, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, revolutionized our understanding of the cosmos. The Church supported his work during his lifetime, and he dedicated his book to Pope Paul III.

Faith Connection: Copernicus saw the study of astronomy as revealing the glory of God's creation. He believed understanding the cosmos helped us appreciate the Creator's wisdom and majesty.

Quote:

"To know the mighty works of God, to comprehend His wisdom and majesty and power; to appreciate, in degree, the wonderful workings of His laws, surely all this must be a pleasing and acceptable mode of worship to the Most High."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Solar system and space

  • Earth's movement and seasons

  • Scientific theories and evidence

  • History of scientific discovery

Reflection Questions: 1. How did Copernicus's faith inspire his scientific work? 2. What does it mean to worship God through understanding creation? 3. Why is it important to follow evidence even when it challenges our assumptions?

docs.title: Louis Pasteur (1822-1895)
docs.text:
Pioneer of Microbiology and Vaccination

Field Microbiology, Chemistry Faith Devout Catholic Major Contribution Germ Theory, Pasteurization, Vaccines STEM Topics Biology, Health, Medicine

Story: Louis Pasteur's discoveries saved countless lives through the development of pasteurization, germ theory, and vaccines for rabies and anthrax. His faith remained central to his life and work. He saw his scientific work as service to humanity—using his God-given gifts to reduce suffering.

Faith Connection: Pasteur explicitly rejected the idea that science and faith were in conflict. He used his talents to serve others, developing vaccines that protected the vulnerable and saving countless lives through his discoveries.

Quotes:

"A little science distances you from God, but a lot of science brings you nearer to Him."

"The more I study nature, the more I stand amazed at the work of the Creator."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Microorganisms and disease

  • Health and medicine

  • Food safety

  • Scientific experiments

Reflection Questions: 1. How did Pasteur use his scientific gifts to serve others? 2. What does Pasteur mean when he says more science brings us closer to God? 3. How can we use science and technology to care for others like Pasteur did?

docs.title: Georges Lemaître (1894-1966)
docs.text:
"Father of the Big Bang Theory"

Field Cosmology, Physics, Mathematics Religious Life Catholic Priest Major Contribution Big Bang Theory STEM Topics Space, Physics, Astronomy

Story: Fr. Georges Lemaître was a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist who first proposed the theory that the universe began from a "primeval atom" or "cosmic egg"—what we now call the Big Bang. He developed this theory independently of and slightly before Edwin Hubble's observations of an expanding universe.

Faith Connection: Lemaître kept his science and theology distinct but complementary. He insisted that the Big Bang theory was a scientific description, not a creation story, showing that science and faith answer different questions. Pope Pius XII wanted to cite the Big Bang as proof of creation, but Lemaître discouraged this, believing science should remain independent in its methods.

Quote:

"The evolution of the world can be compared to a display of fireworks that has just ended: some few red wisps, ashes, and smoke."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Origin of the universe

  • Space and astronomy

  • Scientific theories

  • Faith and science relationship

Reflection Questions: 1. How did Fr. Lemaître show that a person can be both a priest and a scientist? 2. What does the Big Bang tell us about the universe's beginning? 3. Why did Lemaître want to keep science and theology separate but complementary?

docs.title: St. Albert the Great (c. 1200-1280)
docs.text:
Patron Saint of Natural Scientists

Field Natural Science, Philosophy Religious Life Dominican Friar, Bishop, Doctor of the Church Major Contribution Established natural science as legitimate field STEM Topics All STEM areas, Scientific method

Story: St. Albert the Great (Albertus Magnus) was a Dominican friar who became one of the most learned men of the Middle Ages. He wrote extensively on biology, chemistry, physics, astronomy, geography, and more. He insisted on observation and experimentation, not just relying on ancient texts. He taught St. Thomas Aquinas and helped establish that studying nature was a legitimate way to understand God.

Faith Connection: Albert believed that studying nature was a form of worship—we learn about the Creator by studying creation. He saw no conflict between faith and reason, believing both lead to truth.

Quote:

"Natural science does not consist in ratifying what others have said, but in seeking the causes of phenomena."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Any STEM topic (as patron saint)

  • Scientific method and observation

  • History of science

  • Faith and science working together

Reflection Questions: 1. Why is St. Albert called the patron saint of natural scientists? 2. How did St. Albert show that studying nature honors God? 3. What can we learn from St. Albert's approach to learning through observation?

docs.title: Blaise Pascal (1623-1662)
docs.text:
Mathematician, Physicist, and Apologist

Field Mathematics, Physics, Philosophy Faith Devout Catholic Major Contribution Probability, Hydraulics, Calculator STEM Topics Math, Physics, Engineering

Story: Blaise Pascal was a child prodigy who made major contributions to mathematics and physics. He invented an early calculator, developed probability theory with Fermat, and made discoveries in fluid mechanics (Pascal's Law). After a profound religious experience, he devoted much of his life to defending the Catholic faith.

Faith Connection: Pascal saw mathematics and science as revealing the rational order God built into creation. His famous "Pensées" explored the relationship between faith and reason, arguing that faith goes beyond reason but never contradicts it.

Quote:

"In faith there is enough light for those who want to believe and enough shadows to blind those who don't."

Use in Lessons About:

  • Mathematics and probability

  • Physics and pressure

  • Early computers/calculators

  • Engineering design

Reflection Questions: 1. How did Pascal use his mathematical mind to explore both science and faith? 2. What does "Pascal's Law" teach us about how God designed the physical world? 3. How can we use our minds for both scientific discovery and deepening faith?

docs.title: The Jesuit Contributions
docs.text:
Scientists of the Society of Jesus

The Jesuits (Society of Jesus) have made extraordinary contributions to science, including:

Contribution Jesuit Scientists Pendulum Clocks Multiple contributors Barometers Evangelista Torricelli (student of Jesuits) Reflecting Telescopes Improvements and observations Microscopes Development and usage Seismology "Father of Seismology" – Fr. Athanasius Kircher Lunar Features 35 craters named after Jesuit scientists

Use in Lessons About:

  • Any scientific instrument development

  • Astronomy and space exploration

  • Measurement and observation

  • History of scientific institutions

Reflection Question: Why do you think so many Jesuits became scientists? What does this tell us about the Church's relationship with science?

docs.title: 🙏 Prayer for Scientists
docs.text:
Almighty God, who created all things in wisdom, We thank You for the gift of Catholic scientists Who used their talents to discover Your truth And serve their brothers and sisters.

Through the intercession of St. Albert the Great, Patron of natural scientists, Help us to study Your creation with wonder, And use our learning to honor You And serve the common good.

docs.title: 🌈 C-STREAM Differentiation Guide
docs.text:
Location: Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN · Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

Practical strategies for meeting the needs of all learners in your C-STREAM classroom.

October 2026 operating rule: Preserve the stated concept objective while changing access: read aloud, demonstrate one step, gesture, scribe, use larger tools, bilingual response, quiet/seated route or extra wait time. A digital design is not proof of physical testing/program execution. Use the nonreader card and objective-linked assessment. Access supports do not cap achievement; participation/handwriting are not mastery proxies. Use the actual school accommodation plan, not assumptions from a diagnostic label. A = arts including music; M = mathematics.

docs.title: 🎯 Universal Design Principles
docs.text:
Before modifying for individuals, build accessibility into every lesson:

Principle How to Apply Multiple means of representation Show AND tell. Use visuals, verbal, hands-on Multiple means of expression Let students show learning in different ways Multiple means of engagement Offer choice when possible

docs.title: Attention Challenges (ADHD)
docs.text:
Strategy Example Chunk activities Break 30-min lesson into 3 segments with movement Provide fidgets Offer something to hold during listening Use timers Visual countdown for transitions Movement breaks "Stand up and stretch" between activities Clear workspace Only current materials on desk Proximity Seat near you during instructions Written + verbal Post steps AND say them aloud

What works especially well in C-STREAM:

  • Hands-on building naturally engages kinesthetic learners

  • Short segments (explore → build → test → share)

  • Movement built into engineering activities

docs.title: Reading/Writing Challenges (Dyslexia, Dysgraphia)
docs.text:
Strategy Example Reduce writing load Use drawings, verbal responses, check boxes Provide templates Pre-printed worksheets with sentence starters Use visuals Picture instructions, not just text Allow dictation Student speaks, partner or teacher writes Larger print Enlarge worksheets to 125% Color coding Highlight key words or steps Audio options Read instructions aloud, use text-to-speech

Worksheet Modifications:

  • Use Engineering Design Process worksheet with drawing boxes

  • Accept labeled diagrams instead of paragraphs

  • Offer verbal project reflections

docs.title: Processing Differences (Autism Spectrum)
docs.text:
Strategy Example Consistent routine Same structure each C-STREAM session Visual schedule Post lesson flow on board Prepare for transitions "In 2 minutes we will clean up" Reduce sensory input Quiet corner option, headphones available Clear expectations Specific, concrete instructions Social stories "During C-STREAM, we share materials with friends" Warn about changes Preview if doing something different

Sample Visual Schedule: 

1. Prayer (2 min)
2. Wonder Question (3 min)
3. Learn Together (8 min)
4. Build/Create (12 min)
5. Share (3 min)
6. Closing Prayer (2 min)

docs.title: Motor Skill Challenges
docs.text:
Strategy Example Larger materials Use bigger blocks, thicker markers Adaptive tools Scissors with spring return, pencil grips Partner assistance "You design, partner builds" Modified expectations Quality over quantity Alternative methods Stamp instead of write, voice instead of type Stable surfaces Tape paper down, use non-slip mats

Building Modifications:

  • Pre-cut materials for students who struggle with scissors

  • Offer larger KEVA planks or DUPLO instead of small pieces

docs.title: C-STREAM FAQ and troubleshooting
docs.text: October 2026. Start with Quick Start and a completed lesson template. Generalist teachers can teach a clear lesson; not every legacy file is ready. Confirm rotation/calendar and the actual lesson rather than promising no repetition or universal substitute-readiness.

docs.title: Time and classroom management
docs.text:
Running long? Stop new construction, retain the individual check and cleanup, store dry labeled work and continue next meeting. Do not delete evidence collection to add an extra activity or prayer.

Finished early? Ask for a repeated fair test, alternative constraint or explanation of evidence. Faster pupils are not automatically unpaid helpers.

Students excited/arguing? Give instructions before materials, use a stop signal, assign builder/tester/reporter and rotate actual turns. Ask each to show an idea and test alternatives under the same conditions. Refer persistent behavior/safety concerns through actual school procedures.

A child needs more time? Model one step, reduce choices, pre-cut/larger materials, allow gesture/voice/scribe/quiet or seated response. Keep the concept criterion unless documenting an explicit objective change.

docs.title: Missing supplies or technology
docs.text:
Problem Safe response Learning limit Building blocks absent Paper/cardstock/sticks with a stated new constraint Compare evidence; do not silently claim identical load capacity Robot/app/host unavailable Desk-grid arrow cards and pointer Sequence/debugging concepts only; execution/robot mastery deferred Internet absent Teacher-vetted read-aloud source or confirmed offline tool Actual online/source-navigation objective may change Some devices work Document turn/reset time, smaller test rotations or more meetings Each child needs individual real-device evidence if that is O1 Electrical gear damaged Switch off/disconnect; OUT OF SERVICE; safe paper-path model Paper path is not practical circuit-building mastery No safe materials or weather Seated observation fallback Record actual observation objective, not unperformed investigation

Do not open personal accounts, install unapproved apps, bypass safeguards or improvise power supplies. Technology Plan. Borrowing lead times/fees/stock are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed two-week free access. Library planning.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
How do I grade? Use the objective -> prompt -> success condition -> individual evidence chain. Project rubric. Participation, effort, handwriting, neatness and confidence are not mastery. An artistic criterion is used only for an explicit arts objective.

What if the model fails? A child can still explain valid evidence and redesign. A successful team model does not prove each member understands. NE means not yet evidenced; unobserved/absent/device-blocked is not a zero.

How much paperwork? Short roster evidence during work plus one exit check; review termly with Progress Tracker. Named records/photos follow verified school privacy/consent practice; do not assume a digital account or public portfolio.

docs.title: Faith, arts and grade differences
docs.text:
Faith connection feels forced? Use a concrete Catholic decision about dignity, truth, stewardship or service. R identifies the explicit reflection. Prayer supports but does not substitute for this purpose. Verify Church quotations, biographies and standards; never make an experiment theological proof.

Hard science/faith question? Acknowledge uncertainty, distinguish observation from belief/interpretation and consult the verified source record or appropriate school faith educator. Avoid a simplistic "science only how, faith only why" rule or "God is an engineer" analogy.

What does A mean? Arts including music: observational drawing, composition, visual communication, form, rhythmic phrases and performance, not just digital art/decoration. M means mathematics.

K cannot read? Use Show, Try, Tell. An attempt is welcome but does not automatically demonstrate the concept. Assess pointing/sorting/building/telling with the same explicit success condition.

Mixed grades / older students need challenge? Same materials can support different evidence expectations; use the shared progression and actual prerequisites. Add repeat trials, constraints, measurement or tradeoffs, not untaught ratio work or leadership as a substitute for subject learning.

docs.title: Safety and families
docs.text:
No button cells, latex balloons or projectiles in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Stop unsafe activities, isolate hazards and contact the school's responsible adult. Possible battery/magnet ingestion needs urgent emergency escalation. Use indoor alternatives in unsafe Minnesota conditions.

No routine homework, required donations or home purchase/device. Explain concept + action + evidence + Catholic choice using family communication.

docs.title: Kindergarten reference routines
docs.text: Read this page with the selected lesson. It supplies reusable routines, not permission to omit that lesson's exact materials, test or safety instructions. Every minimum pathway works indoors, without independent reading or a device.

docs.title: Twenty-minute substitute gate
docs.text:
1. 0-4 minutes: read the objective, background, test and individual check.
  2. 4-8: locate actual supplies; count the selected enrollment column.
  3. 8-12: inspect materials and confirm accommodations, school contact and any adult-only preparation. A supply estimate is not an owned kit.
  4. 12-16: perform the lesson's demonstration/pretest and distribute kits.
  5. 16-20: draw directions and rehearse the check and cleanup.

If a safety condition or exact material is missing, use only the lesson's named alternative. Record the different/deferred objective; do not improvise unknown substances, electrical connections, outdoor exposure or a human trial.

Common teacher kit: one classroom timer/clock, paper roster and school pencil or school-approved equivalent writing tool, for any enrollment. No pupil device is implied. The audit indexes this common kit separately from student supplies. Adult cutting, secured AA cells and Winter Science tongs are indexed where the selected lesson needs them. Prepared-resource prices do not include these tools or imply verified school stock.

docs.title: Teams and quantities
docs.text:
Pupils Active pair/trio teams Kit budget Additional reserve 10 5 pairs 5 0 15 6 pairs + 1 trio 8 1 20 10 pairs 10 0 25 11 pairs + 1 trio 13 1

Lesson tables use the kit budget, not a lone child working in a "pair." Unless a lesson explicitly adds teacher supplies, demonstrate with one budgeted kit and return it before practice. Never count a reserve twice.

With fewer kits, use groups no larger than three: ⅘/7/9 groups respectively (2 trios + 2 pairs; 5 trios; 6 trios + 1 pair; 7 trios + 2 pairs). Recalculate the per-kit issue quantities. Preserve the test and every child's turn; do not change a learning target merely to fit a materials shortage. If individual turns cannot fit, record missing evidence and schedule follow-up.

docs.title: Nonreader directions and access
docs.text:
Demonstrate one action, say it, let children show it, then add the next action. Use large drawings of an eye, hands, two arrows and a return box. No printout or icon-reading skill is assumed. A child can point, describe, dictate, build or direct an adult to act. Ask permission before physical assistance.

Swap chooser/builder, tester and reporter roles during work. A third child gets a full choice and test turn, not permanent observation duty. Provide a seated route, large parts and a quieter/visual alternative as needed.

docs.title: Individual evidence without a serial exit line
docs.text:
Prepare a roster with the lesson's two or three observable checks. Begin checking during 8-17 minutes, then finish during 17-21 while partners work. Thirteen combined minutes provide an average of about 31 seconds per child at 25 enrollment; actual processing needs may require later follow-up. Record not yet / prompted / independent separately for each check. Do not convert an unobserved response into a pass.

Show what was tested, distinguish prediction from result, and ask one real question. Group products, compliance, handwriting and artistic polish are not mastery. A failed prototype can still produce excellent evidence. The local progression's mastery checkpoints need two dated individual observations; one lesson or a certificate cannot establish grade readiness.

docs.title: Common safety and cleanup
docs.text:
Use teacher-inspected large paper pieces and sound blocks, seated desk tests, no student weight on models and no food/unknown nature materials. Do not taste, sniff closely, collect nests or view the Sun. No small magnets, button cells, lasers, flames, latex balloons, projectiles or mouth-contact instruments. Adults control scissors, batteries and wet setup. Keep paths/exits clear. Follow actual school allergy, hygiene, emergency and accommodation procedures.

At 21-25 minutes, stop the test; count reusable pieces into their labeled kit; cap school-approved glue; retain dated evidence; flatten dry scrap for reuse/recycling; clear tables. Store models by kit number rather than publishing student names. Wet lessons use their own hygiene/cleanup plan.

docs.title: Catholic connection and source use
docs.text: Teach honest evidence, care of creation, dignity, inclusion and service. Prayer is optional according to the school's practice and is not a mastery check. Classroom applications are local, not official religious standards. Use the verified Church teaching register: CCC 159 (faith/reason), 1702/1704 (dignity/reason), 2415-2418 (creation care), 2427-2428 (work), 2468-2469 (truth). Do not attribute original classroom language to a saint or Scripture. An approved religion reading is an optional addition, not a scientific explanation.

docs.title: Continuity and family communication
docs.text:
Keep one dated sheet per child when a lesson specifies it. Use an envelope by class/meeting; no expensive journal is required. Multi-meeting models stay at school. If prior work is unavailable, use the lesson's fresh-evidence route, never invent a past result.

Newsletter statements describe what was actually taught and observed. Family questions are optional and ungraded. No home device, purchase, donation, collection, adult teaching or homework supplies an essential assessment.

docs.title: Materials inventory checklist
docs.text: The authoritative October 2026 planning records are Materials Plan and Materials Inventory CSV. They include normalized names/aliases, unit estimates, 10/15/20/25 stock, annual replacement, storage/safety/batteries, exact kits and \(250/\)500/\(1,000/\)2,500 bills of materials. This checklist does not maintain a contradictory price or loan-stock table.

docs.title: Reported school holdings
docs.text: Reported OLP holdings records 8 individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135, reported on 2026-10-04. This is a school-reported total, not a completed physical inspection. Keep actual holdings separate from the CSV's 10/15/20/25-pupil planning quantities; check contents, condition, location, manufacturer age guidance and battery/power safety before classroom use. For the four selected Grades 3-6 lessons, use the Snap Circuits classroom guide: label SC01-SC08, record the matching manual/project and fitted cell count, and release only checked kits. At 25 pupils use nine teams at five stations in two waves, not nine simultaneous kits or groups larger than three.

docs.title: Beginning-of-year stock check
docs.text:
• Confirm planned schedule/rotation and actual cohorts/enrollment.
  • Count physical stock by normalized ID; record condition/location/date/checker. NOT VERIFIED in the CSV is not zero and is not confirmed ownership.
  • Check school basics assumed by budgets: 25 pencils, 25 blunt scissors, crayons/markers, board, 18 stable supports, teacher timer, cleaning/handwashing.
  • Inspect every reusable kit; complete counted labels and an actual shelf map.
  • Verify supplier packs, current prices, shipping/tax assumptions and yearly consumables. Estimates dated October 2026 are NOT vendor quotations.
  • Verify electrical current protection/ratings, secure battery covers, ingredients, age suitability and accessible response tools before purchasing.
  • Choose only confirmed optional devices/loans. No app license or school account is assumed. Technology Plan.
  • Schedule one-time kit/card preparation and teacher prep tests before substitutes arrive; note shortages explicitly.

docs.title: Before each unit / after each lesson
docs.text: Use Materials List Template. Separate per-student, team, class, teacher-only and optional materials. Nine complete kits accommodate 25 at teams <=3; if switching to pairs, recalculate for 13 pairs. The selected Snap lessons instead use their explicit two-wave allocation. Count fitted/spare batteries separately. Issue exact amounts, record actual use, count returns, dry wet supplies, disconnect/off electrical parts and remove cells for long storage. Mark damaged kits OUT OF SERVICE and notify the responsible adult.

docs.title: Safety and optional donations
docs.text:
No button cells, latex balloons or projectile activities in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Do not use unverified electrical parts, loose high-strength magnets, unknown chemicals, sharp metal/glass or food-soiled recyclables. Donations of screened clean dry cardboard are welcome but the school provides paper/cardstock alternatives. Never require families to bring materials or buy equipment.

Optional request copy: "If convenient, you may donate clean, dry flat cardboard after checking with the teacher. Please send no glass, metal, batteries, magnets, chemical containers or food-soiled items. Donations are optional: every child will have school-provided materials."

docs.title: Loan and audit evidence limits
docs.text: CSCOE planning requires confirmation; there is no guaranteed free loan, fixed stock count or two-week entitlement. Four band audits are available; their as-read counts and specific stock questions are summarized in Materials Plan. Current inventory use counts are explicitly estimated core uses; coverage of all 251 legacy lesson documents has not been established.

docs.title: Parent communication guide
docs.text: Use one family communication system and newsletter template; K-6 unit examples and specific oral questions are supplied there. Retain plain language, welcoming invitations, positive evidence notes and family feedback. No routine homework or donation prerequisite. October 2026.

docs.title: Introduction letter (copy and personalize)
docs.text:
Dear Families,

In C-STREAM, children learn through observing, building, measuring, testing, improving, composing and explaining. C means Catholic identity; R is religion/faith integration; A includes arts and music; M means mathematics. Our Catholic purpose includes dignity, stewardship, truthful reasoning and using gifts to serve others. Faith reflection does not replace scientific evidence. Art includes genuine choices about pattern, form, sound and communication, not just decorating a product.

We use hands-on materials first and devices when they add meaningful learning. Every child has school-provided supplies and classroom work time. There is no routine C-STREAM homework, purchase, device or donation requirement. Newsletters include a specific question you can ask and an optional no-purchase activity. Your child may show learning by speaking, pointing, drawing, modeling or recording, with needed access support.

Questions? Contact [actual teacher/school-approved contact].

docs.title: Showcases and family feedback
docs.text:
Use Student Project Rubric for selected objective-linked evidence, not fixed percentages for attractive displays, confidence, family-funded materials or participation. Work is completed in class; family attendance is optional. Students may show/tell/draw with support. Ask families: "Was the learning clear?" "Was the optional activity accessible?" "What questions remain?" Event planning: STREAM Night.

Source questions about Church teaching, scientists, official standards or diocesan policy are VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Local codes link to Local Standards; they are not official accreditation.

docs.title: C-STREAM quick start guide
docs.text: October 2026. C = Catholic identity; S = science; T = technology; R = religion/faith integration; E = engineering; A = arts including music; M = mathematics. Catholic purpose shapes choices, not only opening prayer. Art involves observation, composition, form, pattern or communication, not just decoration/digital tools.

docs.title: Before the first meeting
docs.text:
1. Confirm weekly/bi-weekly schedule and A/B rotation with the school. Use the lesson index; do not assume the same Week 1 filename or commercial-kit schedule for every band.
  2. Read the actual lesson objective, background, vocabulary, safety, individual check and timed sequence. Use the common lesson format.
  3. Confirm supplies and location with inventory checklist. Default 10/15/20/25 pupils = ⅘/7/9 teams <=3. School provides required supplies.
  4. Perform the teacher pretest and count trays. Have the substitute fallback ready.
  5. Prepare family copy. No routine homework.
Grade Native period Protect inside this time K 25 minutes Oral modeling, each child's action/evidence, 3-minute cleanup 1-2 30 minutes Hands-on turns/test/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup 3-4 40 minutes Evidence-based testing/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup 5-6 45 minutes Reasoning/tradeoffs, individual check, 4-minute cleanup

docs.title: Your first two weeks
docs.text:
Start with a completed band lesson, not a generic untimed welcome sequence. Model "notice -> try -> tell"; nonreader card. State "Today I can..." and give every child a turn to show the objective. Next meeting, use observation/design/measurement appropriate to prerequisites. Failure in engineering is information, not failure of a student.

If a source question arises, say "We need to check that" and record VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The Catholic heritage guide is background for source checking, not a mandatory biography every lesson. No internet image search, unlicensed image or unverified quotation is needed.

docs.title: If conditions change
docs.text:
• Time short: stop new construction; keep individual evidence and cleanup.
  • Kit absent: use the named safe fallback, recording any objective change.
  • Devices absent: unplugged concepts still work; real programming/robot execution evidence must be deferred, not claimed from drawings.
  • Unsafe materials/weather: stop and use a seated indoor task; notify the responsible school adult if safety needs escalation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
STREAM Night is a celebration of student learning that brings families together to experience hands-on Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Art, and Math activities. This guide provides everything you need to plan a successful STREAM Night or family showcase event at Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School.

October 2026 operating conditions: C is Catholic identity, R is explicit religion/faith integration, A includes arts/music, and M is mathematics. This optional event celebrates in-school learning; no home-built project, purchased display board, family attendance or donation affects grades. Use the family copy system and objective-linked rubric. Event costs below are separate planning estimates, not vendor quotes or part of the core classroom budgets. Re-cost for actual attendance, tax and shipping. Confirm staffing, venue capacity, accommodations, safeguarding and photo/consent procedures with the school. Scripture quotations and Church attributions below are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before printing; devotional symbolism is not scientific evidence.

SAFETY: No button cells, latex balloons or projectile stations; no neodymium magnets in K. Adults manage electrical power, small parts and safe bounded tests. Close unstaffed hazardous stations rather than assuming volunteers will arrive. Plan an indoor January version and accessible seated/silent routes. Suspected battery/magnet ingestion or other urgent danger triggers immediate school emergency escalation. Use counted kits.

docs.title: Opening Prayer
docs.text:
Creator God,

Thank you for the gift of wonder and curiosity. Thank you for the minds You have given us to explore Your creation.

Tonight, we celebrate learning together as a community. Help us see Your hand in science, technology, engineering, art, and math.

Bless our families as they discover and create together. May everything we learn draw us closer to You.

We ask this through Christ our Lord. Amen.

docs.title: Closing Prayer
docs.text:
Loving God,

Thank you for this time together as a school family. We are grateful for our students and all they have learned. We are grateful for our teachers who guide them with faith and love. We are grateful for families who support learning at home.

As we go home tonight, help us continue to wonder, to question, and to discover. May we use our talents to serve others and glorify You.

We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

docs.title: OLP Snap Circuits classroom guide
docs.text: Reported stock: 8 individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135, reported 2026-10-04. This means eight student activity kits, not eight six-kit classroom packs. See the holdings record. Physical inspection and classroom approval are still required.

docs.title: Before teaching: release the hardware pathway
docs.text:
Allow 30 minutes for first inspection/pretesting, plus time to obtain any missing instructions or parts; allow 15 minutes for repeat preparation. Leave a prepared kit, approved diagram, component list and this guide for a substitute. A substitute must not invent a circuit or approve unfamiliar parts.

  1. Label the individual kits SC01-SC08. Record the actual manufacturer model, instruction/workbook edition, contents, condition, location and checker. OHM-135 is the supplier item number, not a verified manufacturer model.
  2. Read the matching in-box manufacturer instructions. Select one documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project with a complete return path. Record its project/page number and component IDs on the teacher's setup card. Use the same project in every station; do not mix modules from different systems.
  3. Verify manufacturer age guidance for the actual pupils, battery access, holder protection and the school's electrical-safety requirements. The supplied holder is not assumed equivalent to a screw-secured, current-protected AA holder. If it does not meet school requirements, use the protected-AA alternative or paper route, not improvised covers or protection.
  4. Adult installs only the battery type/count specified for that project. Record b = fitted cells per station and the chemistry/voltage. Count fitted cells as stations * b; reserve complete kits need their own checked cells. Keep replacement cells separately in adult-controlled storage. Do not assume the kit uses the earlier lessons' two-AA allocation.
  5. Pretest the documented switch-OFF/light-off and switch-ON/light-on states twice. An LED project is allowed only if the matching instructions document polarity and required current limiting; never substitute a bare LED for a lamp.
  6. Teach power isolation, not just switch OFF: before changing snap connections, the adult disconnects the battery holder from the build as directed by the manufacturer. Pupils do not handle cells or holder contacts. Adult checks the complete approved layout before reconnecting power.
  7. Issue only the approved project's parts, grid, component list and diagram. Leave motors/fan blades, sound modules, extra loads and unused holders stored. No free wiring, shorts, series/parallel extensions or assumed sensors.

Stop conditions: missing matching instructions, unsuitable age rating, unapproved holder/protection, missing parts, failed pretest, warmth, smell, damage or leakage. Mark the kit OUT OF SERVICE, tell the responsible adult and use a named alternative. A lit lamp alone does not certify safe wiring.

The supplier description lists switches, lamps, LEDs and battery holders and recommends upper elementary. It describes a six-kit classroom pack, not OLP's eight individual kits. It does not verify OLP's exact model, battery allocation or school approval. This guide provides original teaching routines, not a replacement for that model's manufacturer instructions or a claim of official standards alignment.

docs.title: Station capacity: no group larger than three
docs.text:
Use balanced pairs/trios, not a singleton. Each kit is one hardware station. The teacher demonstration uses a station kit before pupil work, not a ninth kit.

Pupils Teams (size distribution) Hardware stations Hardware waves Unissued kits available as reserves 10 4 (two trios, two pairs) 4 1 4 15 5 (five trios) 5 1 3 20 7 (six trios, one pair) 7 1 1 25 9 (seven trios, two pairs) 5 2 3

These numbers assume all eight kits pass preflight. Reserves are not automatically complete or powered. Recalculate when a kit is out of service; do not increase team size or mark a paper turn as electrical operation. One wave cannot serve more than 24 pupils with eight kits.

docs.title: The 25-pupil rotation
docs.text:
Assign teams 1-5 to wave A (15 pupils) and teams 6-9 to wave B (10 pupils). Provide nine team work areas but only five dry hardware stations. Waiting teams work on their own prediction, diagram and audience/design task. The timed lessons include one minute for transfer/reset; supplies move, not live circuits. Adult isolates power and checks stations before the second wave.

Each hardware wave gives a team 12 minutes in Grades 3-4 or 14 minutes in Grades 5-6: follow the approved build, adult inspection, individual switch tests, and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Every child contributes a designated snap connection to the isolated team build and then operates the switch for two OFF/ON cycles. Rotate connector/tester/recorder; a role label alone is not evidence. The teacher checks each team before energizing and again after a repair. Never create a live short as the fault.

At smaller enrollments, all teams use wave A; wave B is extra retesting, feedback and individual checking time, not an additional meeting. If inspections or motor/access needs take longer, record unfinished physical evidence and schedule a supervised completion turn. Do not rush a safety check or report that every child operated a kit unless observed.

docs.title: Individual evidence sheet: draw or copy onto paper
docs.text:
No printer, account, app or additional workbook purchase is required. Each pupil records:

Check Pupil response / teacher observation Full path Label battery, switch, light and conducting return path Prediction OFF -> expected output; ON -> expected output Test OFF/ON observations for cycle 1 and cycle 2 Open-path repair Gap, one approved correction and observed retest result Design/message Intended user/reader; one choice and specific feedback Evidence level Physical contribution and switch test observed / prompted / not yet; paper reasoning recorded separately

Teacher key for the approved simple switched light: OFF opens the path and the light is off; ON closes the path and the light is on. If observation differs, report the actual result. Disconnect power; adult checks the diagram, contacts and cells. Do not substitute parts or bypass protection.

docs.title: Protected-AA alternative: separate equipment, not a Snap conversion
docs.text:
Keep the original protected circuit option if already verified and available. Do not attach Snap parts to its supply or LittleBits modules.

  • Grades 3-4: screw-secured covered 2-AA holder with documented protection, matching cells, switch, enclosed current-limited 3 V LED module and three insulated leads. Pretest holder + -> switch -> module +; module - -> holder -.
  • Grades 5-6: enclosed, current/short-circuit-protected switched 2-AA holder, push switch, adult-prepared sleeved red LED/220-ohm ¼-watt series-resistor assembly and three insulated leads. Pretest the complete series return path. Supply OFF before reconnection; adult checks before ON.

Use the same station/wave counts above. Add one complete spare: ⅚/8/6 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils, 10/12/16/12 fitted AA cells, and 15/18/24/18 leads. This is a selected-path allocation, not a change to the shared purchasing BOM. For Grades 5-6 retain the original four-state evidence: supply OFF with button released/pressed -> off/off; supply ON with button released/pressed -> off/on. Snap's slide switch instead uses two OFF/ON states repeated twice; do not claim push/release behavior or four independently controlled states from that route.

docs.title: Safety and return
docs.text:
Adult supervision, dry seated stations, counted small parts and teacher-managed power throughout. No button/coin cells, household/mains/USB power, soldering, cutting wires, exposed fan blades, battery-terminal shorts or take-home circuits. Never mix cell types/old and new cells or recharge disposable cells. Use manufacturer-directed isolation and adult handling of damaged/hot cells.

Reserve the lesson's final cleanup block: isolate power, count issued parts and cells against each station list, return parts to SC01-SC08, flag discrepancies, and store in a dry adult-controlled location away from water. Adult removes cells for long storage as directed. Only diagrams and paper art go home. Kindergarten remains adult-demonstration only after preflight; no new student circuit-building objective is introduced.

docs.title: Student progress tracker
docs.text: Retain the useful fall/winter/spring growth conversation, but track taught objectives rather than enthusiasm or generic participation. October 2026. Use assessment, rubrics and Local Standards.

docs.title: Lesson evidence roster
docs.text:
Student Date/grade/unit/lesson Objective/local code Exact action/words or artifact Mode/access support ½/¾ or NE Feedback/next check [One row per child; extend to actual enrollment, including 25] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

Levels: 1 Beginning, 2 Developing, 3 Meets Expectation, 4 Extends Learning. Use the lesson's specific descriptors. NE means no adequate evidence yet (absence, unavailable equipment, missed check); it is not a zero. Ordinary read-aloud, gesture, bilingual response, scribe and motor assistance do not lower achievement. Record conceptual hints separately.

docs.title: Termly growth summary
docs.text:
Student/objective/local code Fall evidence/date/level Winter evidence/date/level Spring evidence/date/level Next teaching [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

Examples of appropriate evidence by grade, not new official benchmarks:

Grade Possible individual evidence when corresponding objective taught K Points/sorts by an observed feature; shows a two-action sequence; tells one detail 1 Names the problem/user; compares two results; explains one design choice 2 Records an equal-condition comparison; explains a changed sequence 3 Shows common test conditions and links one redesign to the result 4 Measures in the specified unit and uses results to justify an improvement 5 Compares two designs using taught criteria/constraints 6 Defends a choice with evidence, cost/tradeoff and a taught ethical consideration

This is not an independent progression specification: use the shared grade progression and local definitions for expected outcomes. Real program/robot execution is only recorded when actually demonstrated on a working device. Never fill those cells from an unplugged activity.

docs.title: Workload and privacy
docs.text:
During hands-on time sweep the roster; pair a simultaneous point/show/draw exit response with short targeted conversations. At 25, record unobserved children NE and collect later rather than assuming all groups mastered the concept. Review at project completion and termly; do not require daily long checklists. At expected-mastery checkpoints, retain two dated observations on separate occasions as required by Local Standards, including an individual demonstration and changed context/follow-up explanation. Both must meet the target; one lesson rating is not end-of-grade mastery. Store named records under the school's actual privacy practice. Do not publish names, scores or photographs in newsletters without verified permission.

Behavior/engagement notes may inform support but remain separate from subject mastery. Report "measured the span accurately; next compare repeated trials," not "participates well, therefore proficient."

docs.title: C-STREAM substitute teacher guide
docs.text: C = Catholic identity, R = religion/faith integration, A = arts including music, M = mathematics. Thank you for leading hands-on learning. October 2026. Use the actual scheduled lesson, not a generic assurance that every old lesson is ready. Readiness review.

docs.title: Twenty minutes before class
docs.text:
Minutes Do this 0-4 Read objective, background/vocabulary and native timed steps; identify each child's evidence prompt 4-8 Find the kit at the location supplied by school; count student/team/class/teacher items for enrollment 8-12 Read SAFETY; check accommodations, materials condition and actual school emergency/office contact 12-16 Perform the exact lesson model/pretest, then place counted trays and assign roles 16-20 Draw/read aloud short steps; rehearse individual check, cleanup and the named fallback

School must fill lesson/date [ ], kit/actual location [ ], office/contact [ ], accommodations [ ], emergency instructions [ ] before handoff. Do not assume "STREAM closet," iPads, apps, loan kits or a quick-reference card exists.

Grade 3 example: rebuilt Week 10 Bridge Engineering. Use its precise quantities/span/load/check and 40-minute period. If its kit or prep test fails, use the fallback below and record the changed objective. This guide does not certify all legacy lessons.

docs.title: SAFETY: stop rather than improvise
docs.text: No button cells, latex balloons, projectile activities or neodymium magnets in K. No unknown chemicals, food experiments, glass, hot surfaces, unsafe cold exposure or electrical repair. Teacher controls batteries/clip leads/small loads. Do not use unfamiliar electric/magnetic equipment without a verified pretest. Stop, isolate unsafe materials, move to a seated safe task and notify the responsible school adult. Injury, suspected ingestion of a battery/magnet or other urgent danger requires the school's emergency escalation immediately. Do not send pupils hunting for missing dangerous parts.

docs.title: Fallback A: paper structure comparison
docs.text:
Objective: Compare flat and folded paper under the same span and load. Big idea: Shape can affect a structure; a fair comparison keeps test conditions the same. Catholic connection: Reliable design serves people; shared resources are used responsibly. No "God is an engineer" comparison. Technology Requirement: None. Difficulty: introductory comparison. Prep: 10 minutes if counted stock/supports exist; cleanup included below. Vocabulary: span = gap between supports; load = what a structure supports; compare = notice how results are alike/different.

Background/misconception: Folded and flat paper may respond differently. The result can be the same under a small load; report that honestly. A collapse is information, not failure of the student. If asked why a fold matters, show the changed shape; do not promise that every fold always improves it.

Scope/material Rate 10 pupils 15 20 25 Student response paper (or oral response) 1/child 10 15 20 25 Team paper 2/team 8 10 14 18 Team index-card test loads 10/team 40 50 70 90 Team ruler 1/team 4 5 7 9 Stable support books/blocks 2/team 8 10 14 18 Teacher 2 demonstration sheets, 10 cards, timer, evidence roster One class set in addition to team issue quantities

Pencils/crayons are school basics. Total paper at 25 = 25 + 18 + 2 = 45 sheets; total cards = 90 + 10 = 100. No scissors, coins, tape, devices or donations. Books/supports must be confirmed; without them use fallback B, not an unsafe stack.

Before class: Set stable supports 10 cm apart on each desk; lay one sheet flat across. Fold the second lengthwise into an accordion with adult modeling. Try adding cards one by one at the center in both tests; reset with the same gap and count. Test before class; reduce the gap if neither supports even one card and record that shared change. No escalating to heavy falling weights. K adult places loads; child still predicts/points/compares.

docs.title: Exact native timing (choose the grade column)
docs.text:
Step K 25 1-2 30 3-4 40 5-6 45 What to do/say Hook/purpose 0-3 0-3 0-4 0-4 "What might a fold change?" Explain objective and stewardship Model/vocabulary/safety 3-7 3-8 4-10 4-11 Align supports, show flat/folded examples, demonstrate one load placement Build/test first comparison 7-14 8-18 10-24 11-27 Students take turns placing paper/cards; count or point to result Improve/retest 14-19 18-23 24-32 27-36 Change one paper shape; keep gap/load placement. "What stayed the same?" Individual check 19-22 23-27 32-37 36-41 "Show the result. What stayed the same in the test?" Cleanup/close 22-25 27-30 37-40 41-45 Count cards/rulers/supports, retain dry paper, clear desks, brief thanks

Meets: Each child identifies the observed comparison (including equal results) and shows one common condition. For K, adult reads/models and accepts pointing/gesture. Use Show, Try, Tell. Support: Pre-fold paper, steady supports, scribe or allow a large gesture. Challenge: Repeat the comparison and explain whether it supports the first result; older pupils can compare equal-material versions without untaught ratios. At 25: Nine seated teams, rotating turns; check children during tests plus simultaneous show/draw exit. Mark unobserved evidence NE and leave a follow-up. Troubleshoot: Sliding supports -> stabilize or stop that test; equal results -> record them, not "wrong"; time short -> stop new construction, keep check/cleanup. Family copy: "We compared paper structures using the same gap and loads. Ask: 'What stayed the same, and what changed?' Optional: discuss a folded object already nearby. No home project needed."

docs.title: Fallback B: no devices, no consumable supplies, or unsafe weather
docs.text:
Objective: Make and distinguish a direct observation from a guess. Materials: A familiar safe classroom object/view already present; no handling of hazardous objects. Technology: None. Prep: 2 minutes. Vocabulary/background: Observe = notice directly; guess/inference = an idea that needs more evidence. "Looks wooden" does not prove material composition.

Follow the same native timing columns above: 1. Hook: "What can we actually notice about this desk/door/window view?" 2. Model one observation and one inference; safety: seated, no climbing/touching. 3. Each child notices/points/tells one feature; partners compare. 4. Identify which claim can be checked by looking; refine it. 5. Each child shows one observable feature (older pupils distinguish a guess). 6. Restore room, finish the evidence notes and close.

Meets: Child points/names an observable feature; for a stated older-grade inference objective also explains why a guess needs evidence. Read aloud, model, allow gesture/gaze/home-language response. Challenge: propose a safe way to check a guess. Record objective change; no claim of engineering/programming mastery. Cleanup: no materials to collect; reset seating and leave evidence/NE. Family: "We practiced observing carefully. Ask: 'What did you notice directly?'" At -10 F remain indoors; if there is no safe view, use an ordinary indoor object.

docs.title: Device/supply contingency and return note
docs.text:
Paper algorithms preserve sequence/debugging concepts, not real programming or robot-operation mastery. Defer those objectives if devices fail; do not invent accounts or app permissions. Technology Plan.

Leave lesson/steps completed, actual individual evidence or NE, objectives changed/deferred, restock counts, broken parts OUT OF SERVICE, safety/source questions and the next check. Named evidence stays under school privacy practice. See handoff template and Local Standards; official alignment and unverified Church/supplier claims are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

docs.title: 📝 Teacher Self-Evaluation for C-STEM Excellence
docs.text:
This local self-evaluation tool helps teachers reflect on Catholic identity, hands-on learning, inclusion and instructional planning. It does not establish NCEA/Cognia certification, accreditation or compliance with official standards.

October 2026 status: Treat the following as legacy/local reflection prompts, not a verified official NCEA, Minnesota or Archdiocesan instrument. Attribution, quoted wording and the numbered characteristics/factors are VERIFICATION REQUIRED against a primary source before claiming official alignment. Teacher reflection is separate from student achievement. Use objective-linked evidence and Local Standards, including authentic arts/music (A) and mathematics (M). Do not grade students for apparent joy, participation, interior faith or family practice.

docs.title: 📋 Overview
docs.text:
Purpose: Self-assessment tool for teachers to evaluate and improve their C-STEM instruction

Frequency: Complete at the beginning and end of each semester, or after each unit

Scoring: Honestly rate your current practice to identify areas for growth

docs.text:
Legacy attribution to NCEA and the italicized wording below: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. These prompts are not an official certification checklist.

docs.text:
Lord, help me to be a faithful teacher of Your truth. May I integrate faith and reason seamlessly, Showing my students the harmony of Your creation.
